Title: I hope there are no S:CE hosers in Final Nights

Messages.Author: R. David Zopf
Messages.Body:
Just had to post the counter -point, and have pro-combat advocates
mull over the following thought...

Say your favorite clan did, in fact, get a S:CE hoser that was at
least as good (easy to play) as Immortal Grapple. What I fear is that
the game would swing more and more toward solely combat oriented
themes, with all the juicy intrigue, politics, corruption,
negotiation, etc. taking a back seat. Yes, it might be neat if there
are a few more limited ways to beat a Majesty. Take that concept to a
(not too) distant point, though, and the game devolves into a vampiric
form of Rock'em Sock'em Robots. _Not_ something I'm particularly
interested in playing (How about you?)

I encourage small change ;-) What's your $0.02? Where's the balance
point for you? If combat is too weak, how do you change it without
making other tactics too weak in the process? What's your favorite
fruit?

Regards,
R. David Zopf
guenh...@mindspring.com
Atom Weaver

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <9a7jc4$a72$1...@slb1.atl.mindspring.net>, R. David Zopf
<guenh...@mindspring.com> writes

> Say your favorite clan did, in fact, get a S:CE hoser that was at
>least as good (easy to play) as Immortal Grapple.

And this is where it falls down.

Immortal Grapple is *the* S:CE hoser. You have to be at close range,
sure, but it *completely* stops it.

Telepathic Tracking is a useful power level to consider. It doesn't
*stop* it. You can still play it. Hand jam is thus hard to create.
And they can still escape again. But it gives you a much better shot at
it.

Consider something like this:

Psychic Taunt
Dementation
Combat
Play before range is determined.
If the opposing minion selects a "Strike: Combat Ends" effect for their
strike, that minion takes 1 damage at the end of the Choose Strike
phase.
(S) As above, but this damage is not preventable.

Okay, this card may not be perfect. It may not even be good. But it's
an alternate mechanic that gives S:CE a cost. It doesn't hose it. It
doesn't stop it. But it does make it less "cheap".

I think most people would agree (feel free to shout at me if I'm wrong)
that S:CE is very, very cheap. Giving it some minor costs doesn't hose
it, but it does make it less of a no-brainer in play.

--

Messages.Body:
>Say your favorite clan did, in fact, get a S:CE hoser that was at

>are a few more limited ways to beat a Majesty. Take that concept to a
>(not too) distant point, though, and the game devolves into a vampiric
>form of Rock'em Sock'em Robots. _Not_ something I'm particularly
>interested in playing (How about you?)

S:CE not only deals with 90% of combat, it also eliminates other combat
defenses by being strictly better. Remove S:CE (all together, which I don't
think is likely) and you should see more reliance on dodging and damage
prevention and less use of Immortal Grapple (as it ceases to become
"necessary").

There's nothing necessary about S:CE from a play standpoint (it was a good
interpretation of Majesty, though). By its existence as a common combat
defense it removes the viability of numerous strategies. I'd much rather see
the combat metagame framed by a variety of offensive and defensive combat
options then see it come down to S:CE v. IG, both of which bore me immensely.

>"necessary").

I somewhat agree with Mr. Zopf's statement. I myself don't really play with
S:CE clans (I usually go with Tremere), but it's probably just my conservative
side not wanting to completely "revolutionalize" the game.

I do however think that S:CE does play a valuable role in the game. Yes, it is
powerful, but I think it's necessary.

For example, Mr. Lee suggested that dodging and damage prevention would be
relied upon more.

But take dodging for example. 1. Dodging (like S:CE) is completely hosed by
Immortal Grapple and/or Thoughts Betrayed. 2. Even more importantly, any sort
of additional strikes (mainly Celerity) completely destroys the defense. Unless
I also have additional strikes (and additional dodges), celerity is going to
just about crush anything it goes up against.

I don't mind the damage prevention angle, but the problem is that this is much
more limited. With Dodge, there is the "Dodge" card so anyone can dodge. But
damage prevention is pretty much only for Fortitude (though Protean's Flesh of
Marble, Chimerstry's Apparition, and various Vicissitude cards may help). And
Precognition and Sideslip won't be much use since they can only prevent one.

Looking at it this way, think how powerful the Assamites would be without S:CE.
You can't prevent (if they rely on Blood Sweat or something). If you dodge,
that's fine. They'll just hit you with Blood Sweat with their two other
strikes. Your only hope is to try to outmanuever them which may be just as
hard...

So to conclude. Damage prevention is only available to a few clans. And Dodge
is not sufficient to defend against anything with additional strikes. Thus S:CE
helps keep the combat decks from becoming overly prevalent.

Halcyan 2

Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
I think James Coupe is along the right track on making S:CE cost more.

I'd like to see an Animalism card that doesn't so much destroy Majesty's
usefulness but makes it easier for their opponent to recover somewhat from
any wasted combos played.

I've noticed when playing my Animalism weenie deck lately that S:CE is a
pain. I don't mind that so much... what I mind is that I play three or four
cards and then all become useless when the opposing minion simply 'opts' out
of combat.

So, how about a card that doesn't prevent the opponent from ending combat,
but allows the other minion to somehow keep their card-combo for another
round? Maybe stack the combo next to the minion in question and allow them
to play each card as if it were played that round? Not sure if I'm
explaining that well enough so I'll give an example.

ROUND 1

Devin Bisley bleeds for two with Computer Hacking.
Gideon Fontaine blocks.
Devin Bisley plays Trap, Carrion Crows and Song of Serenity.
Gideon Fontaine plays Majesty to end combat.
Devin plays 'Animal loyalty' (dumb name) to keep Trap, Carrion Crows and
Song of Serenity for use in her next combat.

ROUND 2

Devin Bisley bleeds.
Gideon Blocks.
Devin Bisley sacrifices 'Animal Loyalty' to play Trap, Carrion Crows and
Song of Serenity again.
Gideon panics when he realizes his Methuselah master has run out of Majesty
cards.
Gideon goes to torpor.

Sound reasonable? Powerful, but give it a cost and a rarity that makes
sense. I'd say maybe 2 blood cost and an Uncommon rarity.

This would give the Ravnos, Gangrel, Nosferatu and Tzimisce a slight edge
against S:CE though not without drawbacks. Sure, Gangrel have 'Dog Pack' but
I've never found that card to be worth its cost or common enough. Nossies
have 'Immortal Grapple' and wouldn't need this card (unless they focus on
ANI maybe). Tzimisce and Ravnos could benefit but since both are liable to
lose a lot of blood for many of their 'nasty' cards, they'd have to be more
conservative with its usage. It wouldn't help the Assamites out at all (who
are also vulnerable to S:CE), but you can always give them Potence or
Animalism I guess.

Cheers,
WES

Messages.Author: TigToad
Messages.Body:
The game is inherently balanced in this... effectively:

S:CE is messed up by immortal grapple & things like hidden lurker
Immortal grapple is messed up by damage reduction and manuevers
Damage reduction is messed up by Thaumaturgy & having to have an
excessive number of cards in your deck
Thaumaturgy is hosed by dodges

Etc... the truely greatness of the game to me is that one strategy, no
matter how solid is always able to be pasted by another deck strategy
out there somewhere. The game _needs_ S:CE to keep from combat decks
from running wild. Now, I also really like the way the game limits
these things to, basically, keep from having one clan have access to
more of these abilities than others. (Gangrel actually have
Protean/Fortitude with dog pack being the closests to all of the
above).. but then trying to ever bleed or vote your opponent becomes
very hard since all of your cards help with combat.

Great game from a balance stand point.

Daniel-Tig

Messages.Author: Sorrow
Messages.Body:
> Etc... the truely greatness of the game to me is that one strategy, no
> matter how solid is always able to be pasted by another deck strategy
> out there somewhere. The game _needs_ S:CE to keep from combat decks
> from running wild.

Except that even given the current S:CE hosers, combat *isn't* running wild.
It may have a decent time beating up vamps but it is extremely difficult to
actually
win a given game (most VPs) with a combat deck.

With that said, let's take a look at the current S:CE hosers:

Immortal Grapple: _The_ premier hoser. Though it works only at close range,
it
is useful at both inferior and superior Potence. And with most clans that
have
potence, it's not that hard to stay at close.

Hidden Lurker: not that great because people generally stop blocking after
their
vamp gets hosed. See Todd's recent post in response to an Assamite deck.
It's
an ok card, but it doesn't end up seeing much use.

Fast Reaction: see above. A bit more useful as you generally control the
blocking
but unless you can get a really good strike right off, the fact that the
opposing vamp
can't S:CE is of no consequence. As soon as you press to the second round,
S:CE
can be played.

Telepathic Tracking: requires superior Auspex. While there are alot of
vamps
that have AUS (73; 33 at <= 7 cap), there aren't that many that have combat
support disciplines:

Disc - Num of Vamps (Capacity/ies)

Vic - 5 (5, 6 x2, 7 x2)
Tha - 3 (4, 6 x2)
Obt - 2 (6, 7)
Pro - 3 (6, 7 x2)
Cel - 12 (3, 4, 5 x3, 6 x4, 7 x3)
Ani - 8 (5, 6 x3, 7 x4)

As you can see, somewhat expensive vamps - something which combat decks
can ill afford.

Thoughts Betrayed: requires superior Dominate and also has a pretty steep
cost. Unless you have a way of getting the blood back fast, you can only
play a few of these. Now, let's take a look at the vamp selection we have
that can use this one right off the bat:

Tha - 8 (5, 6 x3, 7 x4)
Pro - 2 (6, 7)
Cel - 3 (5, 6 x2)
Ani - 1 (6)

You have an even smaller selection of vampires.

The reason why I have the vamps start out with AUS or DOM is because
though you can add skill cards, unless you can get some really close to the
start of the game, TT or TB is totally useless and allows S:CE to completely
shut down your deck. And I have the capacity <= 7 because, as I say above,
combat decks cannot afford really large vampires unless they have a major
source of pool gain. When you add this aspect to a deck (large vamps, pool
gain), it slows the combat deck down and this may or may not be a really
bad thing.

> Now, I also really like the way the game limits these things to,
basically, keep
> from having one clan have access to more of these abilities than others.
(Gangrel
> actually have Protean/Fortitude with dog pack being the closests to all of
the
> above)..

Problem with Dog Pack is that it can be blocked and has a high cost.

> but then trying to ever bleed or vote your opponent becomes very hard
since
> all of your cards help with combat.
> Great game from a balance stand point.

I disagree. Even decks using IG have a very, very difficult time winning
games.
Not impossible to do, but it's very difficult. So when you see decks using
_the_
premier S:CE hoser not winning all the time, why is it a safe assumption to
believe
that combat will overrun the meta game if another high tier S:CE hoser, like
IG,
were introduced? Of all the archetypes, combat needs the most help to
become
as viable as bleed and politics are in a tournament setting. I think that
TT went
a ways to help but I don't think it went far enough.

In short, I, for one, do hope there is a S:CE hoser in Final Nights.
Something
still needs to be done to help the combat archetype.

Just my 2 pool.

Sorrow
---

- Narrator

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Sorrow wrote:
> Except that even given the current S:CE hosers, combat *isn't* running wild.
> It may have a decent time beating up vamps but it is extremely difficult to
> actually win a given game (most VPs) with a combat deck.

I don't know about others but it isn't that clear to me that it's of any
importance that "combat decks", per se, be easy to win games with. There's
an infinite number of decks with which you can not win a game. Who told you
a deck that mainly only allows you to rush and beat an opposing vampire into
torpor or oblivion - what I believe you mean you refer to a "combat deck" -
should be any different?

What is of importance is that all the cards have uses. Some cards were simply
misdesigned from the start and are unlikely to ever be useful without errata.
When whole lines of cards have no function because a card like Majesty makes
them too difficult to use, then I'm concerned. I don't think it's accurate to
say cards like "Bum's Rush" and "Ambush" are useless because rush decks are
difficult to win. One could still use a few of them with a bruise and bleed
deck to take out the occasional problematic minion (similar to using Beast,
Leatherface, for instance). Other combat cards like Disarm and aggravated
damage cards can be mean "throw-ins" to decks that have other focuses. The
ones that actually worry me are some of the things used by Assamites and Gangrels,
which IMHO are clans that find striking back against S:CE very difficult. If
S:CE were just a niche tactic, then I'd be OK with that. As it is, S:CE is a
pretty major part of the game, so Gangrel and Assamite combat seems pretty
useless. (No, I don't consider Dog Pack to be a worthwhile answer to S:CE.
It's too expensive and vulnerable. If Dog Packs cost 1, you might have
something...)

So I don't want S:CE majorly hosed. I'd just like see it tinkered with so
that all of the major combat clans can do something about it.

Fred

don't

addressed.

You were the one (apparently) expressing the indirect concept that it's important
to allow combat decks to win the game. The question was addressed to you.

> > a deck that mainly only allows you to rush and beat an opposing vampire
> > into torpor or oblivion - what I believe you mean you refer to a "combat

This doesn't answer the question or respond to my problem with your position. I
so note that you are not referring to a specific type of deck. None the less, of
what benefit is it to the game that a "combat deck", even taken as an archetype,
be made viable? I repeat, there are an infinite number of decks that aren't viable
and won't likely get you a win. I'm sure any number of them can be grouped into a
major (unsuccessful) group archetype. You seem to care about the particular group
of them you call "combat decks". Since you say they're not easy to win with, I'd
say they must be "bad decks". What I want to know is, what differentiates the decks
you're talking about from any other grouping of bad decks. Why should the game be
altered (using new cards or by any other means) to make these decks into viable
decks.

> > What is of importance is that all the cards have uses.
>
> Even "Twising The Knife", as crappy as it is, has a use. This is moot when
> discussing archetypes as a whole, as I was.

That's misrepresenting my point. I mean, it is important that as many cards as possible have
real, true useful uses. I doubt it's possible to bat a thousand on that score but that
should be the goal. I am not referring to just theoretical uses in the perfect situation
which for all practical purposes never comes up.

> > Some cards were simply misdesigned from the start and are unlikely to ever be useful

> > without errata. When whole lines of cards have no function because a card like Majesty

> > makes them too difficult to use, then I'm concerned.
>
> And this is what is currently happening in the game.

But not on the level you seemed to be talking about. When you refer to as large a category
as "combat decks", which has a meaning that can vary greatly from player to player, you're
likely sucking in large numbers of cards which can be used effectively in winning decks. To
the extent that's true, I don't care about what S:CE does to their use in combat decks. If
a Vampiric Speed can be used to good effect in a Brujah deck or a Toreador deck, I couldn't
care less that it can't be used in an Assamite deck. I'm specifically worried about cards
like Weakness or Blood Sweat or Body Flare, which are geared for use by clans that are
pretty much helpless against S:CE IMHO. That's a far cry from worrying about the fate of
"combat decks" in general.

> Unlike the rest of the post, this makes it out as if you were agreeing with
> me...?
>
> > So I don't want S:CE majorly hosed. I'd just like see it tinkered with so
> > that all of the major combat clans can do something about it.
>
> I don't want it to be majorly hosed. I just would like it so that the
> combat archetype had an almost even footing with the other 2 archtypes with
> regards to the possiblity of building a deck that won almost as much.

I'm not sure where we're failing to communicate. What I consider to be the
"combat archetype" is of no particular interest to me. Just certain combat
cards that are not likely to ever have a use, whether in a deck that exists
purely to get into combat and do horrible things to the other guy's minion or
just to support tactics (e.g. vote and bleed) that win you the game in a more
direct fashion.

> The Combat archetype is not even close to being on an even
> footing as the other two archtypes and this is something that needs to be
> addressed. This is the point that I was trying to make.

And I disagree with it. Nothing is bad about the combat archetype not being
on an even footing with whatever other archetypes you feel exist in the game.
What's bad about S:CE to me is causes a lot of other cards that have been printed
to exist in a state that they won't reasonably get used in viable decks. And I
do not believe the number of such cards is all that large.

Fred

Now, I know this is a wide, commonly held belief that "The three deck
archetypes" are Bleed, Vote, and Combat, generally viewed in descending
order of power, though it's more like a 9, an 8, and a 4, respectively, on a
1 to 10 scale of "winningness." Several players, (notably, pure combat deck
players) even go so far as to assume that the game designers had this in
mind, but just botched the implementation, speaking as if this "3 legged
table" metaphor were canon or something.
About all that makes this idea plausible is the inherent describability
of these archetypes.
Bleed deck: "I make a bunch of bleeding actions, removing all my prey's
pool, ousting him."
Vote deck: "I pass a bunch of votes, removing all my prey's pool,
ousting him."
Combat deck: "I kill a bunch of guys, removing all my prey's minions.
Then I hope he spends more pool to bring out more guys for me to kill, and
in the mean time, I bleed him."

Really, every* pure combat deck is, inherently, a Bruise and Bleed deck,
just REALLY heavy on the Bruise (or Beats, if you prefer). But, they're
easy to build, easy to describe, and easy to play. DAMN hard to win with,
though. Which is the issue.
Well, WHY are they hard to win with? Is it because S:CE hoses them? Is
it so painful to point to the fact that combats remove minions, and not
pool? A Methuselah with no minions is pretty helpless. However, a
Methuselah with no pool is not only helpless, he's ousted. Not to mention
also out of minions, then.

Now, to be fair, if you can remove all of your prey's minions, and that
Methuselah wants his deck (that isn't "all masters") to DO anything, he has
to spend pool to bring out more guys. If he can't, he's not long for this
world. That's a bit different than "Bruise and Bleed" if you mean "Bleed
your prey, and if he blocks, kill him," where the Bruise is primarily used
to discourage blocking. In "pure combat" decks, the goal is to actually
kill ALL the minions, so your prey must either bring out more guys (spending
pool) or sit tight until his combat-playing predator is ousted.

This is also the goal for, say, a Cryptic Mission/Society of Leopold
deck. Not a deck people are clamoring need more help.
This is also very similar for "lockdown" decks, that make minions unable
to be used, such as all your prey's minions Haunted and hunting, or Sensory
Deprived.
This is also similar to a pure Shadow Twin deck, which tries to do what
the combat deck does, just skipping over the combats and going straight to
the damage part.
Really the "deck type" for combat decks is "minion removing deck," just
using combat at the way to do it. It's most obvious, most easily built,
most varied and largest "subclass" of these types of decks, but it has the
same ousting strategy: Stack the bodies, and force them to spend pool and/or
die.

But that doesn't make it "the third leg." Now, when you open up your
cards, you get a pile of Masters, and bunch of vamps, a whole lot of
Politics cards, a bunch of cards about stealth and intercept, and a whole
asston of combat cards. You also get a lot of equipment, allies, and
retainers. Why aren't "Ally decks," or "Gun decks" one of the "table legs?"
Well, because they don't oust people by themselves. Allies and guns are
just part of some larger strategy to oust people, and are cards to assist
that goal.
NO combat card says "remove X pool from your prey." Because combat
isn't an ousting strategy. It's an assistance, a vehicle, a means to an
end, just like allies, or equipment. There's a LOT of combat cards,
probably larger than any other single category. But those numbers don't
change the fact that no combat card will oust your prey.
(Let's quickly discuss Fame: A *great* card that lets combat decks
actually do pool damage. Not the original intent, much less wording. It's
change makes an interesting side effect to help combat decks oust, but it's
Uniqueness still limits the viability of "yo-yo" combat decks. It certainly
gives NO support to the assumption that Bleed, Vote, and Combat were ever
intended to be 3 equal Pillars.)

Now, the three words that stymie the combat deck approach are "Strike:
Combat Ends." Somewhat worse off is that Presence, that can both Bleed and
Vote, has one of the best (common) S:CE cards in the game, Majesty.
Meaning, of course, that unless you can stop it, they can go about their
business of bleeding and voting, and cheesily removing their prey's pool,
instead of taking it in the teeth like a man. It also means a great deal of
cards that dodge, press to end, maneuver away, etc, don't get used
(especially the "press to end" cards) since combat never gets even to damage
resolution in one card.
Now, I HAVE to agree with Fred here. The fact that there are many cards
that just don't see much or any use because S:CE *is* a shame. But, hosing
S:CE doesn't solve the problem of combat decks winning or losing. Peter
Bajika and James Hamblin have both effectively used Potence Immortal Grapple
and blow-your-head-off in-one-hit rush decks to get VPs and even win
tournaments, but even they can tell you it's tough. (But not impossible, as
many people will argue) If S:CE was *banned*, that doesn't change that fact
that "pure combat decks" still have to Rush every minion of their prey, and
to be effective, need to torporize or burn that minion THAT combat almost
every time, and (without Fame, a Unique card) they still aren't doing any
pool damage when they Rush someone. The inherent strategy "Remove all
Minions" is simply difficult to win to begin with.
THAT is a different issue, caused by the existence of ONE card, Fame,
that rewards a combat deck with pool damage, assisting the strategy in
ousting your prey (commonly agreed upon as the object of the game; some
upstreamers and Malk-role-playing twits disagree). If you want combat to
become a viable strategy for winning, making it "on par" with Bleed and Vote
to fulfill that flawed prophecy, you should have hooted and hollered more
when Ben Swainbank proposed his War Council:

War Council
Master
Unique Location
Tap when a Vampire is burned to force the controller of the burned
Vampire to burn 2 pool.

(I personally thought it should have been "burned in combat" or
somesuch, or tap for 1 pool "when a vampire goes to torpor or is burned,"
but the idea is in the right direction.)

Of course, that is all under the assumption that V:TES *should* allow
for a strategy that allows beating up your prey's vamps to lead directly
(instead of indirectly) to their ousting. That is, that it become a "viable
strategy." Here I have to waffle. A whole lot of (combat) cards are
considered a waste because they're never played; the reasoning given is that
S:CE hoses them, so you'll never see them. This of course missed the point
that if S:CE were nonexistent, those many cards still wouldn't oust people,
just fight combats. But, if S:CE were gone, and you wanted to defend
against combat, you'd a lot more to defend against combat (well, putting
aside the Daddy-MacDaddy, Obedience), or you'd have to fight back, which
might well result in a whole cornucopia of combat, seeing Body Flare and
even Quick Exit played.
Beating up vamps can be fun and all, but that reduces the game to "king
of the hill" of combats, and then, well, bleeding for one a lot. Moves the
game toward the ideal that if you lose all your minions, you're out of the
game. To borrow from another part of the thread:

> Say your favorite clan did, in fact, get a S:CE hoser that was at
>least as good (easy to play) as Immortal Grapple. What I fear is that
>the game would swing more and more toward solely combat oriented
>themes, with all the juicy intrigue, politics, corruption,
>negotiation, etc. taking a back seat. Yes, it might be neat if there
>are a few more limited ways to beat a Majesty. Take that concept to a
>(not too) distant point, though, and the game devolves into a vampiric
>form of Rock'em Sock'em Robots. _Not_ something I'm particularly
>interested in playing (How about you?)

How about me? Not interested at all.

If people want to try, they can invent their own S:CE hosers. Better
yet, just BAN all S:CE cards in their local playgroup, and see how the games
turn out. Can't convince them to give up S:CE? Is it because they're
afraid of getting beat up? Or just wanting to play a game where you do more
than just fight?

* A "pure combat deck" does exactly as I said. Extraneous examples of
specific combat decks you've played that torp all the vamps and then take
some other cardless pool-removing action besides bleeding that I've
forgotten can be stuck in your ear. Those that take actions requiring cards
to remove pool aren't "pure" combat decks, and are, in all likelihood, a
"Bruise and X" deck.

--
Pat Ricochet
Soul Jar'rn Fool of Atlanta

Hmmm, just for once i don't fully agree with you, Pat. i do, however,
agree with you and Fred PARTIALLY, and even with Andrew davidson, about the undesirability of boosting combat. i hold this position because i
think combat, unintelligently played, is no more than a table-
destabilising factor, which can result in the winner being the lucky
guy/gal who just happens to avoid the worst combat damage. If you've
played in an all-combat tournament you will know what i mean! i hold
the [possibly elitist] view that rush-combat should be something
pretty much restricted to experienced players and/or unjamming playgroups which have got stuck on malky bleed/deflect/counter decks.

But i don't agree with you when you say combat is only a tactic like
putting guns in your deck [sorry if i've misunderstood your argument,
but i don't believe i am being unfair]. Whether this was designed
to be the case or not i don't know, but i think the
following deck-types are viable in VTES at the moment;

Bleed
Vote
Bloat
Combat
Intercept
Swarm
Takeover
Shutdown
Poison

Each deck type has an offense, a defense and a weak spot.

Bleed: Offense: Reduce Prey's Pool by bleeding
Defense: Speed
Weak Spot: Bleed bounce, rush combat, Politics

Vote: Offense: Reduce Prey's Pool by voting
Defense: Various, but often vote-based bloat
Weak Spot: Intercept, not getting vote dominance

Bloat: Offense: Poke-bleeds, Surviving longest
Defense: Too much pool for opponents to whittle down
Weak Spot: Rush-combat, politics

Combat: Offense: Wipe out prey's minions, bleed for 1
Defense: Wipe out predator's minions
Weak Spot: Table-destabilising - may just end up handing
victory to A.N. Other.

Intercept Offense: Stop everything your prey does.
Defense: Stop everything your predator does.
Weak Spot: Table-destabilising - may just end up handing
victory to A.N. Other.

Swarm Offense: have too many minions for your prey to stop
Defense: Have too many minions for your predator to get
through
Weak Spot: Failing to achieve effective swarm.

Takeover Offense: Take over your prey's minions
Defense: Take over your predator's minions
Weak Spot: Expensive and/or slow

Shutdown Offense: Hamstring your prey's minions
Defense: Hamstring your predator's minions
Weak Spot: Table-destabilising - may just end up handing
victory to A.N. Other.

Poison Offense: Turn your prey's minions into liabilities
Defense: Speed
Weak Spot: Politics, relies on rares.

Most of these strategies can be mixed. For example, rush-combat/Fame
is a combat/poison deck. ToGP is a Bloat/Takeover deck. But these are
all real STRATEGIES and the tactics of putting in guns, allies, action
modifiers or whatever are not IMO to be lumped in with the strategic
package. As you and Fred point out, there is no intrinsic reason why
all the above have to be equal, and i'd certainly agree that any
strategy whose weak point is that it's table-destabilising should
NOT be boosted without a long, hard think about the consequences.

As for whether it's desirable or designed to be as i've described,
i think one of the many great things about this game is that it is
bigger than any of us - it is a WORLD within which we are continually
discovering new stuff. One of the implications of this is that the
list i've given above is CERTAINLY wrong - not just because there
are many different incarnations of the strategies with different
weaknesses, but because there WILL be other strategies that remain
to be discovered.

i think it's legitimate to wonder about whether we should plug in
new strategies, boost some strategies at the expense of others,
completely abolish some strategies and so on, but the kind of
discussion i would rather have focusses on neglected cards, and asks
how we might integrate them better into the game. Sometimes this
can be done within the existing rules and card-set just by thinking
a bit harder. Other times perhaps we need new cards or rules to
achieve the same end. That's where this discussion started - people
were thinking aloud about how to make the Assamites more popular.
One idea is that they should get an anti-SCE card. i'd prefer that you
guys get a web-cam up so that EVERYONE can see how Todd plays
them, which would have the additional plusses that people could [a] see
how YOU play the Giovanni, and [b] marvel at the uncanny physical
resemblance of Derek to Angel's Evil Childe in Somnambulist.

Possibly elitist it may be, but I can certainly UNDERSTAND the
position. Anyone who's ever been on the wrong end of an "ah, screw
it, i'm gonna fuck up... THAT crucial minion of yours cross-table"
deck can also certainly sympathise.

And realistically, it's not possible to forbid noobies from playing
combat; so that adds yet another factor to consider when creating.

I'd almost go ahead and pitch out the concept of deck "archetypes"
altogether. I think the original idea was to attempt to classify
decks by the manner in which they ousted their prey; ie bleed, vote,
or beat guys up and hope they bring one out. It now seems likely that
that system of classification simply isn't going to be adequate, and
you'll have to swap back to something like the above; defining briefly
what the deck DOES.

Although again, the mix is best. I think you have to just treat it
like a big set of checkboxes; "my deck does X, Y, and Z". It's not
uncommon to see a deck that mostly bleeds, but occasionally hits you
for something, and carries just enough light intercept to stop very
offensive things from happening. As I wrote in a post that never made
it here (was written at 4am, and i reread it this morning and said
"thank god i didn't send that"), each of these types is simply a leg
of the cow to be considered when building one's deck. A cow with one
leg (weenie dominate bleed) is unstable and can be tipped over easily,
but is easy to make, faster to start, and can give just as much milk
(VPs) as any other cow. And if you put both legs on the same side
(trying to mix combat and shutdown), you might find your cow tipping
over of its own accord, such as when you kill the guy you just Sense
Depped.

...and now you know why I didn't send the other one.

>is a combat/poison deck. ToGP is a Bloat/Takeover deck. But these are

>all the above have to be equal, and i'd certainly agree that any
>strategy whose weak point is that it's table-destabilising should
>NOT be boosted without a long, hard think about the consequences.

And this is a large bit. Intercept carries this problem with it, and
the Tzimisce just got a HUGE boost in Sabbat War. As a result, there
are an awful lot of Tzimisce intercept-and-explode decks running
around out there, and the state of the game has been affected. If you
head to a tournament, you need to consider that you may sit next to
something with more intercept than God, and nothing to do with it all
except stop everything you do.

Fortunately, the Tzimisce are capable of building a deck that not only
intercepts, but also ousts people, so the potential problem ends up
being merely a mirage. But any potential problems were also of
smaller scope, since only one clan needed to be considered.

Providing some sort of global S:CE weakener would be MUCH more risky,
and would need to be considered against the clans that can already
make use of S:CE stoppers. Consider the Assamites, everyone's
favourite target. Obfuscate isn't appropriate. Celerity would affect
the Toreador and !Gangrel, which could be seen as being a good thing;
but it would also affect the Brujah, who simply don't need another way
to thump people. Quietus? possibly.. but then you get back to the
point that the Assamites simply don't NEED to be able to stop S:CE
with only one discipline. You're already in the position of fighting
a clan that can't be dodged (Celerity), can't be prevented (Blood
Sweat), and can't be easily fought back against (long range and
possible "dodge" for initial strike). The only defense starts to end
up BEING S:CE. Frustrating for the Assamites? Yes, but is there a
good alternative?

Also consider this: the problem as defined is partly that there are a
great number of cards that sit by the wayside; presses, guns, numerous
nifty "strike" cards, etc. Will hosing S:CE provide more use for
those cards, or will it simply make the existing S:CE-proof strategies
just that much better, and STILL leave those cards on the side?

Immortal Grapple's strength isn't solely in its ability to zap S:CE.
It's also in its ability to stop weapon strikes, Coma strikes, and all
kinds of other annoying non-hand-strikes... and all you have to do is
stay at close range. Why don't we see more Fleshcraft decks? It
seems like a perfect tool for the Tzimisce; free, and it makes it even
easier for them to do their own job. You should be able to spend
intercept to catch them once, and then just include lots of untap as
opposed to lots of intercept as they frantically take -1 stealth
actions to remove the card. Except that Fleshcraft loses to S:CE,
Dodge, *and* IG... three of the most common combat effects. Then it
becomes "why waste the card slot on it?".

>i think it's legitimate to wonder about whether we should plug in
>new strategies, boost some strategies at the expense of others,
>completely abolish some strategies and so on, but the kind of
>discussion i would rather have focusses on neglected cards, and asks
>how we might integrate them better into the game. Sometimes this
>can be done within the existing rules and card-set just by thinking
>a bit harder. Other times perhaps we need new cards or rules to
>achieve the same end. That's where this discussion started - people
>were thinking aloud about how to make the Assamites more popular.
>One idea is that they should get an anti-SCE card. i'd prefer that you
>guys get a web-cam up so that EVERYONE can see how Todd plays
>them, which would have the additional plusses that people could [a] see
> how YOU play the Giovanni, and [b] marvel at the uncanny physical
> resemblance of Derek to Angel's Evil Childe in Somnambulist.

There is a lot to be said for "playing the clan properly", as opposed
to just looking at the disciplines and making something according to
the disciplines. Sure, the Assamites have OBF/CEL/QUI, but is it
necessary to include lots of OBF when making the deck? Do you WANT to
stay out of combat that much?

There's also a lot to be said for beating Legbiter with a stick and
taking his pint away from him. I'm in favour of that, preferably on a
webcam. :P

-- Derek

I don't think it is necessarily true that removing S:CE promotes combat.
Players adjust in unpredictable ways.

Anyway, there are (as usual) a variety of arguments going on. On the one hand,
I hate what S:CE does in the game. On the other, I find rush combat as it is
done now to be incredibly boring and, as you say, potentially highly
destabilizing. The two relate but not directly.

My interest is in interesting combat. S:CE (which isn't just Majesty) defeats
90% of the possible combat offenses. The predominant corrective answer is
Immortal Grapple rush. Assuming the Immortal Grapple gets played, the deck
annihilates minions. Minion loss, in my mind, is the single most destabilizing
possibility (including through minion theft or Banishment or whatever) and
should be minimized.

So, what I'd like to see is less lethal combat but more combat cards played.
Of course, one way to achieve this is to print more combat cards but make them
defensive oriented. For instance, Personal Scourge could have been interesting
if it prevented a point of damage (at damage resolution) as a strike. While it
won't happen by rule (though I could see some interesting cards based on it),
capping damage would be preferred. Openended damage is yet another reason not
to play high cap vamps as they go down just as easy, often enough.

Yea. You said a lot of the things I was thinking. To add to this, one thing
that bothers me about both rush combat and especially intercept combat are the
way these decks simply do not work well for purposes of gaining victory points
yet they still hose their neighbors. (Or in the case of intercept, they tend
to hose their predator and, if their prey is a bleed deck which doesn't need to
do non-directed actions, will often let their prey run free and easy.) This is
the Jyhad equivalent of a "dog-in-the-manger" attitude. You have a deck which
is very difficult to win with yourself yet you effectively destroy your neighbor's
chances of winning. The VPs tend to fall to other players, such as your
grandpredator in the case of rush combat or your prey in the case of intercept.
I'm not that interested in hosing S:CE just so decks like these will be even
worse news to their neighbors yet probably not do that much better in terms of
victory points themselves. People need to recognize bad/ineffective decks for
what they are. And if classic bleed decks or vote decks need more hosing, then
create cards that hose them a little more directly than simply making rush combat
or intercept combat more effective.

> THAT is a different issue, caused by the existence of ONE card, Fame,
> that rewards a combat deck with pool damage, assisting the strategy in
> ousting your prey (commonly agreed upon as the object of the game; some
> upstreamers and Malk-role-playing twits disagree). If you want combat to
> become a viable strategy for winning, making it "on par" with Bleed and Vote
> to fulfill that flawed prophecy, you should have hooted and hollered more
> when Ben Swainbank proposed his War Council:
>
> War Council
> Master
> Unique Location
> Tap when a Vampire is burned to force the controller of the burned
> Vampire to burn 2 pool.
>
> (I personally thought it should have been "burned in combat" or
> somesuch, or tap for 1 pool "when a vampire goes to torpor or is burned,"
> but the idea is in the right direction.)

To reward the kind of play I'd like to see rewarded, my preference would be for
a card like this to do something like, "Tap when a vampire in combat with a vampire
you control goes into torpor. That vampire does not go into torpor. Combat ends.
Its controller must burn 3 pool." That would be a way to convert combat advantage
into pool loss yet not totally screw the victim from ever having a chance to come
back (as long as he can afford the pool loss).

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Ian wrote:
>>My interest is in interesting combat. S:CE (which isn't just Majesty)
defeats
90% of the possible combat offenses. The predominant corrective answer is
Immortal Grapple rush. Assuming the Immortal Grapple gets played, the deck
annihilates minions. Minion loss, in my mind, is the single most destabilizing
possibility (including through minion theft or Banishment or whatever) and
should be minimized.>>

But if you minimize minion loss, you completely neutralize the combat deck as a
viable strategy option. The whole point of a combat deck is to make others lose
their minions--if you aren't doing this, you will *never* oust them. The only
way to oust someone as a Rush deck is to torporize/burn all of their vampires.
The harder this becomes to do, the more unlikely it is that a combat deck can
actually survive, let alone win. If combat decks become less useful, then S+B
decks become *more* useful, and the game ceases to work well.

As the game stands, IG can be hosed by manuvers, fortitude, Obediance, agg
damage, and more Potence, and IG is the pre-eminent combat option. I suspect
that the only S:CE hoser that folks are looking for at this point out of the
next expansion is something to help the Assamites out, which if comes to pass,
adds yet another option to use against the IG decks--if Assamite decks become
viable (which they currently really aren't, as Psyche isn't really that good of
a S:CE hoser), this makes combat more interesting.

Therein lies the point. The games needs something *else* you can do with combat
besides utterly destroying the opponent's minions and destabilizing the game,
without that great a benefit to yourself. I mean, it is a benefit but of limited
nature: that minion no longer harasses what you're trying to do including bleed
your prey. But if it's your predator's minion, it also can't be used to defend
himself against his predator as needed. And if it's your prey, once you've ousted
him (if you succeed at doing that), you have to start over with the next prey -
who may be all that much better off because your prey was weakened and prevent from
doing much to him from the start.

That's why things like Fame are good. The game needs more stuff like that, perhaps
even more directly useful than Fame for ousting your prey with combat. (Fame has
its drawbacks, unfortunately.)

> The harder this becomes to do, the more unlikely it is that a combat deck can
> actually survive, let alone win. If combat decks become less useful, then S+B
> decks become *more* useful, and the game ceases to work well.

Combat isn't the only thing that keeps S & B in check. Nor does it need to be.
However, if they can solve the problem of giving combat ways to win that aren't
so destabilizing, I don't mind it having that side effect.

Fred

players. Sure, you can make combat more types of combat effective by making
a "generic" S:CE hoser, or even make the Assamites more effective by giving

If you make a card that says "Master. This card cannot be burned by
playing another Master Card. You and your prey and predator are both

both gain none," people WILL play it. Tournaments have plenty of sore

Making a strategy that is capable of being table-unbalancing MORE
capable of it being unbalancing doesn't seem the right way to go. It seems
exactly the WRONG way to go. The Assamites don't need to win every combat

playing tournament-losing Assamite decks. They need ways to survive and

Messages.Author: Pat Ricochet
Messages.Body:
> Hmmm, just for once i don't fully agree with you, Pat. i do, however,
> agree with you and Fred PARTIALLY, and even with Andrew davidson, about the
> undesirability of boosting combat. i hold this position because i
> think combat, unintelligently played, is no more than a table-
> destabilising factor, which can result in the winner being the lucky
> guy/gal who just happens to avoid the worst combat damage. If you've
> played in an all-combat tournament you will know what i mean! i hold
> the [possibly elitist] view that rush-combat should be something
> pretty much restricted to experienced players and/or unjamming playgroups
> which have got stuck on malky bleed/deflect/counter decks.
>
> But i don't agree with you when you say combat is only a tactic like
> putting guns in your deck [sorry if i've misunderstood your argument,
> but i don't believe i am being unfair].

No, you really shouldn't agree with that; I don't quite believe that
myself, and was getting to the "half-baked" part of the post.

But, I let the point stand just to take things "outside the box."
Combat doesn't DO anything by itself. Combat is what happens when one
vampire blocks another. Now, Bum's Rush DOES something. It *deliberately*
gets you into combat. Now, the point, usually, is to torporize the target
minion, but it's the combat cards that help you do that. But if you equip
with a Hawg, 2 sets of IR Goggles, and an RPG Launcher, you can Rush people,
and never play a combat card, and torp damn near anyone who *doesn't* play a
combat card. Really it's a "Rush Combat" deck. Sometimes you hear them
called "Rush decks" or "Combat Decks." The first is correct, and about as
explicit as it needs to be. There really aren't any Rush decks that aren't
Rush Combat. But there are Combat decks that don't Rush.
Notably, Intercept decks. It's just another vehicle for getting into
combat. The question new players find themselves asking (as I asked myself
and the group long ago) is "what do you do, playing an intercept dog, when
you actually *catch* the mailman?" Tear him a new one is certainly one
option. This leads to Tzimisce intercept decks. But you can actually just
leave him alone, and just stop him; in fact, that's sometimes the best thing
against your predator. This leads to Tory/!Tory run-away-Majesty-untap
intercept decks. The first is an "Intercept Combat" deck, where the latter
is not, but is still an Intercept deck.
As several people have noticed, Intercept decks can be as equally
unbalancing to the table as Rush Combat decks. But you don't find as many
people pointing out that "pure" Intercept (Combat) decks ALSO don't win as
many tournaments as vote or bleed. Why not? Same reason as Rush Combat;
because the deck doesn't remove pool from it's prey. But it's an equally
valid deck "archetype" as Combat, Vote, and Bleed. Among other things, it's
as good a counter to Vote and S&B as Rush Combat is. Though, I agree with
Derek that the whole "archetype" thing is pretty pointless, but I want to
take explicit attention to the fact that the idea of deck archetypes is
artificial, and it's painfully artificial, not to mention wrong, that
Combat, Bleed, and Vote are, or were ever meant to be, the "3 equal legs."



Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Fredrick wrote:
>>Therein lies the point. The games needs something *else* you can do with
combat besides utterly destroying the opponent's minions and destabilizing the
game, without that great a benefit to yourself.>>

Destroying your opponents minions, as a Rush deck, provides a great benefit to
yourself--your predator can no longer hurt you as much, and your prey needs to
spend pool to get out more minions (thereby making him that closer to getting
ousted).

I'm a little unclear as to what you see as a possibility for combat *other*
than destroying minions--yeah, Fame is useful, but only in the context of a
deck that can reliably torporize vampires (thus the Destroying is of firstmost
importance, and the Fame secondmost). More cards like Fame would be useful,
sure (say an action modifier that says something like "If a vampire goes to
torpor during this action, that vampire's controller loses 1 pool"), but still
you need to be able to torporize. What other possible use could there be for
combat?

>>I mean, it is a benefit but of limited nature: that minion no longer harasses
what you're trying to do including bleed your prey.>>

The Benefit is immense--as a Rush deck, killing your Predator's vampires keeps
you alive. Killing your prey's vampires gets him ousted. This is the aim of any
strategy in VTES--keeping yourself alive while ousting your prey. Rush decks do
this just like any other deck.

>>But if it's your predator's minion, it also can't be used to defend himself
against his predator as needed.>>

You may have to do that for him. Rush decks are all about table control.

>>And if it's your prey, once you've ousted him (if you succeed at doing that),
you have to start over with the next prey - who may be all that much better off
because your prey was weakened and prevent from doing much to him from the
start.>>

How is this any different from how a Bleed deck operates? If I, as a S+B deck
say, bleed the hell out of my prey, once I've ousted him, I have to start all
over with the next prey, who may be much better off because my prey was
weakened. I'm a little unclear as to the difference.

I fully accept that Rush decks, in the hands of the foolish, *can* destabilize
the game through completely random actions (random cross table rushes or
whatever), but the exact same can be said about a vote deck (who can randomly
oust people across the table with KRC/ConAg) or, say, a TotGP deck, who can
cripple people across the table by stealing all of their vampires. Pretty much
*any* deck can destablize a table when played badly--anyone who takes actions
that are not in their own best interest can destroy a multi-player game. This
is not the sole province of a Rush deck.

>>That's why things like Fame are good. The game needs more stuff like that,
perhaps even more directly useful than Fame for ousting your prey with combat.
(Fame has its drawbacks, unfortunately.)>>

But you'd still have to be able to torporize folks with impunity for such cards
to be worth playing--and if you can torporize folks with impunity, you are
destroying minions.

>>Combat isn't the only thing that keeps S & B in check. Nor does it need to
be.>>

No it isn't, but it is the most effective thing that keeps it in check. It is
Rock to S+B's Scisors. Deflection and Intercept are much less effective at
stopping S+B than combat decks on the whole (as they are passive stratigies
rather than active ones).

>>However, if they can solve the problem of giving combat ways to win that
aren't
so destabilizing, I don't mind it having that side effect.>>

Combat decks, when played intelligently, aren't any more destabilizing than any
other deck strategies. They keep themselves alive while weakening their prey.
Just like every other deck.



...but likely not. That's 5 pool. Or maybe 10 pool if they all have
laptops. More importantly (I guess), it means bleeding out the prey 5
actions earlier, if that makes a difference. And assuming they don't
discover they desperately need the actions to cross-table rush their
grandpredator or do other table management operations to fend off
impending disaster. And it also means they're 5 actions ahead of the
game on their grandprey, too. Though with the number of actions they
have to spend destroying their grandprey's minions and bleeding their
grandprey out whilst continuing to fend off disaster behind them, 5
extra actions may be a drop in the bucket. (Though by that time, if
their grandprey is not able to use S:CE as well, the savings may also
accumulate.)

It's complicated to figure, exactly. No doubt the elimination of S:CE
would make combat decks more viable to some extent. How *much* more
viable is the question. I still think this part of the equation is not
that important in helping decks that use combat to gain more VPs (except
for decks based on clans that can do next to nothing about it), compared
to other stuff you could do for them.

And as for whether it's a "good thing", I don't think it's good enough
and I think it has a definite downside.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
>
> Fredrick wrote:
> >>Therein lies the point. The games needs something *else* you can do with
> combat besides utterly destroying the opponent's minions and destabilizing the
> game, without that great a benefit to yourself.>>
>
> Destroying your opponents minions, as a Rush deck, provides a great benefit to
> yourself--your predator can no longer hurt you as much, and your prey needs to
> spend pool to get out more minions (thereby making him that closer to getting
> ousted).

I disagree. It provides a benefit to you at a cost. It provides a free benefit
to another one of your opponents, your grand predator. All things considered,
the benefit is not that "great", IMHO. Compared to other types of things you
can do for yourself, such as bleed your prey for five.

> I'm a little unclear as to what you see as a possibility for combat *other*
> than destroying minions--yeah, Fame is useful, but only in the context of a
> deck that can reliably torporize vampires (thus the Destroying is of firstmost
> importance, and the Fame secondmost). More cards like Fame would be useful,
> sure (say an action modifier that says something like "If a vampire goes to
> torpor during this action, that vampire's controller loses 1 pool"), but still
> you need to be able to torporize. What other possible use could there be for
> combat?

Now *I'm* a little confused. You just got done lauding the benefits of destroying
a predator's minion in one paragraph and then in the next, you turn around and
minimize the benefit of bleeding your prey for 3 for only torporizing his vampires.
What am I not seeing here? Or rather, what are you *not* seeing here? The
possibilities for cards like this seem clear and obvious to me. The game works
much better when combat decks Fame a prey's vamp and spend all their time putting
the same vamp in and out of torpor. Compared to running around blowing up minions
for no particular gain except their absence, the amount of table destabilization of
the former tactic is practically nil.

> >>I mean, it is a benefit but of limited nature: that minion no longer harasses
> what you're trying to do including bleed your prey.>>
>
> The Benefit is immense--as a Rush deck, killing your Predator's vampires keeps
> you alive.

I just disagree. It helps keep you alive for a moment, but the table destabilization
makes it difficult to predict what will happen in the long run.

I'm not going to argue with you about the point that combat decks find ways to win
using combat. They do. They just aren't very easy ways to win and I feel that the
amount of chaos they cause - in the form of undeserved boons and banes to various
opponents - harms the game in general.

> >>And if it's your prey, once you've ousted him (if you succeed at doing that),
> you have to start over with the next prey - who may be all that much better off
> because your prey was weakened and prevent from doing much to him from the
> start.>>
>
> How is this any different from how a Bleed deck operates? If I, as a S+B deck
> say, bleed the hell out of my prey, once I've ousted him, I have to start all
> over with the next prey, who may be much better off because my prey was
> weakened. I'm a little unclear as to the difference.

That seems deliberately dense to me, to compare the way combat and S & B
operate. Stealth and bleed attacks the remaining pool your prey leaves after
he's brought his minions out - unless you can make huge bleeds in the early going
sufficient to prevent him from bring out as much force as he normally would.
He has as much force as he started out with until the moment he's ousted.
Combat decks, on the other hand, rob the victim (predator or prey), of
desperately needed force which they use against both you and the guy on the
other side. You need to do a bunch of rushes and thus damage before you can
bring your goal into view. It's this time that imbalances the game.

> I fully accept that Rush decks, in the hands of the foolish, *can* destabilize
> the game through completely random actions (random cross table rushes or
> whatever), but the exact same can be said about a vote deck (who can randomly
> oust people across the table with KRC/ConAg) or, say, a TotGP deck, who can
> cripple people across the table by stealing all of their vampires. Pretty much
> *any* deck can destablize a table when played badly--anyone who takes actions
> that are not in their own best interest can destroy a multi-player game. This
> is not the sole province of a Rush deck.

Not in that sense, no. But unlike the bleed deck and the vote deck, the rush
deck *must* destabilize the game for a period of time before it can be successful.
Bleed and vote both attack pool, which has no direct consequences until the moment
you go over the top - if you ever do.

> >>That's why things like Fame are good. The game needs more stuff like that,
> perhaps even more directly useful than Fame for ousting your prey with combat.
> (Fame has its drawbacks, unfortunately.)>>
>
> But you'd still have to be able to torporize folks with impunity for such cards
> to be worth playing--and if you can torporize folks with impunity, you are
> destroying minions.

No. You torporize *one* minion. Then bring it out of torpor. Then torporize

Action Modifier

1 blood

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <9afbe5$8pj$1...@taliesin.netcom.net.uk>, Roger Carhult
<rogc...@student.luth.se> writes

>Since IG decks still doesn't win all that often, I consider it proved that
>S:CE hsoers doesn't make combat deck that good.

Consider:

1) The popular perception is that combat doesn't win
-> people don't play combat, therefore combat *can't* win very
often because it isn't played very often.

2) The received wisdom is that clever and useful play of a combat deck
can only be performed by experienced and talented players. The
standard S&B can be put together by anyone and played to a
relatively good level quite quickly. Combat requires more
thought, skill, planning, diplomacy and strategy.

3) A number of people like to vary the decks they play, for an added
surprise element. Okay, I'll play my Brujah IG Pound for Pound
deck, but sometimes I might want to play with my Malkavian
Derange deck.

Thus:

We have a large set of V:TES players.
(A)
We have a smaller set of player who play combat decks.
(B. B is a subset of A.)
We have a smaller set of players who play combat decks and are also of a
high skill level.
(C. C is a subset of B.)

And at any given point, not all of C will be playing.

The jump between A and B is large, but can be "controlled". That is,
players can be encouraged to play combat decks. The jump between B and
C is hard to control. It is hard to make players "good" (in the current
environment).

Comparatively, I would assert that few people believe that politics
decks can't win, so the drop-off at B is smaller. Similarly, I would
assert that the level of experience, skill etc. needed to play politics
is less than that required for rush combat (in the current environment).

Similarly, I would assert that similar claims can be (rightly) made
regarding stealth and bleed. However, stealth and bleed is hampered by
an additional factor - players dropping out because of perceived cheese.

However, I would still suggest that, globally[0], the set C (players
playing the deck style regularly and having the necessary skill) is such
that C for politics is larger than C for combat, and C for bleed is
larger than C for combat. (I make no such assertion regarding C bleed
vs C politics.)

I would suggest, therefore, that there are two points:

1) Combat decks don't win very often (I will grant that, of course)
2) S:CE hosers don't make combat good (a point under debate)

The reasons behind 1) are very complex, not solely that of 2) even if it
is true.

[0] Groups function somewhat more anecdotally. A group of 20 people may
have certain leanings, another group will do other things. These will
all be influenced by meta-game, relative skill level, card pool, card
availability, creativity, what the "good" players like (that is, if
*all* the good players really, really like Hostile Takeover, a circle
will adjust around that).

--
James Coupe PGP Key: 0x5D623D5D

> Trial by Combat
> Action
> You must control a ready titled vampire. This vampire need not be the
> acting vampire.
> (D) Enter combat with a vampire controlled by another Methuselah. If
> that vampire goes to torpor (or is burned) during this combat, all
> bleeds by that Methuselah are reduced by 1 until your next untap phase.
> If that vampire remains in the ready region at the end of this combat,
> burn 2 pool.

Huh, what? Unless I'm misreading this, if you rush a vamp and that
vamp S:CEs, you burn 2 pool. If this is correct, how does this help
combat decks? It makes them even *more* vulnerable against S:CE
in that if the combat fails, you not only waste the action but also have
to burn 2 pool.
The bleed reduction is ok, but not worth the two pool if S:CE is played.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:

>
> Peter D Bakija wrote:
> >
> > Destroying your opponents minions, as a Rush deck, provides a great benefit to
> > yourself--your predator can no longer hurt you as much, and your prey needs to
> > spend pool to get out more minions (thereby making him that closer to getting
> > ousted).
>
> I disagree. It provides a benefit to you at a cost. It provides a free benefit
> to another one of your opponents, your grand predator. All things considered,
> the benefit is not that "great", IMHO. Compared to other types of things you
> can do for yourself, such as bleed your prey for five.

But bleeding your prey for 5 can be defended against; by bleed bounce,
by intercept, by Archon Investigation, etc. The point of combat is to
try to exploit a weakness in the other deck, namely a lack of combat
defense. If I'm playing a combat deck, I don't care if my opponent has
intercept -- I want to get into a fight. I don't care if they have
bleed bounce or AI. But if I'm playing a bleed deck, those defense
measures influce my game tremendously.

> Now *I'm* a little confused. You just got done lauding the benefits of destroying
> a predator's minion in one paragraph and then in the next, you turn around and
> minimize the benefit of bleeding your prey for 3 for only torporizing his vampires.
> What am I not seeing here?

You're not seeing that the number one priority of a combat deck is to
destroy its prey's vampires. "But," I hear you say, "any decks #1
priority should be to oust its prey." You're right. But the _way_ the
deck does that is by _first_ destroying all of its prey's vampires.
Getting a little pool loss in there is just a bonus.

> Or rather, what are you *not* seeing here? The
> possibilities for cards like this seem clear and obvious to me. The game works
> much better when combat decks Fame a prey's vamp and spend all their time putting
> the same vamp in and out of torpor.

Not necessarily. It's very possible that by concentrating your efforts
on the Famous vampire, you're allowing the other vampires to set up
something which can really hurt you. If, for example, my prey is
playing a deck with guns and I'm light on maneuvers, I don't want them
to be able to get any guns. So my #1 priority is to kill all the
vampires I can, to keep _any_ of them from taking an equip action.

> Compared to running around blowing up minions
> for no particular gain except their absence, the amount of table destabilization of
> the former tactic is practically nil.

No one is claiming that winning with a Rush deck is easy. You are right
that completely destroying any player's minions is destabilizing. The
successful rush player controls that destabilization as much as they
can. But sometimes you can't control it. If my predator is a fast S&B
deck, I pretty much have to destroy every vampire they bring out. If my
prey is playing with a 5th/Tap deck, I need to kill the fatty titled
vampires to keep them from gaining lots of pool. A Rush deck defends
_actively_, which sometimes means destroying all of someone's vampires.

> > The Benefit is immense--as a Rush deck, killing your Predator's vampires keeps
> > you alive.
>
> I just disagree. It helps keep you alive for a moment, but the table
> destabilization makes it difficult to predict what will happen in the long run.

It's hard for a Rush deck to survive until the long run; a lot of things
have to go right for you. Rarely will you want to destroy all of your
predator's vampires. As you say, that usually just gives you a new,
stronger predator. But sometimes you have no choice but to eliminate
your predator.

> I'm not going to argue with you about the point that combat decks find ways to win
> using combat. They do. They just aren't very easy ways to win and I feel that the
> amount of chaos they cause - in the form of undeserved boons and banes to various
> opponents - harms the game in general.

Well, I don't know what to tell you. Anyone can play randomly and give
unexpected benefits to the wrong person. A Malk S&B deck which uses
Malkavian Pranks to keep cross-table allies (and future victims) in the
game is doing the same kind of thing. If I have a heavy bleed deck, and
a Deflection makes me accidentally oust my grand prey, I've
"destabilized" the table, and given my prey an "undeserved boon."

> > How is this any different from how a Bleed deck operates? If I, as a S+B deck
> > say, bleed the hell out of my prey, once I've ousted him, I have to start all
> > over with the next prey, who may be much better off because my prey was
> > weakened. I'm a little unclear as to the difference.

Or because your prey had to keep vampires up to try to block, or had to
get out fewer vampires to conserve pool. I agree with this analogy.

> That seems deliberately dense to me, to compare the way combat and S & B
> operate.

You know, Fred, you seem to have this problem a lot. People disagree
with you, and you think they're deliberately being stupid. Can't you
conceive of a point of view other than your own? Can you accept that
some people aren't convinced by your arguments?

> Stealth and bleed attacks the remaining pool your prey leaves after
> he's brought his minions out - unless you can make huge bleeds in the early going
> sufficient to prevent him from bring out as much force as he normally would.
> He has as much force as he started out with until the moment he's ousted.
> Combat decks, on the other hand, rob the victim (predator or prey), of
> desperately needed force which they use against both you and the guy on the
> other side. You need to do a bunch of rushes and thus damage before you can
> bring your goal into view. It's this time that imbalances the game.

Smart players who realize that their predator is a Rush deck will
influence so as to get out 3-4 vampires on a single turn. This way,
unless the Rush predator is very lucky, the prey will be able to take
actions and "participate." If you bring out vampires one at a time, the
Rush deck can kill them one at a time, while simultaneously handling
their predator.

Bleed decks versus Rush decks... both decks are denying their prey
resources. A bleed deck directly removes pool, which is more directly
effective, but it's also (relatively) easy to defend against. There's
no "Deflection hoser", and there shouldn't be. Combat (well-constructed
and in the right environment) is better at completing its task, but that
task doesn't directly oust people. It's a trade-off.

> Bleed and vote both attack pool, which has no direct consequences until the moment
> you go over the top - if you ever do.

Of course losing pool has direct consequences. I think you are the one
being deliberately dense. If I'm at 15 pool, I'm more willing to buy
things (Hunting Grounds, etc.) which I think will strengthen my
position, or gain me pool in the long run. I'm more willing to tap out,
or feign defenses I don't have in order to affect my prey. If I'm at 3
pool, I can't do these things. If I tap out or pretend to have defenses
I don't have, I'm risking being ousted.

> > But you'd still have to be able to torporize folks with impunity for such cards
> > to be worth playing--and if you can torporize folks with impunity, you are
> > destroying minions.
>
> No. You torporize *one* minion. Then bring it out of torpor. Then torporize
> it again. I believe the difference is pretty obvious.

The difference being you allow your prey to take actions and build up.
While this might have the long-term benefit of having them weaken your
grandprey for you, it usually has the short-term anti-benefit of them
either ousting their prey (which hurts your position by giving your prey
more pool and giving you a new, strong grandprey) or setting up defenses
which hamper your abilities. Keeping their vampires alive lets them
equip bad things, call votes which damage you, steal your vampires,
etc. Why give them the option to hurt you, in the vain hope that
they'll hurt their prey more?

James

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> I just don't care to
> encourage people building decks that will make them bad news to sit next to
> no matter what kind of deck you have. (You can build the fortitude deck to
> defend yourself but it often doesn't help you win, either.) I'd rather see
> such things limited to how you do in outguessing the metagame.

I don't think that the average combat deck is necessarily "bad news." A
potence rush deck is trying to take advantage of a lack of combat
defense (fortitude, maneuvers) in the average tournament deck. There
are plenty of decks which will make the potence player say "oh, shit,
I'm screwed." If Combat is Rock, there are as many Scissors as there
are Papers.

> It sure is. I simply object to the assumption that the combat deck
> archetype "must" be propped up. If people think it does, then tell us
> why first. Then worry about how it needs to be done.

I'm not saying I think Combat (as a strategy) needs any boosting. But
how could the hypothetical existence of more _kinds_ of combat decks be
bad? I can't really play my Gangrel +strength combat deck because I
don't have any way to deal with S:CE. If there's some anti-S:CE
Animalism card, say, in Final Nights, how will that affect things?
Majesty will be just as screwed against this new card as it is against
Grapple, Psyche! and Tracking. It doesn't make the Tzimisce any better;
they can already deal with S:CE. It just means that the game will have
more diversity. There will be more _kinds_ of combat decks -- there may
not be any more combat decks per se. And, even if combat decks become
more prominent, the metagame envrionment will adjust. Ventrue decks
with huge amounts of combat defense will become prominent. And then
those decks will get screwed when the metagame shifts away from combat.

How is this a bad thing?
