Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Fredrick wrote:
>>I disagree. It provides a benefit to you at a cost. It provides a free
benefit
to another one of your opponents, your grand predator. All things considered,
the benefit is not that "great", IMHO. Compared to other types of things you
can do for yourself, such as bleed your prey for five.>>

And bleeding your prey for 5 provides a free benefit for your grand prey--the
five pool that they lost could have been a 5 cost vampire hurting your grand
prey, but because you took that pool, you have denied your prey this
opportunity, and consequently, provided a free benefit to another one of your
opponents. Any action you take against your prey or predator indirectly helps
someone else at the table. Bleeding someone for 5 (denying them a possible 5
point minion) or burning a 5 point minion (denying them an existing minion) has
the same end result--your other opponents benefit. Please explain the
difference.

>>Now *I'm* a little confused. You just got done lauding the benefits of
destroying
a predator's minion in one paragraph and then in the next, you turn around and
minimize the benefit of bleeding your prey for 3 for only torporizing his
vampires.>>

No, no, responding to the following comment:

>>The games needs something *else* you can do with combat besides utterly
destroying the opponent's minions>>

about wanting combat to be useful for something other than destroying minions.
I was pointing out that even *with* Fame, you still need to destroy
minions--Fame does not minimize the need to destroy minions. Fame encourages
you to destroy minions.

>>What am I not seeing here? Or rather, what are you *not* seeing here? The
possibilities for cards like this seem clear and obvious to me. The game works
much better when combat decks Fame a prey's vamp and spend all their time
putting the same vamp in and out of torpor.>>

Not for the Rush deck it doesn't. You are spending 3 actions to cost your prey
6 pool. If you spend those three actions torporizing more than 6 pool worth of
vampires, the three Rush actions are more effective than the Lather, Rinse,
Repeat Fame manuver. Pool loss is pool loss. I fail to see how it is more
beneficial for anyone for this pool loss to be in the form of loose pool than
pool tied up in minions for the same amount. Yes, torporizing a vampire of your
prey gives your grand prey a free bonus (one less vampire to deal with).
Bleeding someone for the same amount does the same thing.

>>Compared to running around blowing up minions for no particular gain except
their absence, the amount of table destabilization of the former tactic is
practically nil.>>

I still fail to see where the "no particular gain" comes in. I play Rush decks
all the time. I do very well with them. I get into the finals of pretty much
every tournament I play in. Sometimes I win. What defines "particular gain" in
VTES more than getting VPs? If killing vampires gets me VPs, I am gaining
something in particular. Victory points.

>>I just disagree. It helps keep you alive for a moment, but the table
destabilization makes it difficult to predict what will happen in the long
run.>>

And deflecting a bleed for 6 helps keep you alive for the moment as well.
Again, please detail the difference.

This concept of "Table Destabilization" is a nebulous one to me. Any deck that
does what it intends on doing is weakening another player. Any time a player's
position is weakened, another player benefits. This is what all decks do. If I
am playing a bleed deck, every pool I remove from my prey is one less pool for
my prey to spend ousting *his* prey. Thus, my grand prey gets a free benefit
from my actions. If I am an intercept deck, and I stop all of my predator's
actions, I am denying him resources and keeping him from doing what he wants to
do. As a result, my grand predator is going to be in a better position, and he
gets a free benefit. How is what a Rush deck does any different?

>>I'm not going to argue with you about the point that combat decks find ways
to win using combat. They do. They just aren't very easy ways to win and I
feel that the amount of chaos they cause - in the form of undeserved boons and
banes to various opponents - harms the game in general.>>

What chaos do they cause? They weaken their prey (just like any other deck) and
slow down their predator (just like any other deck). If by "chaos", you are
referring to folks who randomly Rush folks across the table for no good reason,
and take actions that run contrary to their own best interest, and do so with
no concern as to their ability to win or lose, I again point out that pretty
much *any* deck can do this, and isn't the fault of the Rush deck. It is the
fault of a bad player. A bad player using a vote lock KRC deck can do the exact
same thing--kill folks across the table for no good reason, destabilize the
whole game for no personal gain, and just play stupid.

Again, this is not the fault of the Rush deck. Or of the rules for combat. It
is the fault of bad players.

>>That seems deliberately dense to me, to compare the way combat and S & B
operate.>>

How? How is it dense? Please explain to me the difference between:

A) I bleed you for 6. You now are now denied 6 points of resources.

B) I burn a 6 point vampire. You are now denied 6 points of resources.

Please explain the difference in a strategic sense.

>>Stealth and bleed attacks the remaining pool your prey leaves after
he's brought his minions out - unless you can make huge bleeds in the early
going
sufficient to prevent him from bring out as much force as he normally would.>>

You only have so much pool to spend. How is denying your prey that pool before
he uses it to buy vampires any less destabilizing than denying them that pool
after they bring out vampires?

>>He has as much force as he started out with until the moment he's ousted.
Combat decks, on the other hand, rob the victim (predator or prey), of
desperately needed force which they use against both you and the guy on the
other side.>>

So does a bleed deck. Again, 5 pool lost is 5 pool lost. If I bleed you for 5,
you are denied a 5 point vampire. If I didn't bleed you for 5, you can make
that 5 point vampire. If I didn't bleed you for 5 you can make that 5 point
vampire that you desperately need to use against me and the guy on the other
side. If I do bleed you for that 5, you can't. How is this any different than
you making that 5 point vampire and me killing it?

>>You need to do a bunch of rushes and thus damage before you can
bring your goal into view. It's this time that imbalances the game.>>

How? How does it imbalance the game? I am denying my prey resources. A bleed
deck does the *exact* same thing. I am denying my predator resources. An
intercept deck does the *exact* same thing.

>>Not in that sense, no. But unlike the bleed deck and the vote deck, the rush
deck *must* destabilize the game for a period of time before it can be
successful.>>

Again with the destabilization. A Rush deck weakens its prey and slows down its
predator. Just like any other deck.

>>Bleed and vote both attack pool, which has no direct consequences until the
moment you go over the top - if you ever do.>>

No direct consequences? Wha? If I am bled for 12 pool, I am denied 12 pool
worth of resources I would have had otherwise. How is this not a direct
consequence?

>>No. You torporize *one* minion. Then bring it out of torpor. Then
torporize
it again. I believe the difference is pretty obvious.>>

Obvious, and much less effective. Fame is useful in a pinch, but building a
deck around it is mostly pointless.

>>Maybe. But it still doesn't work very well.>>

Rush decks are the most effective anti S+B decks there are. Very little drives
people away from the Malkavians more effectively that having every one of their
minions destroyed before they take a single action.

> Now THAT'S more like it. (I'd change the wording to "all bleeds by that
>Methuselah'S MINIONS are reduced by 1..." or whatever matches the Protracted
>Racehorses card text.

In addition, I'd like to add the clause that it only reduces bleeds to you.

If it does reduce all bleeds by that Methusaleh, it has the potential to
greatly destabilize the game.

Currently, the only things you can do to reduce others' bleeds are DI, Eagle's
Sight and block, and Ignis Fatuus, all of which are rather limited. But this
new card has the potential to completely shut down any swarm decks (even
cross-table).

While I think it's good that this might help discourage weenie decks, I think
it would give the combat decks way too much table control. And think of the
havoc it would cause if some vindictive or unreasonable Methusaleh was playing.
I'd be pretty annoyed if I was cross-table and about to oust my prey when my
"ally" decides to reduce ALL of my bleeds by one!

Halcyan 2

considered,

you

Hmm. I'm detecting a strong pro-bleed bias here. Oh well, I'll provide the

> > The Benefit is immense--as a Rush deck, killing your Predator's vampires
> > keeps you alive.
>

> I just disagree. It helps keep you alive for a moment, but the table
destabilization

Yet it still keeps you alive. Who knows? Maybe your grand-predator is being

[comparing S&B to combat]

> That seems deliberately dense to me, to compare the way combat and S & B

> operate. Stealth and bleed attacks the remaining pool your prey leaves

after
> he's brought his minions out - unless you can make huge bleeds in the early

Hardly. They both reduce pool, in the long run. How is nuking a 5-capacity
vampire immediately after it's brought out, before it has a chance to act any
different from a bleed for 5? It's still an expenditure of 5 pool that can't
be easily regained.

And how often is a S&B deck *not* able to pound out a huge bleed early on?
Usually they have trouble a little later, when something starts jamming up
their hand...

> sufficient to prevent him from bring out as much force as he normally would.

> He has as much force as he started out with until the moment he's ousted.

A bleed is a pre-emptive rush. You've eliminated the pool before he can get
the vampire out. A rush is an after-the-fact bleed. You've eliminated the
pool after he spent it, but he can no longer get it back with a Minion Tap or
Blood Doll.

> Combat decks, on the other hand, rob the victim (predator or prey), of
> desperately needed force which they use against both you and the guy on the

It's a tactic. Deal.

> other side. You need to do a bunch of rushes and thus damage before you can

> bring your goal into view. It's this time that imbalances the game.

So I deflect all of your bleeds for 5 after I let you stealth them. This is

> > *any* deck can destablize a table when played badly--anyone who takes
> > actions that are not in their own best interest can destroy a multi-player
game. > >This is not the sole province of a Rush deck.

>
> Not in that sense, no. But unlike the bleed deck and the vote deck, the
rush
> deck *must* destabilize the game for a period of time before it can be
> successful.

Depends on what you call destabilization, I suppose. Vote decks often have to
make table-stabilization compromises in order to get their votes through,
though. It happens.

> Bleed and vote both attack pool, which has no direct consequences until the
> moment you go over the top - if you ever do.

Prevents the victim from bringing out the full force that they might have
otherwise. Hmm. I think I've heard that before.

[Fame deck]

> > But you'd still have to be able to torporize folks with impunity for such
cards
> > to be worth playing--and if you can torporize folks with impunity, you are
> > destroying minions.
>

> No. You torporize *one* minion. Then bring it out of torpor. Then
torporize
> it again. I believe the difference is pretty obvious.

It's also not all that efficient, unless you're playing with agg damage and
making the victim pay for the rescue. Otherwise, you're using lots of your
own resources to do that pool damage.

> > the benefit is not that "great", IMHO. Compared to other types of things you
> > can do for yourself, such as bleed your prey for five.
>
> But bleeding your prey for 5 can be defended against; by bleed bounce,
> by intercept, by Archon Investigation, etc. The point of combat is to
> try to exploit a weakness in the other deck, namely a lack of combat
> defense. If I'm playing a combat deck, I don't care if my opponent has
> intercept -- I want to get into a fight. I don't care if they have
> bleed bounce or AI. But if I'm playing a bleed deck, those defense
> measures influce my game tremendously.

That's fine. None the less, I still dispute Peter's assertion that the benefit is
all that wonderful. It's the same problem I have with things like Sudden Reversal.
You burn a card and an MPA and your opponent does likewise. It's good because it was
a master you _really_ didn't want him to play. But you're not his only opponent and
you're not even his only directly-opposed opponent (weird way to put that but I mean
"as opposed to a cross-table/somewhat allied opponent") so someone else on the table
likely benefits even more than you do. I give red marks to "benefits" that work like
that. If you truly need them, OK. But let's not pretend this is the greatest thing
since sliced bread.

> > Now *I'm* a little confused. You just got done lauding the benefits of destroying
> > a predator's minion in one paragraph and then in the next, you turn around and
> > minimize the benefit of bleeding your prey for 3 for only torporizing his vampires.
> > What am I not seeing here?
>
> You're not seeing that the number one priority of a combat deck is to
> destroy its prey's vampires.

This comment (and supporting paragraph) misses the point I just wrote. I'm not
arguing what the "combat deck's" priority is. I'm arguing that it's the wrong
one. That may be the number one priority but it's a difficult way to work.

> > Or rather, what are you *not* seeing here? The
> > possibilities for cards like this seem clear and obvious to me. The game works
> > much better when combat decks Fame a prey's vamp and spend all their time putting
> > the same vamp in and out of torpor.
>
> Not necessarily. It's very possible that by concentrating your efforts
> on the Famous vampire, you're allowing the other vampires to set up
> something which can really hurt you. If, for example, my prey is
> playing a deck with guns and I'm light on maneuvers, I don't want them
> to be able to get any guns. So my #1 priority is to kill all the
> vampires I can, to keep _any_ of them from taking an equip action.

Sure. But this way of looking at the game and how to handle your opposition is
using a total bludgeon to respond to the unknown. You eliminate the possibility
that your opponent can ever do anything to harm you but you necessarily do a whole
lot of other, not necessarily good things at the same time. If you can make it work,
I suppose that's fine. I just don't like what the instability does to the game. It's
never good news to wind up next to this type of a combat deck so far as I know. You
might survive it with a fortitude deck or some such but you never actually *win* that
metagame in terms of gaining by outguessing it. Someone else always "wins" - from
having the thing show up elsewhere on the table in a position that's not next to him.
I don't like strategies that set up these kinds of deals.

> > I'm not going to argue with you about the point that combat decks find ways to win
> > using combat. They do. They just aren't very easy ways to win and I feel that the
> > amount of chaos they cause - in the form of undeserved boons and banes to various
> > opponents - harms the game in general.
>
> Well, I don't know what to tell you. Anyone can play randomly and give
> unexpected benefits to the wrong person. A Malk S&B deck which uses
> Malkavian Pranks to keep cross-table allies (and future victims) in the
> game is doing the same kind of thing. If I have a heavy bleed deck, and
> a Deflection makes me accidentally oust my grand prey, I've
> "destabilized" the table, and given my prey an "undeserved boon."

Of course. But the fact that these things happen unavoidably is no reason to
encourage decks which are much more egregious causes of the problem, which combat
decks undoubtedly are. If someone were to tell me that Malk S & B with lots of
pranks didn't work very well, I sure wouldn't lean over backwards to change the
game so that _that_ worked, either.

> You know, Fred, you seem to have this problem a lot. People disagree
> with you, and you think they're deliberately being stupid. Can't you
> conceive of a point of view other than your own? Can you accept that
> some people aren't convinced by your arguments?

I can conceive of a point of view different from my own. But when someone
tries to compare two obviously different situations, I get kind of frustrated.
I'm pretty damn sure that if Peter knows better than the argument he attempted
to advance: that stealth & bleed causes as much destabilization as combat. If
he wasn't trying to defend the necessity of rush combat decks - which I'm
guessing he likes and is frustrated don't work better than they do with the
current card set - I doubt he'd make such a claim. Arguing about this is a
waste of time, IMO. There's a lot of chaos in the game, period. Combat causes
more than the other types of decks. If you or Peter aren't willing to concede
that, then we're living in different worlds and wasting each other's time trying
to communicate about this. If you are, then drop this lousy line of reasoning
and let's get down to our real differences.

(Rest of the post snipped as it just continues to rehash the comparison.)

Fred

admitting, that's a matter of my personal taste. I don't like decks that
are just a total screw factor to their neighbors. I'd like to have answers
to S & B in the game. I'm just looking for a different answer.

Fred

Ok, thanks to Xian's quote, I was able to find it. This text is from

"The Eternal Struggle: A Players Guide to Jyhad"

taken from the forward written by Richard Garfield. Copyright, all rights
reserved, reproduced without permission, a bunch of legal mumbo jumbo,
yadda, yadda.

Starting on page 14:

"The Beta version of Jyhad(tm) had few political cards relative to what was
eventually published. The political cards were being tested to see if the
flavor they added justified the complexity they added to the rules. I knew
we had to have princes and Justicars, the only question was whether they
added the depth of a political system or were just more of the same. The
political cards were greatly loved and served to throw some curveballs in
the two major strategies that were evolving: the combat monster strategy
and the sneak-and-bleed strategy.
"The combat monster strategy was pretty straightforward: if your vampires
were so deadlyl in combat that no one dared to block them, you could just
waltz over to your prey and bleed him at will. Your predator, on the other
hand, would think twice about sending a vampire to bleed you when she
might have to face one of your servance in combat. The two major clans
used for this purpose were the Gangrel and the well-armed Brujah, though
the Tremere could give a run for the blood. The Gangrel had the edge in
combat over the others, because of their claws and fortitude. After all,
the Brujah do have Presence.
"The sneak-and-bleed strategy was build about the premise that if you
can't catch my minions then I don't have to worry about giving them combat
skills at all. Just needing stealth cards for this gives me plenty of room
in
my deck to devote to enhanced bleedings. This strategy was used most
effectively with Malkavians who had Obfuscate for stealth and Dominate
for the bonus bleeds.
"After Gamma I was pretty sure that I wanted to equalize the pursuit of
the combat monster, sneak-and-bleed, or political decks. Ideally the best
decks would have elements of at least two of these pursuits. After all, a
few enhanced bleed cards in a Brujah combat deck can be an improvement.
"The political cards were even wilder than I anticipated. Sometimes they
were near meaningless while other times you cannot win without political
influence. The political deck has wierd tricks and traps whereas the others
are fairly straightforward, at least in their purest forms."
--Richard Garfield

Straight from the horses mouth.

Sorrow

all--I maintain that combat, when played with actually winning in mind (as
opposed to just playing an idiot rogue) has the same effect on the table as any
other viable strategy--it ousts its prey and slows down its predator.

>>- which I'm guessing he likes and is frustrated don't work better than they

I have no problem with combat decks in the current card set. They work just
fine. Again, I play them all the time and do quite well with them. I never
claimed that they needed to be improved. I simply debated the concept that A)
they are in some way more "destabilizing" (whatever that means) than, say, S+B
deck and B) combat should be tailored to be capable of doing something other
than destroying vampires (your assertion).

>>Arguing about this is a waste of time, IMO.>>

Arguing about everything is a waste of time. Yet here we are on usenet...

>>There's a lot of chaos in the game, period. Combat causes more than the
other types of decks.>>

I'm not quite sure what kind of players you are playing with and what kind of
combat decks you are playing with, but where I come from combat decks are used
to A) oust their prey and B) slow down their predator. Just like every other
deck in the game. If you are playing with people who regularly Rush across the
table, act irrationally, take actions that don't further their own victory,and
generally act chaotically, then that is the players you are playing with, not
the decks they are using.

>>If you or Peter aren't willing to concede that, then we're living in
different worlds and wasting each other's time trying to communicate about
this.>>

Apparently we are. Again, I play combat decks all the time. I do very well. I
regularly win games with them. I play to get VPs. I rarely Rush across table. I
primarily act to destroy my prey and secondarily act to slow down my predator.
I fail to see how my decks are "destabilizing" anything (especially as more
often than not, I win a game where I am capable of killing folks with
reliability). I fail to see how my decks are any more damaging to the game or
environment than a standard S+B deck.

On Wed, 4 Apr 2001 20:20:19 -0500, Sorrow wrote:

>taken from the forward written by Richard Garfield.

>...

>"The combat monster strategy was pretty straightforward: if your vampires

>were so deadly in combat that no one dared to block them, you could just

>waltz over to your prey and bleed him at will. Your predator, on the other
>hand, would think twice about sending a vampire to bleed you when she
>might have to face one of your servance in combat.

This combat monster archetype seems fine to me. It roughly
corresponds to the bruise-and-bleed and intercept decks, right? It's
the Rush deck which is sick and wrong - a degenerate concept based on
overuse of one card.

The new card that I'd like to see would have the effect of deflecting
an "enter combat" action onto another minion. Call it "Mistaken
Identity" or "The Wrong Box". This would hose the Rush deck while
sparing the original combat monster archetype.

As for Garfield, I saw a recent press release from the WotC brand
manager for Magic which, apart from explaining away 2001 budget cuts,
said that Garfield was still working on that game. I don't know if
anyone here has his ear but it would be good to send him some of the
new cards and solicit a state-of-the-nation review.

Andrew

reverse. A rush deck must first neutralize his predator for safety before
turning to his prey. This gives his prey free rein for a while. If his
bleeds can be reduced at the same time you are killing his minions, this
restores the balance.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> > > But bleeding your prey for 5 can be defended against; by bleed bounce,
> > > by intercept, by Archon Investigation, etc. The point of combat is to
> > > try to exploit a weakness in the other deck, namely a lack of combat
> > > defense. If I'm playing a combat deck, I don't care if my opponent has
> > > intercept -- I want to get into a fight. I don't care if they have
> > > bleed bounce or AI. But if I'm playing a bleed deck, those defense
> > > measures influce my game tremendously.
> >
> > That's fine. None the less, I still dispute Peter's assertion that the benefit is
> > all that wonderful.
>
> Benefit of what?

The benefit of destroying an opposing minion Peter was talking about.

> > > You're not seeing that the number one priority of a combat deck is to
> > > destroy its prey's vampires.
> >
> > This comment (and supporting paragraph) misses the point I just wrote. I'm not
> > arguing what the "combat deck's" priority is. I'm arguing that it's the wrong
> > one. That may be the number one priority but it's a difficult way to work.
>
> What should the combat deck do instead?

You mean, "How, in my opinion, should combat cards be incorporated into the
game so they don't cause instability?" I'd like to see them used for such things
as bruise and bleed or things like Fame using the loop I was talking about. You're
right: Fame alone isn't necessarily that good (though the loop works better with
Humanitas and Catacombs). What I'm saying is that I'd like more cards _like_ Fame
to show up in the mix so combat can be used productive to win victory points without
the absolute destruction of minions which causes so much instability.

As for the Fame loop being "dangerous", no, you have not proved it any more dangerous
than any other strategy that doesn't involve messing with people's minions. Stealth
and Bleed is "dangerous" in exactly the same way.

> > I just don't like what the instability does to the game. It's
> > never good news to wind up next to this type of a combat deck so far as I know.
>
> In my experience, many decks are unfazed by having a combat deck on
> either side of them. Against Potence at least, it's not incredibly
> difficult to have some kind of defense; very often a bunch of maneuvers
> is enough to keep you alive long enough to oust your combat prey.
>
> > If someone were to tell me that Malk S & B with lots of
> > pranks didn't work very well, I sure wouldn't lean over backwards to change the
> > game so that _that_ worked, either.
>
> Has someone told you that combat doesn't work very well? It certainly
> wasn't me. The reason some people would like to see a new S:CE hoser is
> just so that MORE KINDS of combat decks can be played, not so that
> "combat" (as a genre) can be more effective.

Allowing "more kinds" of combat decks is no more a priority than allowing
more kinds of decks that can use Malkavian prank. As I've said elsewhere,
though, it does bother me that certain clans have dedicated combat *cards* that
are pretty much useless to play because of S:CE and the fact that they can't
do much about it. That strikes me as a waste of cardboard and should be
rectified. So we may not be that far apart on the particular issue of S:CE
hosers.

>
> > > You know, Fred, you seem to have this problem a lot. People disagree
> > > with you, and you think they're deliberately being stupid. Can't you
> > > conceive of a point of view other than your own? Can you accept that
> > > some people aren't convinced by your arguments?
> >
> > I can conceive of a point of view different from my own. But when someone
> > tries to compare two obviously different situations, I get kind of frustrated.

> > I'm pretty damn sure that if Peter knows better than the argument he attempted
> > to advance: that stealth & bleed causes as much destabilization as combat.
>
> Whatever "destabilization" is. Every deck tries to hurt its prey.
> Hurting your prey weakens them, and makes them less able to hurt _their_
> prey.

"Destabilization", as it's being used all over this thread, refers to the
tendency to cause chaotic and unintended effects on the relationships between
other pairs of players. For instance, removing your predator's ability to defend
himself from his predator as you use rush combat to remove his ability to attack
and bleed you.

> > Combat causes
> > more than the other types of decks. If you or Peter aren't willing to concede
> > that, then we're living in different worlds and wasting each other's time trying
> > to communicate about this. If you are, then drop this lousy line of reasoning
> > and let's get down to our real differences.
>
> Well, once again you follow your standard argument sequence. Step 1:
> put forward outlandish argument filled with holes. Step 2: when others
> try to refute your argument and point out holes, you call them stupid
> for not agreeing with you. Step 3: when others continue to disagree,
> you quit arguing. Why do you even bother?

I don't see much point in debating about this this way. IMO, my argument was not
outlandish, not "filled with holes", and the above does not represent any attempt
to "quit arguing". I simply said that if you cannot accept that combat causes
more destabilization of the game than strategies which attack a Meth's pool
directly, then we have nothing talk about. We simply disagree on how the game
plays, which is not something that we can resolve by arguing with each other.

Fred

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>As I requested in another post, please explain the realistic difference
>between
>denying an opponent 6 pool worth of resources by bleeding them for 6 and
>denying an opponent 6 pool worth of resources by burning a 6 point vampire.

A vampire often doesn't cost 6 pool due to blood management (Blood Doll, etc.).
So, by removing a vampire, you are bleeding your opponent for less than you
would be if you got a similar size bleed through.

But, a vampire can take actions where pool in itself does nothing. By removing
vampires (minions), you remove the ability of your opponent to attempt to oust
his/her prey or defend from being ousted. Look at it this way, is an opponent
with 25 pool and no minions stronger than an opponent with 20 pool and one
minion.

Then, there's the issue of time. Getting really off topic because I haven't
seen a good Banishment rant lately, this is what makes Banishment so strong.
It takes time to bring out minions. Reducing pool has much less effect on how
much a player does (until the player is ousted) than removing minions.

I never get as worked up by a loss of pool as I do a loss of minions because
with minions I can still impact the game. Having nothing but pool removes my
ability to influence the game until I can get a minion back into play. And, if
you kill that to, I really have no interest in doing so. Unless somehow I can
arrange to bring out multiple minions so that I can do something, my game is
over yet I have to sit around and wait to die. Loads of fun.

While its nice and all that some people know precisely how to play combat decks
to prevent excessive destabilization, I really don't see these experts. What I
see are rush and intercept decks that do nothing but affect their predator
because if they take time to look forward, they die. Different if there are
multiple combat decks, but that hasn't come up often enough to note at least in
tournament play. Whether this is because the players lack experience, the
decks are badly constructed, or what, I don't know. I know I lack experience
playing a rush deck. Decks that do nothing but rush bore me immensely.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:

>
> Fredrick wrote:
> >>I disagree. It provides a benefit to you at a cost. It provides a free
> benefit
> to another one of your opponents, your grand predator. All things considered,
> the benefit is not that "great", IMHO. Compared to other types of things you
> can do for yourself, such as bleed your prey for five.>>
>

> And bleeding your prey for 5 provides a free benefit for your grand prey--the
> five pool that they lost could have been a 5 cost vampire hurting your grand

> prey, but because you took that pool, you have denied your prey this
> opportunity, and consequently, provided a free benefit to another one of your
> opponents. Any action you take against your prey or predator indirectly helps
> someone else at the table. Bleeding someone for 5 (denying them a possible 5
> point minion) or burning a 5 point minion (denying them an existing minion) has
> the same end result--your other opponents benefit. Please explain the
> difference.

If you can bleed someone for 5 on the first turn, I agree that that's approximately
the effect it has. In practice, this is not the effect it has once mid-game hits.
People recruit a certain number of vamps and leave as much pool as they're comfortable
sitting on to prevent being ousted. Bleeding for 5 mostly tends to have the effect
of either ousting them or not. And if not, it just makes them more uncomfortable
and may cause them to adjust their emphasis on defense vs. offense. It may also
constrain them from using small amounts of pool for things like locations and
equipment that they might have otherwise paid for. But for the most part, it's
nothing like - for instance - torporizing one or two of their princes, which is
what combat decks do.

> >>What am I not seeing here? Or rather, what are you *not* seeing here? The

> possibilities for cards like this seem clear and obvious to me. The game works
> much better when combat decks Fame a prey's vamp and spend all their time
> putting the same vamp in and out of torpor.>>
>

> Not for the Rush deck it doesn't. You are spending 3 actions to cost your prey
> 6 pool. If you spend those three actions torporizing more than 6 pool worth of
> vampires, the three Rush actions are more effective than the Lather, Rinse,
> Repeat Fame manuver. Pool loss is pool loss. I fail to see how it is more
> beneficial for anyone for this pool loss to be in the form of loose pool than
> pool tied up in minions for the same amount. Yes, torporizing a vampire of your
> prey gives your grand prey a free bonus (one less vampire to deal with).
> Bleeding someone for the same amount does the same thing.

I'm sorry, I just don't think the comparison between destroying a 6-cap minion
and bleeding for 6 is comparable in practice for reasons given above. It's not
like you destroy the minion and you're prey will automatically, necessarily bring
out another 6-cap to replace it with. He may react in all sorts of ways. Nor is
a 6-cap necessarily _like_ bleeding for 6 if it got brought out and Minion Tapped.
5 of those blood may be back in his pool, meaning you've cost him 1 blood, an MPA,
and some transfers. The latter two things get made up rapidly with time.

I'm also not sure where you're getting 3 actions for the cycle. The Fame/torporize/
rescue cycle initiates with an MPA, enough rushes to torporize (not necessarily one,
but definitely easier than burning), and an action to rescue. Then continues with
retorporizing (should be a single rush at that point) and rerescuing.

> >>Compared to running around blowing up minions for no particular gain except
> their absence, the amount of table destabilization of the former tactic is
> practically nil.>>
>
> I still fail to see where the "no particular gain" comes in. I play Rush decks
> all the time. I do very well with them. I get into the finals of pretty much
> every tournament I play in. Sometimes I win. What defines "particular gain" in
> VTES more than getting VPs? If killing vampires gets me VPs, I am gaining
> something in particular. Victory points.

I was referring to short term gain. That is, you don't cost your prey any
pool directly, albeit you may cost him pool indirectly if he decides his response
is to bring out more vampires to replace the destroyed one.

> >>I just disagree. It helps keep you alive for a moment, but the table
> destabilization makes it difficult to predict what will happen in the long
> run.>>
>
> And deflecting a bleed for 6 helps keep you alive for the moment as well.
> Again, please detail the difference.

Obvious. Your predator doesn't lose minions by having his bleed deflected.
(Unless you deflect it into an intercept combat deck. Even then, it would be
unusual for the two players not to pull their punches in a situation like that.)
I find it frustrating to respond to such demands that presume to equate too such
obviously different situations.

> This concept of "Table Destabilization" is a nebulous one to me. Any deck that
> does what it intends on doing is weakening another player. Any time a player's
> position is weakened, another player benefits.

But who benefits and what happens in the game in the interim? When attacking
pool, the victim's resources are basically left in tact until the moment of his
ousting. When defending by other means besides combat, the victim seldom
actually loses any resources at all. Combat creates periods of time when your
neighbors become partially or totally helpless but are not ousted. Those
periods of time are the openings for your non-neighboring players to take
great advantage of, because your grandprey has no predator and because your
grandpredator has a helpless prey. If you can manage the table and ultimate
win enough victory points to win tournaments, that's great. But you can't
tell me that it isn't an undeserved advantage for others to be your grandprey
and grandpredator and an undeserved disadvantage for others to be your predator
and prey - no matter what decks they bring to the table.

> If I am an intercept deck, and I stop all of my predator's
> actions, I am denying him resources and keeping him from doing what he wants to
> do. As a result, my grand predator is going to be in a better position, and he
> gets a free benefit. How is what a Rush deck does any different?

They're not. I have the same problem with intercept decks, actually.

> >>He has as much force as he started out with until the moment he's ousted.
> Combat decks, on the other hand, rob the victim (predator or prey), of
> desperately needed force which they use against both you and the guy on the
> other side.>>
>

> So does a bleed deck. Again, 5 pool lost is 5 pool lost. If I bleed you for 5,
> you are denied a 5 point vampire.

(This point is made over and over. I've refuted it above - a 5 point vampire
and 5 points of pool are two different things, especially in practice. So we
can debate it above. I've snipped the other rehashes of this dispute.)

> >>No. You torporize *one* minion. Then bring it out of torpor. Then
> torporize it again. I believe the difference is pretty obvious.>>
>
> Obvious, and much less effective. Fame is useful in a pinch, but building a
> deck around it is mostly pointless.

You may not find it to be effective and I won't argue with you about it. My
point was not to suggest Fame, used in this way, is a great tactic. My point
was to hold it out as the kind of card combat decks should be given to work
with so that minion destruction doesn't seem like the only way to use combat.
Minion destruction is not very effective, however much success a good player
can have with it, and adds bad elements to the game in general.

> >>Maybe. But it still doesn't work very well.>>
>
> Rush decks are the most effective anti S+B decks there are. Very little drives
> people away from the Malkavians more effectively that having every one of their
> minions destroyed before they take a single action.

I won't dispute that they're good anti stealth & bleed decks. But as I replied
to James Hamblin's post, I prefer the game find another "rock" to S&B's "scissors"
rather than making this one more workable.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> > > I don't think that the average combat deck is necessarily "bad news." A
> > > potence rush deck is trying to take advantage of a lack of combat
> > > defense (fortitude, maneuvers) in the average tournament deck. There
> > > are plenty of decks which will make the potence player say "oh, shit,
> > > I'm screwed." If Combat is Rock, there are as many Scissors as there
> > > are Papers.
> >

> > Combat is usually always bad news to sit next to. Or at worst, mediocre news

> > if you have enough combat cards to survive it. If you "win" the metagame by
> > packing enough combat evasion, the guys who really win are still the ones
> > sitting on the other side of the table.
>
> Speaking as someone who has played rush combat decks a lot, I can tell
> you that this just isn't true. Your deck doesn't have to be 50% combat
> defense to foil a combat deck. You just need to know that effective
> combat decks are out there, and plan for it. If your prey is a combat
> deck which is bashing its head against your defensive wall, there's
> nothing stopping you from ousting them quickly. Combats decks generally
> don't have standard vote or bleed defense; if you can usually survive
> the combats, you can probably oust them. How does that make someone
> across the table win?

Because simply having the answers to the combat deck *doesn't* win you the
game. You may survive the rushes. I suppose if it's your predator and he's
not bleeding you because he's been ineffective at torporizing your minions,
then that's good. But it doesn't help you oust your prey. And the deck
space you need to survive combat robs you of cards you could be using to
win the game.

It's not enough to simply survive to win the metagame. There needs to be
a payoff for guessing right. Guessing right that you're going to hit a combat
deck seldom provides much of a payoff. It mostly just screws the combat deck.
You have to forget the notion you seem to have that this is a zero-sum game.
What's bad for your predator isn't necessarily good for you.

> > > I'm not saying I think Combat (as a strategy) needs any boosting. But
> > > how could the hypothetical existence of more _kinds_ of combat decks be
> > > bad?
> >
> > Assuming by "combat decks" you mean big, bad-boy rush combat that bludgeons
> > all its neighbor's minions to destruction, the answer is because then you'd
> > have more combat decks.
>
> Why? It just doesn't follow. Just because there are more kinds of
> combat decks which can be viable doesn't mean the proportion of combat
> decks at tournaments will increase.

Sure it does. Assuming there are more kinds, they must increase their number
at tournaments. The new decks can come from the ranks of people who played
other combat decks or from those who didn't. If the former, then the net increase
is zero. If the latter, then it's positive. If you're arguing that they'll only
come from the former so the total net increase has a significant chance of being
zero or near zero, that strikes me as unlikely.

I suppose you could be making the point that the increase will be fairly minimal or
that others will cease playing combat decks at all in the shift to the new metagame.
My perception, though, is that if you create a new type of viable deck, it's
unpredictable what it will do to the percentage of existing decks so the most
reasonable assumption to make is that they'll stay steady - thus increasing the overall
number of combat decks if you add a new type of combat deck. If you have a specific
reason you think this would not be true, I'd like to hear it.

> > I don't like decks that
> > are just a total screw factor to their neighbors.
>
> It sounds like you've never seen a combat deck get screwed.

Oh, combat decks absolutely get screwed. It just doesn't necessarily help their neighbors
that much.

Fred

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> James Hamblin wrote:
> >
> > What should the combat deck do instead?
>
> You mean, "How, in my opinion, should combat cards be incorporated into the
> game so they don't cause instability?"

No, I mean: how should a deck dedicated to successful combat win the
game, if not by destroying all of its prey's minions? I don't know what
this whole argument is trying to accomplish; you seem dead-set on making
all-combat decks impossible to play. I'm also not sure _why_ you want
this. You don't like that a combat deck shakes up a table? Live with
it.

> I'd like to see them used for such things
> as bruise and bleed or things like Fame using the loop I was talking about.

Combat _cards_ get used for a lot of things. But Bruise and Bleed isn't
always good, because it's less effective at dealing with combat defense
(due to the smaller amount of combat cards it can include). For a deck
to be able to NEARLY GUARANTEE successful combat, it has to be NEARLY
100% FOCUSED on that goal. Anything less, and you're going to be less
successful in combat. Now, I grant you that the inclusion of bleed
cards will make the deck more effective in other situations. This is
another trade-off.

> You're
> right: Fame alone isn't necessarily that good (though the loop works better with
> Humanitas and Catacombs).

But the deck space and time spent to get these cards isn't really worth
what you get.

> What I'm saying is that I'd like more cards _like_ Fame
> to show up in the mix so combat can be used productive to win victory points without
> the absolute destruction of minions which causes so much instability.

Even if more cards like Fame are printed, the existing combat decks will
still exist. And if, like Fame, these cards require a weakening of the
combat in some area, then they will not be used.

It sounds like you want all combat decks to be Bruise and Bleed decks.
But that's unreasonable.

> As for the Fame loop being "dangerous", no, you have not proved it any more dangerous
> than any other strategy that doesn't involve messing with people's minions. Stealth
> and Bleed is "dangerous" in exactly the same way.

It's dangerous because messing with people's minions is how the combat
deck defends itself. Any player with any deck should want to oust their
prey as quickly as possible. Allowing your prey to take actions or
otherwise "set up" is only going to hurt you. If hurting my prey makes
them ease up on _their_ prey, then that player may become stronger. But
there's nothing in that statement which is specific to combat.

Your arguments seem to be a hair's breadth away from "Wah, combat decks
make me unable to take actions. It's not fair." It's not like combat
cannot be defended against.

> Allowing "more kinds" of combat decks is no more a priority than allowing
> more kinds of decks that can use Malkavian prank.

"Combat" is a common deck genre. Malk. Prank is a specific card.
There's a huge difference. What _is_ a priority is making the
independent clans stronger. One way to do that would be to print cards
which make combat decks easier to build for those clans. One way to do
_that_ would be to print an anti-S:CE card for the Ravnos and/or the
Assamites.

> As I've said elsewhere,
> though, it does bother me that certain clans have dedicated combat *cards* that
> are pretty much useless to play because of S:CE and the fact that they can't
> do much about it. That strikes me as a waste of cardboard and should be
> rectified. So we may not be that far apart on the particular issue of S:CE
> hosers.

Yeah, there will always be wallpaper cards. The fact that there are a
bunch of combat cards which won't work because of S:CE isn't a reason to
print a S:CE hoser. One problem I have is that it's hard to make an
all-Gangrel combat deck, because Dog Pack is slow and expensive.
Protean is a very combat-centric discipline, so maybe it should have a
S:CE hoser. Then again, maybe not.

> > Whatever "destabilization" is. Every deck tries to hurt its prey.
> > Hurting your prey weakens them, and makes them less able to hurt _their_
> > prey.
>
> "Destabilization", as it's being used all over this thread, refers to the
> tendency to cause chaotic and unintended effects on the relationships between
> other pairs of players. For instance, removing your predator's ability to defend
> himself from his predator as you use rush combat to remove his ability to attack
> and bleed you.

The predator point is a valid one. As a Rush deck, you certainly don't
want to weaken your predator so much that they can't defend themselves.
On the other hand, sometimes you have no choice. If my predator is a
weenie Dominate bleed deck, and I'm playing my Potence rush deck, I may
well lose. I'll have to destroy every vampire my predator brings out,
because I have no defense against bleeds for 6 from every minion. Given
this, I may still survive and even get a VP or two. That's a lot better
than other decks which just get rolled over by weenie Dom bleed.

> > Well, once again you follow your standard argument sequence. Step 1:
> > put forward outlandish argument filled with holes. Step 2: when others
> > try to refute your argument and point out holes, you call them stupid
> > for not agreeing with you. Step 3: when others continue to disagree,
> > you quit arguing. Why do you even bother?
>
> I don't see much point in debating about this this way.

It's just frustrating that you seemed to be giving up just because I
disagreed with you.

> IMO, my argument was not
> outlandish, not "filled with holes",

Well, of course not in _your_ opinion. But what about _my_ opinion? If
you're not willing to accept that I have opinions which differ from
yours, why bother having a discussion at all?

> and the above does not represent any attempt
> to "quit arguing". I simply said that if you cannot accept that combat causes
> more destabilization of the game than strategies which attack a Meth's pool
> directly, then we have nothing talk about. We simply disagree on how the game
> plays, which is not something that we can resolve by arguing with each other.

Since "destabilization" is something which I can't exactly define, much
less measure, I can't accept it. But I think attacking someone's pool
makes them turn backwards (or inward) just as much as attacking their
minions.

If I'm a combat deck, and I manage to kill all my prey's minions, I'm
doing well. I'll almost certainly get that VP. Now, if this makes my
grandprey stronger in the meantime, well, that's just part of life as a
combat deck. I don't care if they don't "deserve" to have their prey
killed. I don't care if you think this "advantage" they've received is
"unfair" or not. I've acheived the goal of the game, which is to earn
VP's.

James

ham...@math.wisc.edu

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> Peter D Bakija wrote:
> >

> > Bleeding someone for 5 (denying them a possible 5
> > point minion) or burning a 5 point minion (denying them an existing minion) has
> > the same end result--your other opponents benefit. Please explain the
> > difference.
>
> If you can bleed someone for 5 on the first turn, I agree that that's approximately
> the effect it has. In practice, this is not the effect it has once mid-game hits.
> People recruit a certain number of vamps and leave as much pool as they're
> comfortable sitting on to prevent being ousted.

When I look at my initial vampire draw, I don't say to myself "Ah, I
will get out vampires X, Y, and Z, and then I will safely have 9 pool
remaining." There's no way you can control how much pool you're going
to have or whether you're ever going to be able to get out any more
vampires. Having X amount of pool doesn't prevent you from being
ousted. Being able to defend yourself from your predator and _gain_
pool prevents you from being ousted. If your deck can't handle losing
pool at a regular rate, it's not a good deck.

> Bleeding for 5 mostly tends to have the effect
> of either ousting them or not.

Torp'ing a 5-point vampire tends to have the effect of putting them down
for good (so that they can't get out any more vampires) or not.

> And if not, it just makes them more uncomfortable
> and may cause them to adjust their emphasis on defense vs. offense.

Ditto.

> It may also
> constrain them from using small amounts of pool for things like locations and
> equipment that they might have otherwise paid for.

Ditto. If they know they may have to get out another vampire because
all their current ones are going to die, they're less likely to buy that
pricey master card, etc.

> But for the most part, it's
> nothing like - for instance - torporizing one or two of their princes, which is
> what combat decks do.

You're right. Torporizing their princes is better. And harder.

> I'm sorry, I just don't think the comparison between destroying a 6-cap minion
> and bleeding for 6 is comparable in practice for reasons given above.

Reasons refuted. Your turn.

> It's not
> like you destroy the minion and you're prey will automatically, necessarily bring
> out another 6-cap to replace it with. He may react in all sorts of ways.

Sure. They can get mad and just sit there on a pile of pool, refusing
to get out any more vampires. But then they're not trying to fulfil
their victory conditions. You can't blame this irrational behavior on a
fault in the game. If they want to win the game, they have to try to
play. That means having vampires. Once again, one way to do this is to
get out a bunch of vampires all on the same turn.

> Nor is
> a 6-cap necessarily _like_ bleeding for 6 if it got brought out and Minion Tapped.

Generally, it's a good idea to kill the vampire before it can get minion
tapped. More reasons _not_ to concentrate on a Fame loop.

> 5 of those blood may be back in his pool, meaning you've cost him 1 blood, an MPA,
> and some transfers. The latter two things get made up rapidly with time.

_Not_ killing the vampire may cost you more, even if it has already been
minion tapped. If you let it get Fifth'ed and Tapped again, you're in a
bad place.

> I'm also not sure where you're getting 3 actions for the cycle. The Fame/torporize/
> rescue cycle initiates with an MPA, enough rushes to torporize (not necessarily one,
> but definitely easier than burning), and an action to rescue. Then continues with
> retorporizing (should be a single rush at that point) and rerescuing.

If, as a combat deck, you can't "point and kill" with impunity, you're
not going to be able to win. With this in mind, the Fame "loop" takes 1
action to send the vampire to torpor initially, and then 2 more each
time to "run" the loop (rescue, retorp). Two actions (and a bunch of
cards, and blood) to do 3 pool damage. Seems pretty inefficient to me.

> I was referring to short term gain. That is, you don't cost your prey any
> pool directly, albeit you may cost him pool indirectly if he decides his response
> is to bring out more vampires to replace the destroyed one.

If your prey has no ready vampires and chooses not to bring out any more
vampires, they're not trying to win the game. (Note: sometimes they
have no choice; if they are low on pool, sitting and doing nothing is
acceptable.) I can't control whether people at a tournament are or are
not playing to win. Here's a question for LSJ (or anyone else who runs
tournaments): would it be possible to penalize a player who is not
"playing to win"?

> > And deflecting a bleed for 6 helps keep you alive for the moment as well.
> > Again, please detail the difference.
>
> Obvious. Your predator doesn't lose minions by having his bleed deflected.

And your (combat) predator doesn't lose minions by having his combats
thwarted. Your point?

> I find it frustrating to respond to such demands that presume to equate too such
> obviously different situations.

I find it frustrating that you begin every other sentence telling us how
frustrated you are. If it makes you feel better, convince yourself that
we're all dumb, and we need you to show us "the light".

> > This concept of "Table Destabilization" is a nebulous one to me. Any deck that
> > does what it intends on doing is weakening another player. Any time a player's
> > position is weakened, another player benefits.
>
> But who benefits and what happens in the game in the interim?

I benefit, because my prey is weakened, enabling me to oust them. I
benefit, because my predator is weakened, enabling me to not get ousted.

> When attacking
> pool, the victim's resources are basically left in tact until the moment of his
> ousting.

And, in a way, that's less effective! If he still has minions up, he
can do things which may keep me from ousting him. If my prey has no
ready minions, they can't possibly keep me from killing them.

> When defending by other means besides combat, the victim seldom
> actually loses any resources at all.

...except pool.

> Combat creates periods of time when your
> neighbors become partially or totally helpless but are not ousted.

Your prey being helpless is good for you. Now you can oust them. Your
predator being helpless is only good in the short term. You don't want
them to get ousted unless they're about to kill you. It's difficult to
find the right middle ground between obliterating your predator and
leaving them alone. This is one of the fundamental difficulties with
rush decks.

> Those
> periods of time are the openings for your non-neighboring players to take
> great advantage of, because your grandprey has no predator and because your
> grandpredator has a helpless prey.

Your grandpredator shouldn't have a helpless prey unless you are in a
very bad spot. As for your grandprey? Well, they still have a prey who
is presumably not just sleeping. Plus, once your prey is incapacitated,
you can start taking actions against your grandprey (while still
bleeding your prey).

> If you can manage the table and ultimate
> win enough victory points to win tournaments, that's great.

I can, and have.

> But you can't
> tell me that it isn't an undeserved advantage for others to be your grandprey
> and grandpredator and an undeserved disadvantage for others to be your predator
> and prey

I could say that about a lot of decks. My friend Kevin's weenie
Dominate deck is a nightmare to be sitting next to, unless I'm playing
my intercept deck. So, sure. It's an advantage to _not_ be sitting
next to him.

> - no matter what decks they bring to the table.

Here's the murky part, and it's obviously not true. If someone sits
down as my prey with a shitload of combat defense, they're going to do
pretty well. If I have my potence combat deck, and I sit down next to a
Tzimisce deck with 10 Blood of Acid, I'm going to get wrecked.

> > If I am an intercept deck, and I stop all of my predator's
> > actions, I am denying him resources and keeping him from doing what he wants to
> > do. As a result, my grand predator is going to be in a better position, and he
> > gets a free benefit. How is what a Rush deck does any different?
>
> They're not. I have the same problem with intercept decks, actually.

What is your problem? There are a bunch of decks you don't like. So
what? You find them boring. Good for you. That doesn't mean people
shouldn't play them or that they shouldn't exist.

> > Obvious, and much less effective. Fame is useful in a pinch, but building a
> > deck around it is mostly pointless.
>
> You may not find it to be effective and I won't argue with you about it. My
> point was not to suggest Fame, used in this way, is a great tactic. My point
> was to hold it out as the kind of card combat decks should be given to work
> with so that minion destruction doesn't seem like the only way to use combat.
> Minion destruction is not very effective, however much success a good player
> can have with it, and adds bad elements to the game in general.

I think minion destruction is very effective. If you can keep someone
from being able to take any actions, or gain any pool, you can easily
kill them. There is only an "unbalancing" effect to your right if the
combat deck has a speedy deck as their predator. And the combat deck is
doing the table a FAVOR by eliminating a deck which probably has a fair
chance of sweeping the table. This seems like a balancing element, not
a "bad element."

> > Rush decks are the most effective anti S+B decks there are. Very little drives
> > people away from the Malkavians more effectively that having every one of their
> > minions destroyed before they take a single action.
>
> I won't dispute that they're good anti stealth & bleed decks. But as I replied
> to James Hamblin's post, I prefer the game find another "rock" to S&B's "scissors"
> rather than making this one more workable.

S&B is already pretty easily screwable. Archon Investigation is a
horrible card, and makes you never want to bleed for more than 3, lest
your vampire get burned and your prey _gain_ pool. Let's not get into
that now. There's also bleed bounce, which is impossible to defend
against. Permanent intercept is much easier to come by than permanent
stealth. And then, of course, there's combat.

Bleed is a fun deck to play. It's very straight forward; it's usually
either great or terrible. It shouldn't get screwed any more than it
already is.

James
--
James Hamblin
ham...@math.wisc.edu

"You seem to think you know it all

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> James Hamblin wrote:
> >
> > Combats decks generally
> > don't have standard vote or bleed defense; if you can usually survive
> > the combats, you can probably oust them. How does that make someone
> > across the table win?
>
> Because simply having the answers to the combat deck *doesn't* win you the
> game.

Simply having bleed defense doesn't win you the game, either.

> You may survive the rushes. I suppose if it's your predator and he's
> not bleeding you because he's been ineffective at torporizing your minions,
> then that's good. But it doesn't help you oust your prey.

Since when does being able to defend against your predator help you oust
your prey?

> And the deck
> space you need to survive combat robs you of cards you could be using to
> win the game.

Having Deflections robs you of space you could be using for game-winning
cards, too. What's the difference?

> It's not enough to simply survive to win the metagame. There needs to be
> a payoff for guessing right.

Why? If you survive, you get a victory point. That's a pretty good
payoff.

> Guessing right that you're going to hit a combat
> deck seldom provides much of a payoff.

It makes you not dead.

> It mostly just screws the combat deck.
> You have to forget the notion you seem to have that this is a zero-sum game.
> What's bad for your predator isn't necessarily good for you.

If your predator can't kill you, then you're not dead. Being not dead
is good.

> > Why? It just doesn't follow. Just because there are more kinds of
> > combat decks which can be viable doesn't mean the proportion of combat
> > decks at tournaments will increase.
>
> Sure it does. Assuming there are more kinds, they must increase their number
> at tournaments.

No! You're completely wrong!!! According to this logic, every time an
expansion gets printed, then since new decks are possible, then EVERY
deck type must increase in proportion. Which is, of course, impossible.

> The new decks can come from the ranks of people who played
> other combat decks or from those who didn't.

Wait, what were the people who were not playing combat decks before
playing? Bleed decks? But wait, they also printed a new bleed card, so
by your reasoning there must be _more_ bleed decks. Do you see why this
makes no sense?

[snip more insanity]

> I suppose you could be making the point that the increase will be fairly minimal or
> that others will cease playing combat decks at all in the shift to the new metagame.
> My perception, though, is that if you create a new type of viable deck, it's
> unpredictable what it will do to the percentage of existing decks so the most
> reasonable assumption to make is that they'll stay steady - thus increasing the
> overall number of combat decks if you add a new type of combat deck. If you have a
> specific reason you think this would not be true, I'd like to hear it.

How can I be more specific?!? It's impossible for the proportions of
EVERY type of deck to increase or stay steady unless they all stay
steady. I'm not saying that there won't be more combat decks if more
combat cards are printed, just that it doesn't follow.

> > It sounds like you've never seen a combat deck get screwed.
>
> Oh, combat decks absolutely get screwed. It just doesn't necessarily help their
> neighbors that much.

Well, having a prey that's getting screwed is good. It makes them
easier to kill. Having a predator that's getting screwed is good. It
makes it harder for them to kill you.

This really is all very simple...

<< A vampire often doesn't cost 6 pool due to blood management (Blood Doll,
etc.).
So, by removing a vampire, you are bleeding your opponent for less than you
would be if you got a similar size bleed through. >>

Completely true, but not the point. We aren't here trying to prove that
bleeding for 6 is more effective than blowing up a 6 point vampire. We are here
trying to prove than under the best circumstances, blowing up a 6 point vampire
has the same effect as a 6 point bleed.

Under the worst circumstances (that 6 point vampire gets minion tapped for 6
before it gets blown up), blowing up that 6 point vampire is considerably less
effective than a 6 point bleed. No one is here debating that.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Fredrick wrote:
>>If you can bleed someone for 5 on the first turn, I agree that that's
approximately the effect it has. In practice, this is not the effect it has
once mid-game hits. People recruit a certain number of vamps and leave as much
pool as they're comfortable sitting on to prevent being ousted.>>

Exactly. Generally one (I know I do) looks at the amount of pool they have,
estimates what is a safe "cushion" of pool to sit on to avoid ousting, and then
spends the rest on vampires. Assuming that X is your safe pool cushion, the
amount you spend on vampires is (the amount you currently have)-X. If the
amount you currently have is 6 less than it was before (because you were bled
for 6), you are getting out 6 points less of vampires, or getting yourself 6
points closer to ousting. Losing 6 pool is 6 points less of resources you have
access to, regardless of *when* you lose the pool.

>>Bleeding for 5 mostly tends to have the effect of either ousting them or
not.>>

But if you don't lose that pool, you have the option of getting out another 5
point vampire. You don't have to, but you can if you feel it is safe to do so.
Without that 5 pool, you don't have this option at all.

You can make all the situational examples in the world where losing 6 pool does
not *necessarily* equate losing a 6 point vampire, but in the end, if you have
6 pool, you have access to 6 more points of resources than you did before. If
you lose 6 pool, you are losing a potential 6 points of vampires. Whether you
lose this 6 pool before it is a vampire or after makes no difference in the
long run.

>>I'm sorry, I just don't think the comparison between destroying a 6-cap
minion
and bleeding for 6 is comparable in practice for reasons given above.>>

I think you are mistaken. 6 pool is 6 pool. If you lose 6 pool from bleeding,
you can't ever spend that 6 pool on a vampire. If you lose 6 pool from getting
a 6 cost vampire burnt (that you haven't Minion Tapped or Blood Dolled or used
his blood to do other stuff with), you are in the exact same spot you were when
you were bled for 6--without a 6 point vampire.

>>Nor is a 6-cap necessarily _like_ bleeding for 6 if it got brought out and
Minion Tapped.>>

People keep bringing this up. It confuses me in this conversation--yes, if the
minion tap goes off *before* the 6 point vampire is burned, you are in *much*
better off than if you had been simply bled for 6. If I bleed you for 6, you
lose 6 pool and have nothing to show for it. If I beat up a 6 point vampire who
has been minion tapped, you still have 6 pool, *plus* a 6 point vampire who may
or may not get burned. This is much less damaging than just losing 6 pool from
a bleed in the first place. As I am attempting to illustrate how blowing up a 6
point vampire is equivalent to being bled for 6, I fail to see how introducing
the minion tap element does anything other than make the 6 point bleed seem
*much* more effective than the Rush.

>>I'm also not sure where you're getting 3 actions for the cycle.>>

Torporize/rescue/Torporize again for 6 pool loss (7, actually) with 3 actions.
The maximum pool damage with the minimum of actions. I could have couched it as
2 actions per 3 pool loss, but that seems even less effective, so I used the 3
actions for 6 damage model.

>>I was referring to short term gain. That is, you don't cost your prey any
pool directly, albeit you may cost him pool indirectly if he decides his
response
is to bring out more vampires to replace the destroyed one.>>

Short term gain: My prey is now weaker and easier to oust. Long term gain:
Eventually, I will oust my prey. Killing their vampires provides both.

>>But who benefits and what happens in the game in the interim?>>

If you are playing correctly, you are benefiting. You seem to be under the
impression that folks who play Rush decks do so with no logic or need to act in
their own best interest. When playing a Rush deck, you do the same things to do
with any other deck that tries to win--take the actions that provide you with
the most benefit at the time. If you aren't doing this, you are playing poorly.

>>When attacking pool, the victim's resources are basically left in tact until
the moment of his ousting.>>

But each pool you remove is one less pool available to spend on these
resources. If I lose lots of pool to a bleed deck, I have fewer resources. If I
get my vampires burned by a Rush deck, I have fewer resources. The effective
difference is zero.

>>When defending by other means besides combat, the victim seldom
actually loses any resources at all.>>

Except their pool, which denies them resources.

>>Combat creates periods of time when your neighbors become partially or
totally helpless but are not ousted.>>

Bleed decks create periods of time when you are ousted.

I think I see where you are coming from here--you don't like having your
vampires blown up, but you are perfectly happy getting bled for 30 in 5 actions
and ousted. Either way you are removed from the game. When the bleed deck does
this, you have to sit around at the table for an extra 10 minutes before you
are ousted. When the bleed deck does this, you are removed from the game 10
minutes earlier. You see this as much better. Check.

>>If you can manage the table and ultimate win enough victory points to win
tournaments, that's great. But you can't tell me that it isn't an undeserved
advantage for others to be your grandprey and grandpredator and an undeserved
disadvantage for others to be your predator and prey - no matter what decks
they bring to the table.>>

An undeserved advantage? If I am winning, who cares? If I am letting other
people win, I am not playing correctly. As I have pointed out many times
before, playing dumb and making other people win is not the sole province of
the Rush deck. Anyone can play dumb with any deck and make other people win.
You seem to think that Rush decks are the only ones that allow for this. I
assure you that this is an incorrect assumption.

>>They're not. I have the same problem with intercept decks, actually.>>

Ahh. I see. You prefer games where everyone is a S+B deck.

>>(This point is made over and over. I've refuted it above - a 5 point vampire
and 5 points of pool are two different things, especially in practice. So we
can debate it above. I've snipped the other rehashes of this dispute.)>>

Nope. 5 pool is a 5 point vampire. Without the 5 pool, you can never spend it
on a 5 point vampire. Thus, you are denied a 5 point vampire. Losing 5 pool
before it is a vampire is one less 5 point vampire you will ever make. Losing 5
pool (in the form of a vampire) after it is a vampire is one less 5 point
vampire you will ever have.

>>You may not find it to be effective and I won't argue with you about it. My
point was not to suggest Fame, used in this way, is a great tactic.>>

Fame is perfectly effective. I use it all the time. What it is effective for is
squeezing those last few pool out of your prey to oust them. What it is not
effective for is attempting to oust your prey by rescuing their vampires every
turn. You are much better off just killing stuff.

>>I won't dispute that they're good anti stealth & bleed decks. But as I
replied
to James Hamblin's post, I prefer the game find another "rock" to S&B's
"scissors"
rather than making this one more workable.>>

This one is perfectly workable. No one is trying to make it *more* workable.
They are just trying to diversify a bit. As it stands, if you want to make a
good combat deck, you make a Pot IG deck. That is your only option. Folks are
hoping that there can be other options. Not me, necessarily, but that is what
this all came out of.

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>Ian wrote:
><>
>
>Completely true, but not the point. We aren't here trying to prove that
>bleeding for 6 is more effective than blowing up a 6 point vampire. We are
>here
>trying to prove than under the best circumstances, blowing up a 6 point
>vampire
>has the same effect as a 6 point bleed.

What are the "best" circumstances? Whatever they are, they sound irrelevant to
any debate because blowing up the vampire will rarely have the same effect as
the bleed. It could be that blowing up the vampire is more or less effective,
but identically effective just doesn't happen that often in real games.

In one of your other posts you (ad infinitum) keep saying 6 pool = 6 pool, 5
pool = 5 pool, whatever. But, a 6 cap vampire isn't 6 pool. It was an
investment of 6 pool to get a minion in play that can act, react, etc. Nor is
6 pool necessarily 6 pool. When you lose 6 pool does matter. How much pool
you had when you lost it does matter - compare losing 6 pool when at 7 versus 6
pool when at 6.

>Under the worst circumstances (that 6 point vampire gets minion tapped for 6
>before it gets blown up), blowing up that 6 point vampire is considerably
>less
>effective than a 6 point bleed. No one is here debating that.

What was the original issue that sparked this diversion from S:CE hosers again?
Rush combat is/is not obnoxious or something? Rush combat has to destroy all
of its predator's and prey's minions because it can't do anything else to
survive and gain VPs?

Personally, I would like to see mild rush as a common feature in games. I
would not like to see decks that do nothing but rush. This applies similarly
to: plus bleed, votes, intercept, other?. I'd like to see the rushes and/or
the intercept combats result in some pain but not in crippling, one sided
fights. I'd like to see fewer extremes in the game. S:CE and IG are too
examples of extreme cards.

>remaining." There's no way you can control how much pool you're going
>to have or whether you're ever going to be able to get out any more

Remove the word "safely" and this is precisely what I do. I aim to spend a bit
less than 20 pool on bringing vampires out in most cases. Obviously, decks

> > more diversity. There will be more _kinds_ of combat decks -- there may
> > not be any more combat decks per se. And, even if combat decks become
> > more prominent, the metagame envrionment will adjust. Ventrue decks
> > with huge amounts of combat defense will become prominent. And then
> > those decks will get screwed when the metagame shifts away from combat.
> >
> > How is this a bad thing?
>
> It is a bad thing, because if all combatclans have access to S:CE hosers
> there'äs simply no reason anymore to include S:CE's as defence. S:CE will
> become obsolete since you use them to avoid combat clans, not exactly
> Malkavians and such a like. So please explain to why anyone would want to
> include S:CE in their deck then (ignore Majesty's untap effect since it's a
> secondary effect and most other S:CE cards that don't have this and they'd
> be useless).

There are S:CE hosers and then there are S:CE hosers. The most
effective combat decks seem to involve Immortal Grapple, since it's (a)
free, (b) usable at inferior, and (c) prevents the S:CE from being
played at all. But it's also hosed by maneuvers.

This is all beside the point. If another S:CE hoser gets printed, S:CE
isn't going to be more hosed. Now instead of having your S:CE hosed by
Immortal Grapple, maybe it's hosed by "Aid from Ferrets," the new
Animalism anti-S:CE card. The point is that, when putting S:CE in a
deck, you have to account for the anti-S:CE cards. Usually this means
putting in maneuvers.

It's important (to me anyway) that any hypothetical new anti-S:CE card
have some kind of drawback, like IG's range requirement or Thoughts
Betrayed's high cost. Without this, it becomes too easy to screw S:CE
and the balanced is tipped too far, IMO.

So assuming a balanced S:CE hoser gets printed, you'll still want to
play S:CE for the same reasons you want to play it now. You won't get
hosed any more unless the metagame shifts heavily in favor of combat.
