Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
>
> Fredrick wrote:
> >>If you can bleed someone for 5 on the first turn, I agree that that's
> approximately the effect it has. In practice, this is not the effect it has
> once mid-game hits. People recruit a certain number of vamps and leave as much
> pool as they're comfortable sitting on to prevent being ousted.>>
>
> Exactly. Generally one (I know I do) looks at the amount of pool they have,
> estimates what is a safe "cushion" of pool to sit on to avoid ousting, and then
> spends the rest on vampires. Assuming that X is your safe pool cushion, the
> amount you spend on vampires is (the amount you currently have)-X. If the
> amount you currently have is 6 less than it was before (because you were bled
> for 6), you are getting out 6 points less of vampires, or getting yourself 6
> points closer to ousting. Losing 6 pool is 6 points less of resources you have
> access to, regardless of *when* you lose the pool.

That's exactly incorrect. Losing 6 pool is *not* the same as losing a 6 cap
vampire once it's out: you can't shove that sucker back into the uncontrolled
area and get your 6 pool back. You just live with 6 less pool in your cushion.

> >>Bleeding for 5 mostly tends to have the effect of either ousting them or
> not.>>
>
> But if you don't lose that pool, you have the option of getting out another 5
> point vampire. You don't have to, but you can if you feel it is safe to do so.
> Without that 5 pool, you don't have this option at all.

You don't have the option but so? It's not like someone with 6 pool is going to
say, "Hey, I have a 5 cap vampire upside down so I might as well burn 5 to bring
it out." The 6 is their cushion. If they get bled for 5, they have one left
and they have to make do. Either way, that bleed for 5 is not the same as
destroying a 5 cap vampire.

> You can make all the situational examples in the world where losing 6 pool does
> not *necessarily* equate losing a 6 point vampire, but in the end, if you have
> 6 pool, you have access to 6 more points of resources than you did before.

No, I don't agree. If you're trying to state that you see that as "X blood worth
of resources" equal in value to approximately X pool, I'd say you're being simplistic
and naive and ignoring the way the game seems to work in real life. At least I would
say I've found the source of our dispute.

> If
> you lose 6 pool, you are losing a potential 6 points of vampires. Whether you
> lose this 6 pool before it is a vampire or after makes no difference in the
> long run.

It absolutely does. Even if it doesn't make a difference to the victim who loses
either (which it does), it sure makes a difference to his other opponent, who either
does or does not have to contend with the 6-cap that's currently out and ready to go.
Or not.

> >>Nor is a 6-cap necessarily _like_ bleeding for 6 if it got brought out and
> Minion Tapped.>>
>
> People keep bringing this up. It confuses me in this conversation--yes, if the
> minion tap goes off *before* the 6 point vampire is burned, you are in *much*
> better off than if you had been simply bled for 6. If I bleed you for 6, you
> lose 6 pool and have nothing to show for it. If I beat up a 6 point vampire who
> has been minion tapped, you still have 6 pool, *plus* a 6 point vampire who may
> or may not get burned. This is much less damaging than just losing 6 pool from
> a bleed in the first place. As I am attempting to illustrate how blowing up a 6
> point vampire is equivalent to being bled for 6, I fail to see how introducing
> the minion tap element does anything other than make the 6 point bleed seem
> *much* more effective than the Rush.

No one is trying to claim it a 6 point bleed isn't more effective than rush. The
trouble we're having in communicating is that you insist on looking that the game
only from the standpoint of counting resources and in terms of winning vs. losing.
You're missing the points I'm trying to make. Of course bleeding for 6 is more
effective - that's why stealth and bleed can be won with by morons and it takes
very good players to win with combat.

The point *I'm* trying to make isn't that combat is too effective. It's that combat
often gives arbitrary advantage to other players in the game besides the one using
it. I think that's bad.

You can't compare what torporizing a 6 cap does to a player vs. what a bleed for 6
does. The bleed is often more fatal in the long run. But in the short run, the
player continues to defend himself effective - as effectively as he can at least -
from whatever the other players on the board want to do to him.

> >>I'm also not sure where you're getting 3 actions for the cycle.>>
>
> Torporize/rescue/Torporize again for 6 pool loss (7, actually) with 3 actions.

Then rescue and torporize again is 2 actions - 2 actions in a cycle, OK?

Anyway, it's not the point. As I said, I'm not claiming Fame is currently the
best way for combat to go. I'm just holding it up as the prototype for the sorts
of combat-related card I'd like to see designed. So that combat decks don't have
to utterly destroy minions to be have a chance at being successful.

> >>But who benefits and what happens in the game in the interim?>>
>
> If you are playing correctly, you are benefiting. You seem to be under the
> impression that folks who play Rush decks do so with no logic or need to act in
> their own best interest.

I'm saying it's pretty difficult for them, WHATEVER their logical abilities, to
avoid benefiting other players by the actions they need to take to win the game.
If you destroy your predator's minion, it's not there to bleed you AND it's not
there to defend against his predator. You can cross table bleed to go correct
that imbalance, but it's hard. Generally, the reason these decks fail all the
time in the hands of mediocre players is just that the damn thing is hard to
work right. Because it's hard to work right without handing victory points to
a third party, THAT'S reason enough not to encourage it.

A lot of people have trouble with concept but I'll argue it with my dying
breath: if a card, tactic, or strategy makes the game suck, I don't give a
shit how balance it is. Just making the game suck is criminal enough.

I don't think rush combat decks are the worst thing of this nature to come down
the pike in the last 50 years (Blood Moon in Magic probably owns that title),
though I think intercept wall decks come close. I'm just saying I'm not in
favor of doing anything to prop this form of deck up.

> An undeserved advantage? If I am winning, who cares?

I care. For one thing, in this game victory points count (at least in
tournaments), so even if there's a tendency to slip an undeserved VP to your
grandpredator before sweeping the rest of the table, that's a raw deal for
those who don't happen to be your grandpredator. And *that*, of course,
assumes you're God and can always win with your wonderful combat deck.

> If I am letting other people win, I am not playing correctly.

Or maybe you got bad luck or maybe someone packed fortitude and outguessed
you in the metagame. Or maybe you *aren't* playing correctly. In any event,
chaos is chaos, no matter what causes it. In the final, of course, the one
with the most VPs to that point can use their advantage with strategy to
get a better result. In most games, though, sitting next to the combat deck (or
not) is just luck of the draw.

> >>I won't dispute that they're good anti stealth & bleed decks. But as I
> replied to James Hamblin's post, I prefer the game find another "rock" to S&B's
> "scissors" rather than making this one more workable.>>
>
> This one is perfectly workable. No one is trying to make it *more* workable.
> They are just trying to diversify a bit.

I think there's some dispute on that. I believe we started out with Ian expressing
regret that Immortal Grapple is the only effective combat counter to S:CE because it
leads to minion loss. So I perceive it's a question of saying, "We want to find
some way to make other clans (e.g. Assamites) have their own answer to S:CE. We
just don't want it to look like Immortal Grapple." If that's what you mean by
"diversify", fine.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >

> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> > > What should the combat deck do instead?
> >
> > You mean, "How, in my opinion, should combat cards be incorporated into the
> > game so they don't cause instability?"
>
> No, I mean: how should a deck dedicated to successful combat win the
> game, if not by destroying all of its prey's minions? I don't know what
> this whole argument is trying to accomplish; you seem dead-set on making
> all-combat decks impossible to play. I'm also not sure _why_ you want
> this.

Then you need to go back and reread the thread. This is a waste of time.
You're demanding that I defend things I never said and don't believe in.
I don't want to make all-combat decks impossible to play. I just don't want
to lift a finger to make such decks more viable, that's all.

> > What I'm saying is that I'd like more cards _like_ Fame
> > to show up in the mix so combat can be used productive to win victory points without
> > the absolute destruction of minions which causes so much instability.
>
> Even if more cards like Fame are printed, the existing combat decks will
> still exist.

Perhaps. But if they were useful enough to use with the existing combat cards and
make effective, viable decks out of, no one would have to worry about how viable
pure thug rush combat decks were. Which in my mind would be just fine.

> And if, like Fame, these cards require a weakening of the
> combat in some area, then they will not be used.

It all depends on how the card is designed. As always.

> > As for the Fame loop being "dangerous", no, you have not proved it any more dangerous
> > than any other strategy that doesn't involve messing with people's minions. Stealth
> > and Bleed is "dangerous" in exactly the same way.
>
> It's dangerous because messing with people's minions is how the combat
> deck defends itself. Any player with any deck should want to oust their
> prey as quickly as possible. Allowing your prey to take actions or
> otherwise "set up" is only going to hurt you.

As is true of any deck, including stealth and bleed and voting and anything except perhaps
a dedicated intercept deck. They all allow your prey to take actions and set up.

> > Allowing "more kinds" of combat decks is no more a priority than allowing
> > more kinds of decks that can use Malkavian prank.
>
> "Combat" is a common deck genre. Malk. Prank is a specific card.
> There's a huge difference.

Not for these purposes. The point is that it's something in the game that tends to increase
the randomness in its effects on others, even if they both do something positive for those
who use them.

> > As I've said elsewhere,
> > though, it does bother me that certain clans have dedicated combat *cards* that
> > are pretty much useless to play because of S:CE and the fact that they can't
> > do much about it. That strikes me as a waste of cardboard and should be
> > rectified. So we may not be that far apart on the particular issue of S:CE
> > hosers.
>
> Yeah, there will always be wallpaper cards. The fact that there are a
> bunch of combat cards which won't work because of S:CE isn't a reason to
> print a S:CE hoser.

Not a general S:CE hoser, no. But one which specifically makes that particular
"bunch" of combat cards useful would be reasonable, yes. My best result would
be to do it in a way that would make them useful for other purposes besides
just rush/KILL/CRUSH/DESTROY/rinse/repeat type decks.

> One problem I have is that it's hard to make an
> all-Gangrel combat deck, because Dog Pack is slow and expensive.
> Protean is a very combat-centric discipline, so maybe it should have a
> S:CE hoser. Then again, maybe not.

It should. I agree with you on this point.
>
> > > Whatever "destabilization" is. Every deck tries to hurt its prey.
> > > Hurting your prey weakens them, and makes them less able to hurt _their_
> > > prey.
> >
> > "Destabilization", as it's being used all over this thread, refers to the
> > tendency to cause chaotic and unintended effects on the relationships between
> > other pairs of players. For instance, removing your predator's ability to defend
> > himself from his predator as you use rush combat to remove his ability to attack
> > and bleed you.
>
> The predator point is a valid one. As a Rush deck, you certainly don't
> want to weaken your predator so much that they can't defend themselves.
> On the other hand, sometimes you have no choice. If my predator is a
> weenie Dominate bleed deck, and I'm playing my Potence rush deck, I may
> well lose. I'll have to destroy every vampire my predator brings out,
> because I have no defense against bleeds for 6 from every minion. Given
> this, I may still survive and even get a VP or two. That's a lot better
> than other decks which just get rolled over by weenie Dom bleed.

Yep, I agree with all that. To which I'll add, this is a sad state of affairs:
outguess your predator in the metagame and the only result is that your grand predator
gets a free victory point. (And if *he's* a weenie Dom bleed deck, too?) This is
exactly the problem with looking to rush combat to serve as a "major leg" in the
three-legged metagame in Jyhad. It doesn't work very well.

> > > Well, once again you follow your standard argument sequence. Step 1:
> > > put forward outlandish argument filled with holes. Step 2: when others
> > > try to refute your argument and point out holes, you call them stupid
> > > for not agreeing with you. Step 3: when others continue to disagree,
> > > you quit arguing. Why do you even bother?
> >
> > I don't see much point in debating about this this way.
> > IMO, my argument was not outlandish, not "filled with holes",
>
> Well, of course not in _your_ opinion. But what about _my_ opinion?

Well, we're not going to convince each other so why do you bother bringing up
such opinions? What's the point?

> If you're not willing to accept that I have opinions which differ from
> yours, why bother having a discussion at all?

Precisely. You're the one who went off on my so-called "standard argument sequence".
It had no function. So, as I said, I don't see much much point in debating about
this this way. So again, I suggest we move on.

> > I simply said that if you cannot accept that combat causes
> > more destabilization of the game than strategies which attack a Meth's pool
> > directly, then we have nothing talk about. We simply disagree on how the game
> > plays, which is not something that we can resolve by arguing with each other.
>
> Since "destabilization" is something which I can't exactly define, much
> less measure, I can't accept it. But I think attacking someone's pool
> makes them turn backwards (or inward) just as much as attacking their
> minions.

But notice that one seldom attacks one's *predator's* pool as combat decks
attack their predator's minions. There's another reason it's impossible to
equate combat decks with bleed decks and attempt to draw comparisons between
bleeding and destroying minions. As for bleeding one's prey and having them
turn backwards, that happens. But they still have the minions they had before.
And the effect is often different if they think they can avoid being ousted
without defending with everything or that it won't make a difference what they
leave behind to defend. The prey without minions has no such choice to make.

> If I'm a combat deck, and I manage to kill all my prey's minions, I'm
> doing well. I'll almost certainly get that VP. Now, if this makes my
> grandprey stronger in the meantime, well, that's just part of life as a
> combat deck.

For reasons stated above, combat decks are often worse about this than
other types of decks in this sense.

> I don't care if they don't "deserve" to have their prey killed. I don't
> care if you think this "advantage" they've received is "unfair" or not.

Well, I do. As I said, it's a matter of taste. But this falls under the
category of (as stated in my response to Peter Bakija), "Things that make
the game suck." People getting victory points based on the pure luck of
where they sit tends to make Jyhad suck when they happen. Pure play-balance
isn't the only thing to worry about.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >

> > > Combats decks generally
> > > don't have standard vote or bleed defense; if you can usually survive
> > > the combats, you can probably oust them. How does that make someone
> > > across the table win?
> >
> > Because simply having the answers to the combat deck *doesn't* win you the
> > game.
>
> Simply having bleed defense doesn't win you the game, either.

Well, it depends on the type of bleed defense you have. Bleed bounce actually
does. But aside from that, most bleed defense isn't usually as involved as the
amount of combat defense you need to stay away from a combat deck. (Assuming
you're not using S:CE against a combat deck unprepared for S:CE, of course.)

> > You may survive the rushes. I suppose if it's your predator and he's
> > not bleeding you because he's been ineffective at torporizing your minions,
> > then that's good. But it doesn't help you oust your prey.
>
> Since when does being able to defend against your predator help you oust
> your prey?

You mean by bleeding or voting? If you don't have to dedicate much of your
deck to it, it simply gives you more time to do your ousting against a prey
you hope is less prepared for your particular means of ousting him.

> > And the deck
> > space you need to survive combat robs you of cards you could be using to
> > win the game.
>
> Having Deflections robs you of space you could be using for game-winning
> cards, too. What's the difference?

Numbers. Pure and simple.

> > > Why? It just doesn't follow. Just because there are more kinds of
> > > combat decks which can be viable doesn't mean the proportion of combat
> > > decks at tournaments will increase.
> >
> > Sure it does. Assuming there are more kinds, they must increase their number
> > at tournaments.
>
> No! You're completely wrong!!! According to this logic, every time an
> expansion gets printed, then since new decks are possible, then EVERY
> deck type must increase in proportion.

No, that's a bad analogy. When a new expansion gets printed, new types come and
go as they become playable or not in the new environment. But *YOU* just got through
saying there were "more kinds of combat decks". I naturally just ASSUMED (silly me)
that you were sanely referring to, more PLAYABLE kinds of combat decks - meaning more
types of playable combat decks came than went. Yet there's nothing in this suggestion
to state that there would be more types of playable bleed or vote or other types of
decks, merely more types of playable combat decks. Hence the rest of my reasoning.

> > In fact
> > The new decks can come from the ranks of people who played
> > other combat decks or from those who didn't.
>
> Wait, what were the people who were not playing combat decks before
> playing? Bleed decks? But wait, they also printed a new bleed card,
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

No, they didn't. Unless you're changing the proposal on me, which is a stinky,
sneak attack to pull. If you want to consider the concept of the new S:CE hoser
in the backdrop of Final Nights, which has new bleed cards and other new combat cards -
so even without it the new hoser there were going to be new combat decks - then
say so. In which case, I'd say we really can't predict anything about what the
environment after Final Nights so why make any statements about it at all?

Fred

I don't really agree. The thing is that as it is now, there's clans that
doesn't have access to S:CE hosers. This may be bad for that clan froma
combat perspective (e.g. Ravnos) but it also makes the S:CE worthwhile to
include because you know there's times you will play against combat decks
and that the S:CE will actually be useful. If you face a Brujah with IG's
then you know you'll almost never get to use your S:CE's. You could include
maneuvers as you said but that doesn't help, because any viable IG-deck has
tons of maneuvers in it to counter that (not hard with celerity either).
Since it's a combat deck it's fair to assume the combat deck can put in more
maneuvers (since they can combine the card with other effects, such as
additional strikes (Pursuit) shich makes the maneuver card useful evne in
environments where maneuvers aint needed, which isn't the case for the
S:CE-deck) than the S:CE can have, or else that S:CE deck will turn out to
be a pure defensive deck that can achieve nothing but avoid combat.
Now there's other S:CE hosers, but they're not any better for the S:CE-deck.
Some hosers mean that you have to put in just more S:CE than before (Psyche
and TT) which gain waters down S:CE to become pretty meaningless to include
in a deck (I'd rather go for Obedience or fortitude than S:CE for example).
Thoughts Betrayed has it's cost, but it's not that impossible to get the
spent blood back through Taste of Vitae. My point is (again) that more
hosers makes S:CE pretty much useless since every combat deck will include
them if they can (as it is now Ravnos for example really cannot) and this
will lead to that any deck who wants to avoid combat goes for Flesh of
Marble, Oebedince or Fortitude instead. While a hoser for Ravnos strengthens
them, it also means that the Setities for example get smacked even more
(because they neither have dom, fortitude or protean) and I don't think it's
fair to strenghten for example Ravnos at the cost of the setite (when they
already have big problems defending themselves). I jsut don't see how S:CE
would be any good in the future if all combat decks have easy access to S:CE
hosers. It would just be a waste of cardslots and it will lead to that
certain clans become more powerful than they already are. A good example is
the Venture, because they don't need their S:CE to still be good, since they
have fortitude as well. Now everyone who wants to survive in a tournament
against combat will start playing Ventrues because they can both survive
combat, vote AND bleed well. Everything you need to win. Now thye cannot
intercept well but they got defelctions so who cares? There's usually not
many other things but bleeds you really need to stop through blocking.

So again, tell me how S:CE will be USEFUL in the future of all combat decks
have S:CE hosers. You seemt o think they will be because you can exploit the
weakness of the particular hoser. In IG's case that would be maneuver. But
that's not true, because all hosers have different weaknesses so as a S:CE
player you need to get cards to exploit all of them which S:CE simply isn't
worth. It would be much easier to just stick with fortitude clans if you
fear combat, which makes things pretty boring even for combat decks if just
about every defensive deck has fortitude or protean in it. Just as most
defensive decks have S:CE's now. I agree a *few* more hosers could be good,
but ONLY if they're for Chimerstry and Quietus...certainly not for animalism
that is used by so many clans!

Fine. Having _vote_ defense doesn't win you the game. And it

Pat Ricochet wrote:
> The quote in question that Sorrow wanted to rub my nose in. So rubbed;
> my bad, there is a quote to support a "3 legs design" argument.

I disagree, if the reference to the text is any indication. The text quoted
by Sorrow refers to a "combat monster" as a deck that simply uses combat cards
to be fearsome and make your prey fear intercepting your bleeds and make your
predator fear bleeding you. If that's all a "combat deck" is supposed to be,
I'm fine with it. It's the translation of that into rush decks (I don't find
intercept decks very rewarding to the people that run them so I'm not going to
bother worrying about them) where the emphasis is on going out and starting
combat and blowing opposing minions to kingdom come that I question whether
needs to be supported or considered one of the three important fundamental
strategies.

> However, as many people have said, the game has gone on since then, and
> a large collective experience has grown on the game, not to mention a ton of
> new cards and vampires. (Leggy has proposed theories that the game is
> bigger and more complex than us, which I basically agree with) Arguing the
> Canon of Garfield at this stage is going to lead to even less than most
> arguments do.

Well, no, "because Garfield intended it that way" isn't really a reason to make
the game play as he envisioned it. Not if his vision has turned out to be a
problem. Still, those of us who've questioned the necessity of viewing the game
as having the three fundamental strategies of bleed, vote, and combat challenged
others who see the game that way to document that it was intended as such from
the start. At least for academic purposes, it's interesting to see how they
came to that point of view.

If this is the only reference to it from Garfield's writings, though, I'd say
it represents a bit of a misunderstanding where rush combat decks are concerned.

Fred

> > you're not using S:CE against a combat deck unprepared for S:CE, of course.)
>
> Most of the decks around here have some combat defense, mostly because I
> and my deck exist. But the defense they have doesn't detract from their
> deck's strategy; having a defense is _part_ of your strategy.

Agreed. But pure rush combat decks are geared to and, apart from S:CE, usually
can get past the amount of combat defense that doesn't detract from their
strategy. The have to. If just any Joe-schmuck deck could stop a Brujah rush
monster, it wouldn't ever be possible to win with. To defend against pure combat
takes up a great deal of deck space that, if you actually encounter the deck,
still leaves you at a disadvantage. If your prey is rush combat and you have
enough of whatever types of combat cards you need to survive it, you're still
really screwed if your predator if your predator is stealth/bleed. How are
you ever going to fit both combat and enough intercept or bleed bounce to
survive? This is something you could probably do reasonably enough if caught
between bleed and vote.

> > > Since when does being able to defend against your predator help you oust
> > > your prey?
> >
> > You mean by bleeding or voting? If you don't have to dedicate much of your
> > deck to it, it simply gives you more time to do your ousting against a prey
> > you hope is less prepared for your particular means of ousting him.
>
> There are many decks with minimal (or no) defenses, which just point
> forward and try to oust as quickly as possible. They make a risk,
> thinking that it's better to just remove all defenses and just be very,
> very fast. So you don't _have_ to dedicate a large amount of space to
> combat defense. It depends on what you want to do.

Sure. But it's hard to resolve where such decks belong in a reasonable
metagame. They may work well against bleed and vote as predators if they're
fast enough on offense and don't run into the wrong prey. But probably never
against rush combat. And you and Peter will likely say that's just losing the
metagame and I can't disagree with that. But it isn't what happens when you
lose the metagame that's at issue here. My point that we're debating here is
how you can't _win_ the metagame against combat as its neighbor. You just
make it hard on the combat deck without much benefit to yourself.

>
> > > Having Deflections robs you of space you could be using for game-winning
> > > cards, too. What's the difference?
> >
> > Numbers. Pure and simple.
>
> It's not like 30% of your deck has to be combat defense to stave off a
> rush deck. Some Maneuvers and some S:CE work fine.

First of all, the role of S:CE and S:CE hosers is what started the whole debate.
Now you're touching on the reason the game needs a one-card combat hoser that's
hard to prepare for without significantly weakening your combat deck for other
purposes.

As for maneuvers plus S:CE to get around Immortal Grapple, yes and no. If you
have a dogged rush combat deck, you maneuver away and use the S:CE so he just
holds on to the IM. But Brujah rush, for example, usually has more maneuvers
than you do unless you really do take up large amounts of your deck for combat
defense. And even so, the rush deck has the options of Psyches, which get a
lot more effective if you're prone to running out of S:CE _or_ of the maneuvers.
So to really plan for combat, yes, we are talking about a lot of deck space.

> > > > > Why? It just doesn't follow. Just because there are more kinds of
> > > > > combat decks which can be viable doesn't mean the proportion of combat
> > > > > decks at tournaments will increase.
> > > >
> > > > Sure it does. Assuming there are more kinds, they must increase their number
> > > > at tournaments.
> > >
> > > No! You're completely wrong!!! According to this logic, every time an
> > > expansion gets printed, then since new decks are possible, then EVERY
> > > deck type must increase in proportion.
> >
> > No, that's a bad analogy.
>
> It's not an analogy! It's simple mathematics. It's impossible for
> EVERY deck type to increase IN PROPORTION. The numbers have to add up
> to 100%, so they can't all go up.

At this point, I don't even know what point you're trying to make. I just said
that if more combat deck types are viable - meaning you've added more viable
combat decks than you've taking away in your modification of the game environment -
and the other types of other decks (stealth/bleed, vote, etc.) don't increase or
decrease - you didn't originally indicate that they did - then it's likely the number
of combat decks in tournaments overall increases. Not necessarily but it seems like
a pretty reasonable assumption. All this talk about what happens when whole new
expansions are printed is a completely different subject. Tell me what situation
you're talking (and DON'T CHANGE IT IN THE MIDDLE) and I'll tell you what I think
will happen.

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Ian wrote:
>>In one of your other posts you (ad infinitum)>>

What is the point of having an opinion if you aren't going to defend it?

>>keep saying 6 pool = 6 pool, 5 pool = 5 pool, whatever. But, a 6 cap vampire
isn't 6 pool.>>

It was at some point. When it *is* 6 pool (and not a 6 point vampire), and it
gets taken away from you, it never becomes a 6 point vampire. If it is a 6
point vampire (assuming it still has all of its blood on it) that gets burned,
it was a 6 point vampire, and now it is no longer. You are in the exact same
situation as if you had been bled for 6--without 6 pool, and without a 6 point
vampire.

>>What was the original issue that sparked this diversion from S:CE hosers
again?>>

I dunno. I stopped paying attention to that a long time ago...

>>Personally, I would like to see mild rush as a common feature in games. I
would not like to see decks that do nothing but rush.>>

Hmm. Sad. I love those decks. I love seeing those decks. The last tournament I
went to was teeming with those decks. It was great.

>>I'd like to see fewer extremes in the game. S:CE and IG are too examples of
extreme cards.>>

It's all about the dizzying highs and devestating lows for me. Pah on those
soft, creamy middles.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Fredrick wrote:
>>That's exactly incorrect. Losing 6 pool is *not* the same as losing a 6 cap
vampire once it's out: you can't shove that sucker back into the uncontrolled
area and get your 6 pool back. You just live with 6 less pool in your
cushion.>>

But if you lost that 6 pool earlier, you are down 6 pool. If you spend 6 pool
for a 6 pool vampire, you are also out 6 pool, but have a 6 point vampire. If
that vampire dissapears for whatever reason, you are in the exact same spot you
were in when you were bled for 6--without 6 pool, and without a 6 point
vampire.

>>You don't have the option but so? It's not like someone with 6 pool is going

to
say, "Hey, I have a 5 cap vampire upside down so I might as well burn 5 to
bring
it out." The 6 is their cushion. If they get bled for 5, they have one left
and they have to make do. Either way, that bleed for 5 is not the same as
destroying a 5 cap vampire.>>

Right. If I feel that my "safety cushion" is 14 pool, I'll spend 16 pool on
vampires. If I lose some of that 16 pool, I spend that much less on vampires.
If, on the second turn, I am bled for 5 (not that unlikely...), and I still
wish to maintain my safety cushion of 14 pool, I now only have 11 pool to spend
on vampires.

On the other hand, if I spend 16 pool on vampires, and get a 5 point vampire
burned (assuming I did not remove any blood from that vampire), I am in the
exact same spot--with a 14 pool cushion, and 11 points of vampires.

>>No, I don't agree. If you're trying to state that you see that as "X blood
worth
of resources" equal in value to approximately X pool, I'd say you're being
simplistic
and naive and ignoring the way the game seems to work in real life. At least I
would
say I've found the source of our dispute.>>

Hmm. I thought the source of our dispute was that I am stubborn and
tenacious...

Right. Having X pool gives you access to X resources. If you lose 6 pool, you
now have access to X-6 resources. If you have X pool in resources, and lose 6
points of resources, you now have access to X-6 resources.

>>No one is trying to claim it a 6 point bleed isn't more effective than rush.
The
trouble we're having in communicating is that you insist on looking that the
game
only from the standpoint of counting resources and in terms of winning vs.
losing.>>

Well, that pretty much describes the game--resources and winning or losing...

>>The point *I'm* trying to make isn't that combat is too effective. It's that
combat often gives arbitrary advantage to other players in the game besides the
one using it. I think that's bad.>>

I have conceded that point, but pointed (ahem...) out that non-combat decks are
perfectly capable of doing the exact same thing. If I am playing a speedy bleed
deck, and I bleed my prey for 15 by turn 4, it is very likely that my prey will
have very few vampires (i.e. resources) on the table. As a result, my grand
prey is getting a free ride for a few turns. Thus, I am giving my grand prey an
arbitrary advantage. Ignoring all other apsects of this post, please, please,
explain how you see this as somehow different than when a Rush deck demolishes
its prey's vampires and gives its grand prey the same free ride. Please.

>>You can't compare what torporizing a 6 cap does to a player vs. what a bleed
for 6 does.>>

I certainly can. I do it all the time. If I bleed you for 6, that is one fewer
6 point vampire you can bring out, regardless if you do or not. If I blow up a
6 point vampire, that is one fewer 6 point vampire you have brought out. The
end result is the same--without 6 pool, and without a 6 pool vampire.

>>I care. For one thing, in this game victory points count (at least in
tournaments), so even if there's a tendency to slip an undeserved VP to your
grandpredator before sweeping the rest of the table, that's a raw deal for
those who don't happen to be your grandpredator.>>

A raw deal? Everyone gets a raw deal in this game all the time. That is the
nature of the game. If I am sitting at a 5 player table, and I can arrange a
way to go 4-1 in vps, even if it means screwing some poor guy who just gets
caught in the cross fire, I'll do it every time. I do do it all the time. That
is the nature of the game.

>>And *that*, of course, assumes you're God and can always win with your
wonderful combat deck.>>

I love when people get snarky. Cracks me up.

>>Or maybe you got bad luck or maybe someone packed fortitude and outguessed
you in the metagame. Or maybe you *aren't* playing correctly. In any event,
chaos is chaos, no matter what causes it. In the final, of course, the one
with the most VPs to that point can use their advantage with strategy to
get a better result. In most games, though, sitting next to the combat deck
(or
not) is just luck of the draw.>>

Yes. Just like every other deck.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> James Hamblin wrote:
> >
> > Fine. Having _vote_ defense doesn't win you the game. And it
> > shouldn't. The fact that Deflections can make a bleed deck accidentally
> > kill the wrong person is one of the major drawbacks of that archetype.
>
> I don't think deflections kill the wrong person. There is some of that if the
> stealth/bleeder isn't careful about his bleeds

Careful how? "Oh, I won't ever bleed for 6 because that might get
deflected and oust the wrong person." That sounds like a pretty
mediocre strategy.

> but if so, the stealth/bleeder's
> grandprey is also guessing wrong in the metagame. At least he's involved in
> his own fate.

Not really. He's only involved if he has bounce or intercept, and
managed to stay untapped.

...and is the implication here that if you are the "victim" of a combat
deck, then you have no say in your fate? That's hogwash.

> But yea, as I said on the onset, there is chaos in the game. It's just that
> combat causes more than the usual amount.

How do you know?

> > Most of the decks around here have some combat defense, mostly because I
> > and my deck exist. But the defense they have doesn't detract from their
> > deck's strategy; having a defense is _part_ of your strategy.
>
> Agreed. But pure rush combat decks are geared to and, apart from S:CE, usually
> can get past the amount of combat defense that doesn't detract from their

> strategy. They have to.

Well, they have to try. There are many ways to shut down a combat deck
that don't require scores of cards in your deck. A non-additional
strike Potence deck is shut down by a single Superior Mettle, for
example. And now that IG doesn't last the whole combat, it's usually
enough to last the first round, or at least force the combat deck to
expend a _lot_ of resources to kill your vampire.

> If just any Joe-schmuck deck could stop a Brujah rush
> monster, it wouldn't ever be possible to win with.

Any Joe-schmuck deck with the right defenses can stop a Brujah rush
deck. If everyone at tournaments played with enough combat defense,
Rush decks _would_ be impossible to win with.

> To defend against pure combat
> takes up a great deal of deck space that, if you actually encounter the deck,
> still leaves you at a disadvantage.

How is it a disadvantage to be able to have the combat deck _not_ kill
you?

> If your prey is rush combat and you have
> enough of whatever types of combat cards you need to survive it, you're still
> really screwed if your predator if your predator is stealth/bleed.

Why? You should have bleed defense, too.

> How are
> you ever going to fit both combat and enough intercept or bleed bounce to
> survive?

Even if you put 15 Deflections in your deck, chances are you'll get
caught with your pants down at some point. Even if your deck is 50%
combat defense, the combat player will occasionally be able to make a
kill. What's the difference? Even if you can thwart every other
combat, that is often enough to stymie the combat deck; you'll still
have enough minions out to rescue, take damaging actions, etc.

> This is something you could probably do reasonably enough if caught
> between bleed and vote.

Only because intercept _can_ serve as both vote and bleed defense. What
if you're not using intercept at all? Same problem.

> > There are many decks with minimal (or no) defenses, which just point
> > forward and try to oust as quickly as possible. They make a risk,
> > thinking that it's better to just remove all defenses and just be very,
> > very fast. So you don't _have_ to dedicate a large amount of space to
> > combat defense. It depends on what you want to do.
>
> Sure. But it's hard to resolve where such decks belong in a reasonable
> metagame.

Huh? They belong in the hands of the person playing them.

> They may work well against bleed and vote as predators if they're
> fast enough on offense and don't run into the wrong prey. But probably never
> against rush combat.

Dude. The example I gave was specific. There is a fast
forward-pointing bleed deck in our group which can routinely oust my
combat deck. So probably _not_ never, huh?

> And you and Peter will likely say that's just losing the
> metagame and I can't disagree with that. But it isn't what happens when you
> lose the metagame that's at issue here. My point that we're debating here is
> how you can't _win_ the metagame against combat as its neighbor. You just
> make it hard on the combat deck without much benefit to yourself.

You can _totally_ win the metagame. In Ithaca, when almost every other
deck was a combat monster, Josh Duffin made a super-resilient Ventrue
deck that kicked all of our asses. Repeatedly. Then the metagame
shifted. That's how it works.

> > It's not like 30% of your deck has to be combat defense to stave off a
> > rush deck. Some Maneuvers and some S:CE work fine.
>
> First of all, the role of S:CE and S:CE hosers is what started the whole debate.
> Now you're touching on the reason the game needs a one-card combat hoser that's
> hard to prepare for without significantly weakening your combat deck for other
> purposes.

You're saying there needs to be a combat hoser? That's insane. I'll be
the first one to say combat is reasonably effective in the right hands,
but it certainly doesn't need to be hosed more.

> As for maneuvers plus S:CE to get around Immortal Grapple, yes and no. If you
> have a dogged rush combat deck, you maneuver away and use the S:CE so he just

> holds on to the IG.

But he used up a Rush action and probably some pre-range cards like Torn
Signpost or Fists of Death.

> But Brujah rush, for example, usually has more maneuvers
> than you do unless you really do take up large amounts of your deck for combat
> defense.

Most good Potence-based rush decks don't have that many maneuvers (not
counting Bum's Rush maneuvers). This too is a metagame choice; in most
situations the maneuvers just clog up your hand. You _want_ to be at
close, so if they don't maneuver, you don't get to play your maneuver
card.

> And even so, the rush deck has the options of Psyches,

Only if it can guarantee its vampires have CEL as well as pot/POT.
Which ups the average capacity. Which makes it more vulnerable to
speedy predators. And so on.

> which get a
> lot more effective if you're prone to running out of S:CE _or_ of the maneuvers.
> So to really plan for combat, yes, we are talking about a lot of deck space.

In order to be _completely_ unaffected by combat decks, then yes, you
need to devote lots of deck space to defense. But in practice, as I
mentioned above, being able to stop every other combat is usually
enough.

[snip me bashing my head against the wall]

> At this point, I don't even know what point you're trying to make.

I guess it was the former, then.

Here is the point. If new deck subtypes become viable (Ravnos Rush, for
example), it increases the total number of decks in each type. It does
_not_ necessarily increase the frequency with which decks of that type
appear at tournaments.

I don't see how you could possibly refute the previous paragraph.

I suspect that even if decks like "Ravnos Rush" become viable, the
number of combat decks at tournaments will largely stay the same.
They'll still be just as hard to play well and win with.

[snip more of you not understanding stuff]

>

> >
>

You seem to object strenuously to how combat decks win games. I guess I

> > Even if more cards like Fame are printed, the existing combat decks will

>

In what way will they not still exist?

> But if they were useful enough to use with the existing combat cards and
> make effective, viable decks out of, no one would have to worry about how viable
> pure thug rush combat decks were. Which in my mind would be just fine.

The "pure thug rush decks" would be just as effective as they are now.
Making cards which give combat decks alternate paths to victory would
only, if anything, make combat decks more effective. Aren't you against
that?

> > "Combat" is a common deck genre. Malk. Prank is a specific card.
> > There's a huge difference.
>
> Not for these purposes. The point is that it's something in the game that tends to
> increase the randomness in its effects on others, even if they both do something
> positive for those who use them.

Now who's comparing obviously different situations?

Malkavian Prank is extremely random. You can't get much more random
that "someone picks a number and someone else tries to guess it." Even
though a combat deck's actions can cause unforseen consequences, this is
far from "random."

> > Yeah, there will always be wallpaper cards. The fact that there are a
> > bunch of combat cards which won't work because of S:CE isn't a reason to
> > print a S:CE hoser.
>
> Not a general S:CE hoser, no. But one which specifically makes that particular
> "bunch" of combat cards useful would be reasonable, yes. My best result would
> be to do it in a way that would make them useful for other purposes besides
> just rush/KILL/CRUSH/DESTROY/rinse/repeat type decks.

Give a specific example of a "bunch" of combat cards you would like to
see be made effective.

> Yep, I agree with all that. To which I'll add, this is a sad state of affairs:
> outguess your predator in the metagame and the only result is that your grand
> predator gets a free victory point.

Not necessarily. Remember that the point is to _not_ cripple your
predator unless it's absolutely necessary (for exactly the reason you
state).

I don't see what this has to do with guessing and the metagame.

> (And if *he's* a weenie Dom bleed deck, too?)

Then you may have to rush one of _their_ minions to keep your predator
alive.

> This is exactly the problem with looking to rush combat to serve as a "major leg" in
> the three-legged metagame in Jyhad. It doesn't work very well.

Uh, OK. If you say so. I think you need to explain what this has to do
with the previous part.

> > Since "destabilization" is something which I can't exactly define, much
> > less measure, I can't accept it. But I think attacking someone's pool
> > makes them turn backwards (or inward) just as much as attacking their
> > minions.
>
> But notice that one seldom attacks one's *predator's* pool as combat decks
> attack their predator's minions.

Well, every deck must have _some_ way of defending itself. A combat
deck's defense is an active one; kill their vampires before they get a
chance to act against you. It is by far the most unpredictable and
volatile defense method. But a good player can make it work.

> There's another reason it's impossible to
> equate combat decks with bleed decks and attempt to draw comparisons between
> bleeding and destroying minions. As for bleeding one's prey and having them
> turn backwards, that happens. But they still have the minions they had before.
> And the effect is often different if they think they can avoid being ousted
> without defending with everything or that it won't make a difference what they
> leave behind to defend. The prey without minions has no such choice to make.

That's the way the combat deck wins. If your prey has no minions, they
can't keep you from killing them.

> > If I'm a combat deck, and I manage to kill all my prey's minions, I'm
> > doing well. I'll almost certainly get that VP. Now, if this makes my
> > grandprey stronger in the meantime, well, that's just part of life as a
> > combat deck.
>
> For reasons stated above, combat decks are often worse about this than
> other types of decks in this sense.

OK. So what?

> > I don't care if they don't "deserve" to have their prey killed. I don't
> > care if you think this "advantage" they've received is "unfair" or not.
>
> Well, I do. As I said, it's a matter of taste. But this falls under the
> category of (as stated in my response to Peter Bakija), "Things that make
> the game suck." People getting victory points based on the pure luck of
> where they sit tends to make Jyhad suck when they happen. Pure play-balance
> isn't the only thing to worry about.

This happens _all_ the time. It has _nothing_ to do with combat decks
specifically. That's where the "rock/paper/scissors" analogy comes
from. Many times another deck will be the Paper to your Rock, and
you'll just lose. My intercept deck is the Paper to my friend's weenie
Dominate deck's Rock. If I'm his prey, he can't possibly win. Neither
of these decks is a combat deck.

don't get something you didn't have before which is a major difference. A
similar thing are stocks, you haven't made a profit on a stock until you
actually sell it (with profit). Simply owning a stock that has gone up 100%
haven't made you go profit or gain *anything* because in theory the stock
could fall 50% the very next second. That's also why you don't pay tax (for
those countries who have profit taxes on stocks) until you sell the stock
and made an actual profit.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> >
> > I don't want to make all-combat decks impossible to play. I just don't want
> > to lift a finger to make such decks more viable, that's all.
>
> You seem to object strenuously to how combat decks win games. I guess I
> misinterpreted your objectives.

That's correct.

>
> > > Even if more cards like Fame are printed, the existing combat decks will
> > > still exist.
> >
> > Perhaps.
>
> In what way will they not still exist?

The "perhaps" was not intended to dispute that they still might exist. If combat-
oriented player decide to use the alternate paths to victory because they just like
playing combat-oriented decks but want a better chance to win, then you wouldn't
see as many of the rush-type combat decks.

> > But if they were useful enough to use with the existing combat cards and
> > make effective, viable decks out of, no one would have to worry about how viable
> > pure thug rush combat decks were. Which in my mind would be just fine.
>
> The "pure thug rush decks" would be just as effective as they are now.
> Making cards which give combat decks alternate paths to victory would
> only, if anything, make combat decks more effective. Aren't you against
> that?

You should understand the answer to that by now. Think that through, yourself. At
the top, you indicated that you understood my problem was with "how combat decks win
games" - i.e., by destroying opposing minions leaving the victim player helpless against
both the combat deck and his other opponent's action thus creating instability. If
combat decks do not win by these means but some other means (e.g. Fame cycles destroying
victim's pool), obviously I'm not against that. It's not what I'm objecting to.

> > > "Combat" is a common deck genre. Malk. Prank is a specific card.
> > > There's a huge difference.
> >
> > Not for these purposes. The point is that it's something in the game that tends to
> > increase the randomness in its effects on others, even if they both do something
> > positive for those who use them.
>
> Now who's comparing obviously different situations?

You have to understand the point of the comparison. No two different situations are
the same, by definition. Malkavian Prank and rush combat strategies share one thing
common, which is the thing I'm objecting to.

> Malkavian Prank is extremely random. You can't get much more random
> that "someone picks a number and someone else tries to guess it." Even
> though a combat deck's actions can cause unforseen consequences, this is
> far from "random."

It's not exactly "random" in the same way, granted. But it has essentially random
effects in that you really don't know beforehand what your victim's other neighbor
is going to do when you blow up your victim's minions. If you did, you could adjust
your deck and tactics to compensate and make the results of playing combat decks much
more predictable than I perceive they are now.

> > > Yeah, there will always be wallpaper cards. The fact that there are a
> > > bunch of combat cards which won't work because of S:CE isn't a reason to
> > > print a S:CE hoser.
> >
> > Not a general S:CE hoser, no. But one which specifically makes that particular
> > "bunch" of combat cards useful would be reasonable, yes. My best result would
> > be to do it in a way that would make them useful for other purposes besides
> > just rush/KILL/CRUSH/DESTROY/rinse/repeat type decks.
>
> Give a specific example of a "bunch" of combat cards you would like to
> see be made effective.

Assamite combat cards. Gangrel combat cards.

> > Yep, I agree with all that. To which I'll add, this is a sad state of affairs:
> > outguess your predator in the metagame and the only result is that your grand
> > predator gets a free victory point.
>
> Not necessarily.

In this situation - combat with a stealth/bleed predator, it is. I was talking about
this situation exactly.

> I don't see what this has to do with guessing and the metagame.

Well, I've touched on it a number of times but OK, I'll repeat myself again much more
explicitly so you'll have a chance to understand:

The metagame is about guessing. You guess what you think will work based on your
experience with whatever group of people you're about to play with and your opponents
do likewise. The thinking is that this is a matrix game: guess right and you're supposed
to be rewarded. Guess wrong and you get punished. The trouble I find with combat is
that its neighbors seldom get rewarded no matter what they guess. If they guess right
vs. the combat deck, much of the payoff still seems to go to the guys across the table,
who in fact tend to get paid off no matter whether the combat decks neighbors guess
right or wrong. Combat decks are just bad news to sit next to and good news to set
across from, no matter whether they themselves win or lose.

Of course, if the combat deck does well, that's always somewhat bad for the guys across
the table in the same way that if anyone on a table really does well, it's bad for
everyone else. But relatively speaking, it's much worse for the combat deck's neighbors
because the guys across the table at least have some chance of grabbing a VP before
getting sucked under.

I don't find this works the same way with any other deck - with one exception - where
you tend to have a chance to get rewarded well if you guess right vs. your neighbor.
The exception is intercept wall decks (whether combat-oriented or just something like
Obedience and untap or Majesty and untap) which don't do that much for themselves,
totally screw their predators, and may or may not screw with their prey depending on
how much the prey's deck depends on undirected actions. Intercept wall decks, in my
experience, just don't win period and they almost always take their predator down with
them.

> > > Since "destabilization" is something which I can't exactly define, much
> > > less measure, I can't accept it. But I think attacking someone's pool
> > > makes them turn backwards (or inward) just as much as attacking their
> > > minions.
> >
> > But notice that one seldom attacks one's *predator's* pool as combat decks
> > attack their predator's minions.
>
> Well, every deck must have _some_ way of defending itself. A combat
> deck's defense is an active one; kill their vampires before they get a
> chance to act against you. It is by far the most unpredictable and
> volatile defense method. But a good player can make it work.

Yea, I understand. It's just the additional instability (and I'll grant it's
_additional_ instability over and above the chaos that already exists in the
game) that I don't personally care for.

> > > If I'm a combat deck, and I manage to kill all my prey's minions, I'm
> > > doing well. I'll almost certainly get that VP. Now, if this makes my
> > > grandprey stronger in the meantime, well, that's just part of life as a
> > > combat deck.
> >
> > For reasons stated above, combat decks are often worse about this than
> > other types of decks in this sense.
>
> OK. So what?

Same as anything else people don't like in the game. If it's just me, screw it.
But I hear others (e.g. Ian) don't really care for it either it. If it's a lot
of people, White Wolf would want to consider carefully to whether this is really
the type of game they want to design cards for and facilitate.

> > > I don't care if they don't "deserve" to have their prey killed. I don't
> > > care if you think this "advantage" they've received is "unfair" or not.
> >
> > Well, I do. As I said, it's a matter of taste. But this falls under the
> > category of (as stated in my response to Peter Bakija), "Things that make
> > the game suck." People getting victory points based on the pure luck of
> > where they sit tends to make Jyhad suck when they happen. Pure play-balance
> > isn't the only thing to worry about.
>
> This happens _all_ the time. It has _nothing_ to do with combat decks
> specifically.

What happens "all the time"? Luck? You're failing to make a distinction.
The luck of the metagame is a necessary element to CCGs. The luck of having
to sit next to someone who happens to be playing a specific type of deck that's
always bad news to its neighbors, on the other hand, is not necessary.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:

>
> Fredrick wrote:
>
> Right. If I feel that my "safety cushion" is 14 pool, I'll spend 16 pool on
> vampires. If I lose some of that 16 pool, I spend that much less on vampires.
> If, on the second turn, I am bled for 5 (not that unlikely...), and I still
> wish to maintain my safety cushion of 14 pool, I now only have 11 pool to spend
> on vampires.

Again (believe I made this point elsewhere multiple times), that's fine if the
bleeds come early enough to make that decision. But once the 16 pool is already
spent on vampires, you can't put them back in the uncontrolled area and retrieve
your pool. That's what I meant by "mid or late game".

...

> >>No one is trying to claim it a 6 point bleed isn't more effective than rush.
> The trouble we're having in communicating is that you insist on looking that the
> game only from the standpoint of counting resources and in terms of winning vs.
> losing.>>
>
> Well, that pretty much describes the game--resources and winning or losing...

Not really. It's a multiplayer game, which makes things a lot more complex
because the way the players play has _varying_ effects on the other players in the
game. And I emphasize "varying" to signify that the way play has an effect which
varies from one player to the next in the same game. How this works can be more
fun or less fun depending on the way the game plays. I find the effects that rush
combat has on the game to be less fun in this sense.

> >>The point *I'm* trying to make isn't that combat is too effective. It's that
> combat often gives arbitrary advantage to other players in the game besides the
> one using it. I think that's bad.>>
>
> I have conceded that point, but pointed (ahem...) out that non-combat decks are
> perfectly capable of doing the exact same thing. If I am playing a speedy bleed
> deck, and I bleed my prey for 15 by turn 4, it is very likely that my prey will
> have very few vampires (i.e. resources) on the table. As a result, my grand
> prey is getting a free ride for a few turns. Thus, I am giving my grand prey an
> arbitrary advantage. Ignoring all other apsects of this post, please, please,
> explain how you see this as somehow different than when a Rush deck demolishes
> its prey's vampires and gives its grand prey the same free ride. Please.

Just pure play experience. You just often don't see the bleed or vote deck demolish
its prey's resources so quickly that they don't even have a chance. And such
decks do not usually attack their predator's resources at all (or at least not very
much compared to rushing backwards), giving their predator a fighting chance to
outrace them if nothing else.

> >>I care. For one thing, in this game victory points count (at least in
> tournaments), so even if there's a tendency to slip an undeserved VP to your
> grandpredator before sweeping the rest of the table, that's a raw deal for
> those who don't happen to be your grandpredator.>>
>
> A raw deal? Everyone gets a raw deal in this game all the time. That is the
> nature of the game. If I am sitting at a 5 player table, and I can arrange a
> way to go 4-1 in vps, even if it means screwing some poor guy who just gets
> caught in the cross fire, I'll do it every time. I do do it all the time. That
> is the nature of the game.

Combat decks make it significantly worse. We'll never prevent sickness and
injury altogether either but we still put a ton of effort into medicine. Go
figure. Some problems can't be solved, such as the game having randomness.
But there's necessary randomness and UNnecessary randomness. And I put rush
combat decks into the latter class.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> > > Fine. Having _vote_ defense doesn't win you the game. And it
> > > shouldn't. The fact that Deflections can make a bleed deck accidentally
> > > kill the wrong person is one of the major drawbacks of that archetype.
> >
> > I don't think deflections kill the wrong person. There is some of that if the
> > stealth/bleeder isn't careful about his bleeds
>
> Careful how? "Oh, I won't ever bleed for 6 because that might get
> deflected and oust the wrong person." That sounds like a pretty
> mediocre strategy.

I don't know what you do when you have a stealth bleed deck and hit a prey
with bleed bounce. Personally, I watch how much I'm bleeding for with each
given vampire. Yes, I refuse to bleed for 6 in this situation. I will keep
my bleed for maybe 2 or 3 or maybe only 1 if my grandprey is teetering on the
edge.

> > but if so, the stealth/bleeder's
> > grandprey is also guessing wrong in the metagame. At least he's involved in
> > his own fate.
>
> Not really. He's only involved if he has bounce or intercept, and
> managed to stay untapped.

Oh cripes, this is not rocket science. He's involved the same way anyone's
involved in the metagame. You plan for your defense against stealth bleed.
I'm just saying that the same defense comes into play whether it's your
predator's bleed or your grandpredator's deflected bleeds.

> ...and is the implication here that if you are the "victim" of a combat
> deck, then you have no say in your fate? That's hogwash.

Nope. That's the point I'm making about combat decks. You can plan for them
but you don't get as much of a metagame payout if you guess right. This is
a point of discussion below.

> > > Most of the decks around here have some combat defense, mostly because I
> > > and my deck exist. But the defense they have doesn't detract from their
> > > deck's strategy; having a defense is _part_ of your strategy.
> >
> > Agreed. But pure rush combat decks are geared to and, apart from S:CE, usually
> > can get past the amount of combat defense that doesn't detract from their
> > strategy. They have to.
>
> Well, they have to try. There are many ways to shut down a combat deck
> that don't require scores of cards in your deck. A non-additional
> strike Potence deck is shut down by a single Superior Mettle, for
> example.

There's various fortitude cards that will shut down a combat deck for a
whole combat but none of them that you would sanely include in large numbers
just for one type of combat deck.

> And now that IG doesn't last the whole combat, it's usually
> enough to last the first round, or at least force the combat deck to
> expend a _lot_ of resources to kill your vampire.

I'm not sure what this has to do with not using lots of cards to defend
against a combat deck. The point isn't about making the combat decks lose.
It's about gaining advantage from the fact that the combat deck is your
neighbor.

> > If just any Joe-schmuck deck could stop a Brujah rush
> > monster, it wouldn't ever be possible to win with.
>
> Any Joe-schmuck deck with the right defenses can stop a Brujah rush
> deck.

Stopping the deck is one thing. But having a deck that wins *because* a
Brujah combat deck sat next to it is a different thing. Especially in the
context of it being reasonable against other types of decks. That is,
it's well-known in most CCGs that even though deck X may have a nemesis,
call it deck Y, which hoses it doesn't imply that deck X isn't overpowered.
(Please go through the whole paragraph and don't jump to respond that
combat decks aren't overpowered. I know that.) If deck Y isn't reasonable
to play against anything else, it really isn't much of a hoser. In the
case of combat decks, it isn't that they're overpowered. It's just that
anything you might play that might possibly make it a positive advantage
to be between two combat decks would get slaughtered by anything else.
Mostly, in the metagame you just try to do things to _survive_ a combat
deck. But I've never found a way to survive a dedicated rush combat deck
that works against anything else at all.

> If everyone at tournaments played with enough combat defense,
> Rush decks _would_ be impossible to win with.

But that wouldn't help their neighbors. It would be the players across
the table that would benefit, as always.

> > If your prey is rush combat and you have
> > enough of whatever types of combat cards you need to survive it, you're still

> > really screwed if your predator if your predator is stealth/bleed. How are

> > you ever going to fit both combat and enough intercept or bleed bounce to
> > survive?
>
> Even if you put 15 Deflections in your deck, chances are you'll get
> caught with your pants down at some point. Even if your deck is 50%
> combat defense, the combat player will occasionally be able to make a
> kill. What's the difference?

What do you need to know? The difference is that you usually *WON'T* get
caught with your pants down against bleed instead of being getting caught
with your pants down ALL THE TIME. The difference is the combat player
making an occasional kill rather than ripping you apart from the first
action. That's plenty of difference for me.

> > This is something you could probably do reasonably enough if caught
> > between bleed and vote.
>
> Only because intercept _can_ serve as both vote and bleed defense.

That's not what I meant. You can also fit both bleed bounce and various
vote-only defenses (e.g. Delaying Tactics, your own voting vamps and vote-
producing cards, both masters and reaction cards and so forth) in the
same deck.

> > > There are many decks with minimal (or no) defenses, which just point
> > > forward and try to oust as quickly as possible. They make a risk,
> > > thinking that it's better to just remove all defenses and just be very,
> > > very fast. So you don't _have_ to dedicate a large amount of space to
> > > combat defense. It depends on what you want to do.
> >
> > Sure. But it's hard to resolve where such decks belong in a reasonable

> > metagame. They may work well against bleed and vote as predators if they're

> > fast enough on offense and don't run into the wrong prey. But probably never
> > against rush combat.
>
> Dude. The example I gave was specific. There is a fast
> forward-pointing bleed deck in our group which can routinely oust my
> combat deck. So probably _not_ never, huh?

It depends on your combat deck, I guess. Unless the combat deck is based on
larger vampires, I've never seen a weeny bleed deck that works well enough against
a combat deck. The combat deck just rushes and eats them too fast for them to
make much headway - even if you bring 4 out in the same turn.

I guess this an example of differing perceptions. This is completely outside
of my experience. Or maybe the problem is your combat deck, I don't know. It
doesn't seem like a reasonable claim to me.

> > And you and Peter will likely say that's just losing the
> > metagame and I can't disagree with that. But it isn't what happens when you
> > lose the metagame that's at issue here. My point that we're debating here is
> > how you can't _win_ the metagame against combat as its neighbor. You just
> > make it hard on the combat deck without much benefit to yourself.
>
> You can _totally_ win the metagame. In Ithaca, when almost every other
> deck was a combat monster, Josh Duffin made a super-resilient Ventrue
> deck that kicked all of our asses. Repeatedly. Then the metagame
> shifted. That's how it works.

This is irrelevant to the point I'm making. If the rest of the table is combat
decks then the same disadvantage of having a combat deck as neighbor exists
everywhere so it cancels itself out. And yes, if someone's playing the combat-
hoser strategy it stands to reason he'd do well. But in a metagame environment
not dominated by combat, none of this matters. It's _still_ a pure disadvantage
to sit down next to a combat deck except with the combat-hoser deck, which will
be too disadvantaged at any other times to really bother using.

> > > It's not like 30% of your deck has to be combat defense to stave off a
> > > rush deck. Some Maneuvers and some S:CE work fine.
> >
> > First of all, the role of S:CE and S:CE hosers is what started the whole debate.
> > Now you're touching on the reason the game needs a one-card combat hoser that's
> > hard to prepare for without significantly weakening your combat deck for other
> > purposes.
>
> You're saying there needs to be a combat hoser? That's insane. I'll be
> the first one to say combat is reasonably effective in the right hands,
> but it certainly doesn't need to be hosed more.

Again, that's because you insist on looking at the game only in terms of which decks
have how much chance to win. I'm looking at the game in terms of the amount of
chaos caused by the different deck types. I agree, in terms of deck advantage
combat does not need to be hosed more. In terms of how to plan a deck that's a
reasonable metagame choice and wins *because* it's next to a combat deck, combat
decks do indeed need to be hosed more. The answer is not to worry about how much
chance rush combat decks have to win the game and find some other answer to stealth/bleed
decks.

> Here is the point. If new deck subtypes become viable (Ravnos Rush, for
> example), it increases the total number of decks in each type. It does
> _not_ necessarily increase the frequency with which decks of that type
> appear at tournaments.

It certain doesn't decrease them. I already conceded (in the middle of
all that text that you went off on) that it might not increase them, though
that strikes me as unlikely. Classifying deck types into "subtypes" and stating
that the overall decks in the type might not increase in number is implicitly
suggesting that the only ones interested in playing the deck are those who already
play decks of that type. My perception of the reality of CCGs is that if a new
deck type becomes viable, it will find players who formerly played decks of
completely different natures. Maybe some players are stuck on stealth/bleed or
voting decks (or bloat or whatever), but a lot of people - me for instance - will
play anything that seems viable. Thus you will pretty much automatically see
at least a few players move from other types of decks to the new one and can't
help but increase the number of combat decks in general. By how much is debatable.

Fred

In general, if I didn't want people like James to call me an idiot, I wouldn't
post. That's part and parcel of the game. You want to express an opinion
about something, it can and will be held up for ridicule by those who disagree.

Still, I don't think such comments get one anywhere in the long run. I do
it when I'm frustrated with trying to get something across. Ironically (but
likely not coincidentally), I have the exact same issue with James: that I
make the same point over and over and he still asks the exact same questions
of me that seem to ignore that point from the last post...and the post before that.

It's no use pointing fingers and blaming each other for out lack of ability
to communicate. I would say we both need to open our minds and listen to other
person but I'd like to think we're already trying to do just that. So failing
that answer, my instinct is do whatever I can to move the discussion along with
each post so we're not arguing about the exact same damn thing we were in the
last exchange of posts. (It can be hard, though...)

Messages.Body:
Fredrick wrote:
>>Again (believe I made this point elsewhere multiple times),>>

Of course you made it multiple times--I just chose to not accept it as a valid
one :-)

>>that's fine if the bleeds come early enough to make that decision. But once
the 16 pool is already spent on vampires, you can't put them back in the
uncontrolled area and retrieve your pool. That's what I meant by "mid or late
game".>>

That doesn't matter one way or the other. Bleed decks kill you by denyng you
resources--your pool. If you lose it now or later, it is still less pool you
have to spend on stuff you want. If you aren't ever bled for anything, you will
have a lot more stuff/resources (vampires, master cards, whatever) than if you
are bled for a lot. It doesn't matter when you lose the pool--if you lose it
early, you lose the access to the resources early. If you lose the pool late,
you lose access to the resources later. It doesn't matter. Each pool you lose
is one less pool you have to spend on something useful.

Rush decks kill you by denying you resources--your vampires. If you lose a
vampire, you lose a vampire that cost you X pool, you have lost X pool in
resources. The rush deck does it after the fact, while the bleed deck does it
before the fact. The end result is the same--you are denied resources.

>>Not really. It's a multiplayer game, which makes things a lot more complex
because the way the players play has _varying_ effects on the other players in
the
game. And I emphasize "varying" to signify that the way play has an effect
which
varies from one player to the next in the same game. How this works can be
more
fun or less fun depending on the way the game plays. I find the effects that
rush
combat has on the game to be less fun in this sense.>>

Which is a reasonable belief--I never claimed that it was *fun* getting whacked
by a Rush deck. In fact, it is not particularly fun at all. You sit around and
get your vampires killed, and then get ousted. That isn't the point. I am
completely unconcerned with whether this sort of deck is fun or not in this
context. It also isn't fun getting run over by a weenie bleed deck in 4 turns.
It also isn't particularly fun getting all of your vampires stolen by TotGP,
and sitting around till you are ousted. That certainly isn't what I'm
discussing here. I'm discussing what is *effective*, not what is *fun*.

>>Just pure play experience. You just often don't see the bleed or vote deck
demolish its prey's resources so quickly that they don't even have a chance.>>

I see that quite often, actually. If my predator is a well designed, quick
Dom/Obf deck, I can easily lose upwards of 15 pool by turn 3. Sure, if I have
bleed defenses, this won't happen, but on the other hand, if I have combat
defenses, I won't get all my vampires killed, either.

>>And such decks do not usually attack their predator's resources at all (or at
least not very much compared to rushing backwards), giving their predator a
fighting chance to outrace them if nothing else.>>

So? VTES is a mutli-player game, and by virtue of this, you deal with multiple
players. You have two neighbors in every game. Some people are happy simply
interacting with their prey, and leaving their predator to do whatever they
want. Some are not. If killing my predator keeps me alive and helps me win, I
will kill them. If they feel they are getting a raw deal (because I'm not
simply leaving them alone), that is sad, but I'm certainly not going to stop
killing them. You should expect that both of the players sitting next to you
are going to interact with you. Perhaps they'll intercpet your actions. Perhaps
they'll deflect all of your bleeds. Perhaps they'll beat up your vampires.
Expecting that your prey is going to leave you alone strikes me as a bad idea.

>>Combat decks make it significantly worse. We'll never prevent sickness and
injury altogether either but we still put a ton of effort into medicine. Go
figure. Some problems can't be solved, such as the game having randomness.
But there's necessary randomness and UNnecessary randomness. And I put rush
combat decks into the latter class.>>

I see. You don't like Rush decks, and you don't like intercept decks. You
basically don't seem to like any situation where a player can have any
significant impact upon their predator at all, as you see this as "random".
Check. You don't like situations where your grand predator gets an "undeserved
advantage", because you did something bad to your predator. Check.



Messages.Author: Roger Carhult
Messages.Body:

> Investigation worded that way :
> cost : 3 pool. Play when a vampire with DOM/PRE is trying to bleed you for
4

bleed.

he's

Ummm AI has a pool COST. If you had 10 pool you now have 7 pool left after

come true, you're still poorer than you were before. Gain = you're richer

> to prevent 3 damage. I don't want to bother about taxes or stock exchange.
> Preventing a huge bleed and burning a big bleeder at the same time IS a

No it isn't a gain. You prevent somehting that's is a prevent, not a gain.
