And I really hope you don't work with something involving economy =)

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> James Hamblin wrote:
> >
> > You seem to object strenuously to how combat decks win games. I guess I
> > misinterpreted your objectives.
>
> That's correct.

So let me try again; your objective is to provide a way to win with
combat which is _so_ much more effective than the current method that
people will largely stop playing with that method. Correct?

> The "perhaps" was not intended to dispute that they still might exist. If combat-
> oriented player decide to use the alternate paths to victory because they just like
> playing combat-oriented decks but want a better chance to win, then you wouldn't
> see as many of the rush-type combat decks.

It seems like we're splitting hairs here. Bruise and Bleed is a
sufficiently different way to "win using combat," but people still play
rush-type decks. There are a _lot_ of criteria this "new winning
method" would have to satisfy before people will give up rush decks.
For example:

* It must not be card-intensive. It must be a single card which is
either reusable for moderate effect, or usable once for great effect.
* It must provide an advantage which is repeatedly better than bleeding
for 1-2 per action. (For example, the "Fame loop" only provides 1.5
loss pool per action, usually at a cost of 2 blood from you, hence why
it's not that good.)

> > The "pure thug rush decks" would be just as effective as they are now.
> > Making cards which give combat decks alternate paths to victory would
> > only, if anything, make combat decks more effective. Aren't you against
> > that?

[snip you misunderstanding me]

What I mean is, the _existing_ rush combat decks will be just as
effective as they are now. This new method of victory must be more
effective for people to want to switch.

> > Malkavian Prank is extremely random. You can't get much more random
> > that "someone picks a number and someone else tries to guess it." Even
> > though a combat deck's actions can cause unforseen consequences, this is
> > far from "random."
>
> It's not exactly "random" in the same way, granted. But it has essentially random
> effects in that you really don't know beforehand what your victim's other neighbor
> is going to do when you blow up your victim's minions. If you did, you could adjust
> your deck and tactics to compensate and make the results of playing combat decks
> much more predictable than I perceive they are now.

I really don't like your use of the word "random" like this. The good
rush players can make the compensations you're talking about.

> > Give a specific example of a "bunch" of combat cards you would like to
> > see be made effective.
>
> Assamite combat cards. Gangrel combat cards.

Is it just me who doesn't see the Assamites as needing a S:CE hoser?
They have Psyche! What they need is a few more vampires with the right
skills.

Gangrel combat cards are already somewhat effective; at least they see
play. Wolf Claws is very common, and the maneuver/press cards are
played as well. You were talking about cards which are currently
_useless_.

> > > Yep, I agree with all that. To which I'll add, this is a sad state of affairs:
> > > outguess your predator in the metagame and the only result is that your grand
> > > predator gets a free victory point.
> >
> > Not necessarily.
>
> In this situation - combat with a stealth/bleed predator, it is. I was talking
> about this situation exactly.

It's not necessarily true that your grandpredator gets a VP. You make
it sound like a foregone conclusion, which it certainly is not. If
anything is "the problem" in this scenario, it's the weenie deck with no
defenses, not the combat deck.

> The metagame is about guessing.

I don't think it's that random. My conception of "the metagame" is: I
have a vision of what decks I think I'll be facing, and I'll plan my
defenses correctly. It's at worst an educated guess.

> You guess what you think will work based on your
> experience with whatever group of people you're about to play with and your
> opponents do likewise. The thinking is that this is a matrix game: guess right and
> you're supposed to be rewarded.

We have established that you don't think "not dying" is reward enough.
As much as you, for example, might plan on weenie decks being prominent
at the tournament, you may still only not die due to your planning.
Again, the combat deck is not the problem. It's your conception that
you deserve a reward for being smart and planning ahead.

> Guess wrong and you get punished. The trouble I find with combat is
> that its neighbors seldom get rewarded no matter what they guess. If they guess
> right vs. the combat deck, much of the payoff still seems to go to the guys across
> the table, who in fact tend to get paid off no matter whether the combat decks
> neighbors guess right or wrong. Combat decks are just bad news to sit next to and
> good news to set across from, no matter whether they themselves win or lose.

You've said all this before, and I've argued against it. Your reward is
that you don't die. You slow the combat deck down so that they can't
oust you, and get ousted by their predator instead. The people across
the table are irrelevant, much as they are between any other pair of
decks.

> Of course, if the combat deck does well, that's always somewhat bad for the guys
> across the table in the same way that if anyone on a table really does well, it's
> bad for everyone else. But relatively speaking, it's much worse for the combat
> deck's neighbors because the guys across the table at least have some chance of
> grabbing a VP before getting sucked under.

Any deck which is slow to oust has this problem. It's not specific to
combat.

> I don't find this works the same way with any other deck - with one exception -
> where you tend to have a chance to get rewarded well if you guess right vs. your
> neighbor. The exception is intercept wall decks (whether combat-oriented or just
> something like Obedience and untap or Majesty and untap) which don't do that much
> for themselves, totally screw their predators, and may or may not screw with their
> prey depending on how much the prey's deck depends on undirected actions. Intercept
> wall decks, in my experience, just don't win period and they almost always take
> their predator down with them.

If someone is playing a deck which can't win, then of course they're
going to screw up the table. Not all intercept decks have this
problem. Often, an intercept deck _can_ oust its prey, if it's built
correctly. You have no control over stupid people who are going to
screw up the game because they're not trying to win. Just because
stupid people can do more damage with a combat deck is no reason to
sanction the deck.

> > Well, every deck must have _some_ way of defending itself. A combat
> > deck's defense is an active one; kill their vampires before they get a
> > chance to act against you. It is by far the most unpredictable and
> > volatile defense method. But a good player can make it work.
>
> Yea, I understand. It's just the additional instability (and I'll grant it's
> _additional_ instability over and above the chaos that already exists in the
> game) that I don't personally care for.

You keep going back and forth on this. Are rush combat decks a
_problem_ for the game, or are they not? If so, then argue that point.
If this is just you not liking something, then I can safely pigeonhole
you with all the 4CL people.

> Same as anything else people don't like in the game. If it's just me, screw it.

See my previous paragraph.

> But I hear others (e.g. Ian) don't really care for it either it. If it's a lot
> of people, White Wolf would want to consider carefully to whether this is really
> the type of game they want to design cards for and facilitate.

It's been the same game for years and years. It would be highly
daunting and/or highly unstabilizing to make the kind of fundamental
change you seem to be advocating. Daunting to do it well, unstabilizing
if it is not done well.

> > > People getting victory points based on the pure luck of
> > > where they sit tends to make Jyhad suck when they happen. Pure play-balance
> > > isn't the only thing to worry about.
> >
> > This happens _all_ the time. It has _nothing_ to do with combat decks
> > specifically.
>
> What happens "all the time"?

"People getting victory points based on the pure luck of where they sit"

happens all the time. It has nothing to do with combat decks
specifically.

> The luck of having

> to sit next to someone who happens to be playing a specific type of deck that's
> always bad news to its neighbors, on the other hand, is not necessary.

Back to this. It is _not_ always bad news to sit next to a combat
deck. I have explained this repeatedly. Back in Ithaca, when everyone
had psychotic combat decks, Josh Duffin made a Ventrue deck with lots of
combat defense and wrecked us all. He _wanted_ to sit next to combat
deck; otherwise, all his combat defense cards went to waste. So, we
started making non-combat decks and mixing things up. And the metagame
evolved, as it's supposed to.



Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
>
> James Hamblin wrote:
> >
> > Careful how? "Oh, I won't ever bleed for 6 because that might get
> > deflected and oust the wrong person." That sounds like a pretty
> > mediocre strategy.
>
> I don't know what you do when you have a stealth bleed deck and hit a prey
> with bleed bounce. Personally, I watch how much I'm bleeding for with each
> given vampire. Yes, I refuse to bleed for 6 in this situation. I will keep
> my bleed for maybe 2 or 3 or maybe only 1 if my grandprey is teetering on the
> edge.

...which seems like a pretty mediocre strategy to me. As I said.

> > > but if so, the stealth/bleeder's
> > > grandprey is also guessing wrong in the metagame. At least he's involved in
> > > his own fate.
> >
> > Not really. He's only involved if he has bounce or intercept, and
> > managed to stay untapped.
>
> Oh cripes, this is not rocket science. He's involved the same way anyone's
> involved in the metagame. You plan for your defense against stealth bleed.

Just like you plan your defense against combat. Doesn't mean it will
always work.

> > Well, they have to try. There are many ways to shut down a combat deck
> > that don't require scores of cards in your deck. A non-additional
> > strike Potence deck is shut down by a single Superior Mettle, for
> > example.
>
> There's various fortitude cards that will shut down a combat deck for a
> whole combat but none of them that you would sanely include in large numbers
> just for one type of combat deck.

Once again I'm repeating myself: you don't need scores of combat defense
cards to screw a combat deck.

> > And now that IG doesn't last the whole combat, it's usually
> > enough to last the first round, or at least force the combat deck to
> > expend a _lot_ of resources to kill your vampire.
>
> I'm not sure what this has to do with not using lots of cards to defend
> against a combat deck. The point isn't about making the combat decks lose.
> It's about gaining advantage from the fact that the combat deck is your
> neighbor.

I guess I finally understand, though it seems psychotic. You're saying
you don't like rush decks, because there's no way to make a deck which
makes you say "hurray!" every time a combat deck sits down next to you?
That's insanity.

> Mostly, in the metagame you just try to do things to _survive_ a combat
> deck.

Surviving is good enough. If you can survive a combat deck, you neuter
it. If you can survive 1 out of every 2 or 3 combats, you stand a good
chance of beating it.

> But I've never found a way to survive a dedicated rush combat deck
> that works against anything else at all.

Why should _combat_ defense cards work against anything but a _combat_
deck? You seem to want Jyhad to be some kind of happy fairy land where
you get to not think and never get screwed.

> > If everyone at tournaments played with enough combat defense,
> > Rush decks _would_ be impossible to win with.
>
> But that wouldn't help their neighbors. It would be the players across
> the table that would benefit, as always.

So if I have a deck with lots of intercept, and my predator is a vote
deck which I'm able to completely shut down, how is that different?

> > Even if you put 15 Deflections in your deck, chances are you'll get
> > caught with your pants down at some point. Even if your deck is 50%
> > combat defense, the combat player will occasionally be able to make a
> > kill. What's the difference?
>
> What do you need to know? The difference is that you usually *WON'T* get
> caught with your pants down against bleed instead of being getting caught
> with your pants down ALL THE TIME. The difference is the combat player
> making an occasional kill rather than ripping you apart from the first
> action. That's plenty of difference for me.

Dude. You don't need to have gobs of combat cards to keep from getting
ripped apart. But there's no way to guarantee that you won't get caught
against either strategy. If combat decks are killing you _absolutely_
every time you get into a fight, then you must be playing with zero
combat defense.

> That's not what I meant. You can also fit both bleed bounce and various
> vote-only defenses (e.g. Delaying Tactics, your own voting vamps and vote-
> producing cards, both masters and reaction cards and so forth) in the
> same deck.

Then you can fit combat defense cards into the same deck.

OK, I agree that combat defense cards don't do much unless there's a
combat deck next to you. But that's part of the metagame. Your
Delaying Tactics and Dread Gazes don't do shit unless there's a vote
deck around, either.

> > Dude. The example I gave was specific. There is a fast
> > forward-pointing bleed deck in our group which can routinely oust my
> > combat deck. So probably _not_ never, huh?
>
> It depends on your combat deck, I guess. Unless the combat deck is based on
> larger vampires, I've never seen a weeny bleed deck that works well enough against
> a combat deck. The combat deck just rushes and eats them too fast for them to
> make much headway - even if you bring 4 out in the same turn.

It's not going to win every time. But it has a very good chance.
_Especially_ if the weenie player is smart and gets all their vampires
out all on the same turn.

> I guess this an example of differing perceptions. This is completely outside
> of my experience. Or maybe the problem is your combat deck, I don't know. It
> doesn't seem like a reasonable claim to me.

Yeah, that's right. I've only been playing rush combat decks since the
game was first released. Yeah, my deck must just be for shit. <sigh>

> > You're saying there needs to be a combat hoser? That's insane. I'll be
> > the first one to say combat is reasonably effective in the right hands,
> > but it certainly doesn't need to be hosed more.
>
> Again, that's because you insist on looking at the game only in terms of which decks
> have how much chance to win. I'm looking at the game in terms of the amount of
> chaos caused by the different deck types.

Well, I don't have a "chaosometer", so I can't use the magical chaos
scale to make judgements about the game. The more "trump cards" which
are released, the stupider this game will become. Archon Investigation
is a trump card which was totally unnecessary. The way to fix AI is not
to print an anti-AI card. There are many combat strategies, some of
which are screwed by S:CE, some by Fortitude, some by maneuvers, etc. A
better-than-S:CE trump card would be succeeded by a
better-than-Immortal-Grapple anti-trump, and so on. Then we'd really be
playing rock/paper/scissors.

> In terms of how to plan a deck that's a
> reasonable metagame choice and wins *because* it's next to a combat deck, combat
> decks do indeed need to be hosed more.

Why does such a deck need to exist? I don't ever sit down and say
"hurray! my predator is a malkavian stealth bleed deck!" Even if I have
Deflections and/or other bleed defense, that defense doesn't _make_ me
win.

> The answer is not to worry about how much chance rush combat decks have to win the
> game and find some other answer to stealth/bleed decks.

It's not like the raison d'etre for combat decks is "to kill
Malkavians." There's plenty of ways to do that already.

> I already conceded (in the middle of
> all that text that you went off on) that it might not increase them, though
> that strikes me as unlikely.

Then there's nothing more to argue. The rest of your paragraph is you
_still_ not understanding that 1+1=2. All I said was that the existence
of new combat cards would not NECESSARILY increase the frequency with
which combat decks appeared at tournaments. If the printing of new
cards was the only thing which caused such increases in frequency, then
by that logic _all_ decks would increase in frequency (percentage-wise)
after the release of every set, which is impossible, since the total
percentage must add up to 100%.

If you read that paragraph and still disagree, do us both a favor and
keep it to yourself, before I have to shoot myself.



which are screwed by S:CE, some by Fortitude, some by maneuvers, etc. A
better-than-S:CE trump card would be succeeded by a
better-than-Immortal-Grapple anti-trump, and so on. Then we'd really be
playing rock/paper/scissors.

> In terms of how to plan a deck that's a

> reasonable metagame choice and wins *because* it's next to a combat deck, combat
> decks do indeed need to be hosed more.

Why does such a deck need to exist? I don't ever sit down and say

"hurray! my predator is a malkavian stealth bleed deck!" Even if I have
Deflections and/or other bleed defense, that defense doesn't _make_ me
win.

> The answer is not to worry about how much chance rush combat decks have to win the

> game and find some other answer to stealth/bleed decks.

It's not like the raison d'etre for combat decks is "to kill

Malkavians." There's plenty of ways to do that already.

> I already conceded (in the middle of

> all that text that you went off on) that it might not increase them, though
> that strikes me as unlikely.

Then there's nothing more to argue. The rest of your paragraph is you

_still_ not understanding that 1+1=2. All I said was that the existence
of new combat cards would not NECESSARILY increase the frequency with
which combat decks appeared at tournaments. If the printing of new
cards was the only thing which caused such increases in frequency, then
by that logic _all_ decks would increase in frequency (percentage-wise)
after the release of every set, which is impossible, since the total
percentage must add up to 100%.

James

> That doesn't matter one way or the other. Bleed decks kill you by denyng
you
> resources--your pool.

<...>

it
> before the fact. The end result is the same--you are denied resources.

....must.... disagree.....

Simple maths:

6 pool = 6 pool

a 6-cap vamp= 6 pool + six transfers + a potential X actions + a potential Y
reactions

difference: six transfers + a potential X actions + a potential Y reactions

I know this is oversimplified. 6 pool can, for instance, potentially buy
stuff,etc.

V:TES is not M:TG. In Magic there's the possibility to do tons of stuff
without creatures, even to make creatureless decks. In V:TES the only thing
you can do without minions is play master cards.

Here lies IMO the biggest problem with rush decks: they deny you the chance
to do ANYTHING WHATSOEVER. Both vote and bleed decks attack your pool but
they leave their prey the chance to get VP's for himself and to react to
things happening on the table.

But, in the end, I just have to agree with legbiter: rush combat is not for
newbies or intelectually challenged veterans.

Jeroen

>>V:TES is not M:TG. In Magic there's the possibility to do tons of stuff

you can do without minions is play master cards.>>

No one has made any reference to M:TG in any of this thread.

>>Here lies IMO the biggest problem with rush decks: they deny you the chance

A) If you have combat defense, they don't do this.

B) Bleed decks do the exact same thing--if you are ousted in 4 turns by a S+B

do ANYTHING WHATSOEVER. 'Cause you are ousted. Thus most people plan on
defending themselves against bleed decks. If they have no bleed defense, and
run into a (fairly common) bleed deck, they are denied the chance to do
anything whatsoever--because they are quickly ousted. Rush decks work exactly
the same way--if you don't have defenses, you get destroyed, and quickly. Just

idea to have to include bleed defense, where they feel it is unreasonable and

let alone get a VP. 'Cause I'm dead. If I have no vote defense, and I sit next
to a weenie vote push deck, I will be ousted quickly. Again, I will not have

against this" equation. Most folks include some sort of bleed defense (bounce,
intercept, rampant pool gain, out race) in their deck strategy. Most folks
include some sort of vote defense (intercept, vote weight, delaying tactics,

>>But, in the end, I just have to agree with legbiter: rush combat is not for
newbies or intelectually challenged veterans.>>

Umm, ok. But vote decks, that can cause just as much random damage, are ok? How
about Anarch Revolt decks? I have seen Anarch Revolt cause *far* more "random"

I guess.

wrote:

>>>difference: six transfers + a potential X actions + a potential Y
>reactions>>
>
>If you still have the six pool ('cause it wasn't bled from you), you still have
>the option of getting the 6 point vampire. If you don't have the 6 pool, you
>don't.

...whether or not you were ever intending to get the 6 point vampire
in the first place. Bleed decks can hamstring you somewhat by
bleeding for tons early on. After enough turns, though, you
potentially already have the vampires you've intended to get out, and
now that bleed for 6 is, while still aggravating, not quite as
limiting. And you ALWAYS get to have your first-choice vampire who
can at least make the deck hobble along, no matter how much you're
bled for in the first three turns.

>If you are bled for 6, you are now without 6 pool, and without anything to show
>for it--no 6 point vampire, no other 6 points of resources. If you get a 6
>point vampire blown up, you are in the exact same spot--without 6 pool, and
>without anything to show for it.

For this paragraph, I'll define "blown up" as burned. If you have a 6
point vampire BURNED, you are in the position you mention: you have
effectively been bled for 6 at the 'start' of the game, making you
unable to get that 6 point vampire. However, there's an additional
cost: you might have chosen to get that specific 6 point vampire, and
passed up some other supporting vampires instead. This gives an
additional destabilizing effect to Rush decks, as opposed to bleed
decks. If I have Dolphin Black, Boy Toy, and Yorik out, and someone
poofs Dolphin, I no longer have any intercept capability until I fetch
another vampire with Auspex. If my only option is to influence out
Claven, then I've STILL lost my superior Auspex; and that probably
matters a great deal, since Eagle's Sight and a number of other toys
depend on AUS.

With one well-placed action, Rush can effectively remove a deck's
ability to function. If, in the situation above, I was the Rush
deck's predator, then he is probably almost REQUIRED to kill Dolphin
before he gets repeatedly bled for 4 at stealth. But in killing
Dolphin, he also removes my deck's ability to defend against my
predator effectively. Against a fast predator, I'm probably on a
death-spiral. So a 6-cap vampire being burned is generally worth much
more than 6 pool - situational costs invariably come into play here.

>Yes, you lose the transefers as well, but transfers are a renewable resource
>that cost you nothing, so kind of moot. And if you were bled for 6 instead, the
>use of the transfers was never even an option.
>
>Again. If I am bled for 6, that is a 6 point vampire I will never have. If I
>make a 6 point vampire, and it is blown up, I am in the same spot that I would
>have been if I had never made the 6 point vampire in the first place, and
>instead, bled for 6--without 6 pool and without a 6 point vampire.

No. You are screwed much worse, since you've lost the 6 point vampire
that you wanted/needed and probably don't have another copy of in your
uncontrolled region. If you had a bleed deck behind you, you simply
wouldn't get 6 pool worth of OTHER vampires. You would still get the
vampire you wanted, however. Again, in the above case, if I were bled
for 12 before I were able to get a vampire, I would still have gotten
Dolphin Black. Then I would have just failed to transfer out Boy Toy
or Yorik unless I thought I wasn't going to get bled for another 10.

Big difference.

Now, if we define 'blown up' as "sent to torpor", then we discover the
reason why Rush decks tend to not win. Vampires will come back unless
you kill ALL of their minions, so they are physically unable to
perform the rescue actions. In the above case, if you torporize
Dolphin, the first thing I'll do on my turn is rescue with Yorik. She
comes back out, and if I had only been Disarmed or had a Blood Doll
handy to blow through the straw, she'll be bleeding for 4 again at
stealth. In this case, I've merely lost 8 blood and 1 pool... which
is significantly less than 6 pool.

And if you kill ALL of someone's minions, then you definitely end
their game. This has an enormous destabilizing effect on the table;
if you kill all your prey's minions, your grandprey will have
completely free rein for the time it takes you to bleed out the
remaining 10+ pool. If you kill all your predator's minions, your
grand-predator will likely use the time to set up carefully so that he
blows through your predator and then you all in one turn. And if you
start rushing your grand-predator's minions, then you are going all
over the road and are starting to look like a "reckless" deck. I bet
I could turn a table against someone who was doing -that-, no matter
how necessary it was.

>>>Here lies IMO the biggest problem with rush decks: they deny you the chance
>to do ANYTHING WHATSOEVER.>>
>
>A) If you have combat defense, they don't do this.
>
>B) Bleed decks do the exact same thing--if you are ousted in 4 turns by a S+B
>deck that bleeds you sucessfully for 5 an action, you are denied the chance to
>do ANYTHING WHATSOEVER. 'Cause you are ousted. Thus most people plan on
>defending themselves against bleed decks. If they have no bleed defense, and
>run into a (fairly common) bleed deck, they are denied the chance to do
>anything whatsoever--because they are quickly ousted. Rush decks work exactly
>the same way--if you don't have defenses, you get destroyed, and quickly. Just
>like when you are sitting next to a bleed deck without bleed defense. The only
>difference is for some reason, people seem to think it is reasonable and a good
>idea to have to include bleed defense, where they feel it is unreasonable and
>unfair to have to include combat defense. Go figure.

It's easier to include bleed defense than it is combat defense.

To stop bleed decks cold, I simply include 6 Wakes and 8 Deflections.
The Wakes can be used for other things if nobody's behind me. If I'm
out of Wake, I leave a guy untapped. I don't always NEED to have both
cards in hand to survive. And most decks can be counted on to bleed
for 1, so I can chuck Deflections on those actions if nothing else.
The 14 cards I have to include to protect against bleed are not a
major opportunity cost.

To stop a Rush deck cold, I need to have about 30% of my deck be
combat defense. Note that the 14 cards mentioned above are
significantly short of 30% of even a 60-card deck... and most decks
are more than 60 cards. If I make it be REAL combat defense, then I'm
going to run into some trouble when I don't sit next to a Rush deck.
Mostly, I'm going to try desperately to get into combat so I can cycle
all my maneuvers, prevent cards, and S:CE that are cluttering my hand
and that normally just vanish without me making any effort when I sit
near Rush.

...This comes from the point of view of the combat deck, by the way.
=) I've found that if your deck has "light combat defense", it means
that I just have to use a little strategy and planning to thump your
guys, but I'll still get 'em... just a touch slower. You really need
about 30% of your deck being "go away" cards to seriously stop things,
and that's gonna be too much.

>I fail to see how Rush decks are exempt from the "I want to have defenses
>against this" equation. Most folks include some sort of bleed defense (bounce,
>intercept, rampant pool gain, out race) in their deck strategy. Most folks
>include some sort of vote defense (intercept, vote weight, delaying tactics,
>rampant pool gain) in their deck strategy. Few people include combat defense
>other than Majesty in their deck strategy. Why? You got me. I always assume it
>is because they want me to kill them.

This, by the way, is no longer an accurate assertion. The Atlanta
qualifier can be described in one word: messy. And I don't recall
seeing a single Majesty played all day.

-- Derek

simple: in a 90 card deck
bleed defence: say max. 8 cards (bounce and bloat)
vote defence: 2-3 cards + the bloat from above
rush defence: 8 against IG decks (manuevres and obedience), other rush
decks: another 6-8 S:CE. Exception when you play a deck with for: 10
prevention cards

with 10 cards you're defended against bleed AND vote, to protect yourself
from rush you'll need 14 cards. That would make a total of 24 purely
defensive cards (26.666666%) And because 8 of these cards only protect you
from 1 type of rush deck it's easy to see why they're the ones left out.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> > > You seem to object strenuously to how combat decks win games. I guess I
> > > misinterpreted your objectives.
> >
> > That's correct.
>
> So let me try again; your objective is to provide a way to win with
> combat which is _so_ much more effective than the current method that
> people will largely stop playing with that method. Correct?

Not exactly. I don't like rush combat decks but I'm not spitting blood to get rid of
them. My primary objective is simply to find a way to win using the combat cards we
have in the game in a way that isn't as destabilizing and mutually destructive as rush
combat. If it has the benefit of inducing fewer players to play rush combat, I sure
wouldn't mind that as a side-effect.

So I'm clear about this, I'll there's bad things in this game and there's all-caps
BAD THINGS. Rush combat is not the latter. We got into this (I think) because I'm
one of the ones that disputes that combat is this important third major deck archetype
that I perceive the combat deck players would like see put on an equal footing with
vote and bleed by being given cards which make combat more unstoppable. I'm just trying
to point out that there's another aspect of the game to look at besides which types
of decks are effective enough to win how many victory points.

> There are a _lot_ of criteria this "new winning
> method" would have to satisfy before people will give up rush decks.
> For example:
>
> * It must not be card-intensive. It must be a single card which is
> either reusable for moderate effect, or usable once for great effect.
> * It must provide an advantage which is repeatedly better than bleeding
> for 1-2 per action. (For example, the "Fame loop" only provides 1.5
> loss pool per action, usually at a cost of 2 blood from you, hence why
> it's not that good.)

Yea, that makes sense. And I think both criteria are achievable.

> > > Malkavian Prank is extremely random. You can't get much more random
> > > that "someone picks a number and someone else tries to guess it." Even
> > > though a combat deck's actions can cause unforseen consequences, this is
> > > far from "random."
> >
> > It's not exactly "random" in the same way, granted. But it has essentially random
> > effects in that you really don't know beforehand what your victim's other neighbor
> > is going to do when you blow up your victim's minions. If you did, you could adjust
> > your deck and tactics to compensate and make the results of playing combat decks
> > much more predictable than I perceive they are now.
>
> I really don't like your use of the word "random" like this. The good
> rush players can make the compensations you're talking about.

Yes, I understand that. But even so, they fail some of the time and the mediocre
players fail an awful lot. So random things come from combat decks, even if it's
not the same type of randomness that comes from the matrix games in Malkavian Prank.

> > > Give a specific example of a "bunch" of combat cards you would like to
> > > see be made effective.
> >
> > Assamite combat cards. Gangrel combat cards.
>
> Is it just me who doesn't see the Assamites as needing a S:CE hoser?
> They have Psyche! What they need is a few more vampires with the right
> skills.

Psyche's actually a pretty mild S:CE card. The experience I had with Assamites
is a deck that wanted to maneuver to long and launch Taste of Deaths. It's too
many moving parts to combine with enough Psyches to cancel out an opponent's
Majesties. A lot of Quietus combat involves spending blood which gets real
self-defeating real fast if they just S:CE, even if you have the Psyche in
hand.

> Gangrel combat cards are already somewhat effective; at least they see
> play. Wolf Claws is very common, and the maneuver/press cards are
> played as well. You were talking about cards which are currently
> _useless_.

I guess I'm not seeing how Wolf Claws really help. OK, you have to pay for them
until you know they work, but so? If you could use Psyches with Gangrel, that
might be doable since you don't need to spend blood on combat cards and you can
save the claws until they work. But without the discipline cards, that combination
doesn't exist. From what I've seen, protean and animalism combat cards are pretty
close to useless against a deck with a significant number of Majesties, which makes
them pretty useless in general.

> > > > Yep, I agree with all that. To which I'll add, this is a sad state of affairs:
> > > > outguess your predator in the metagame and the only result is that your grand
> > > > predator gets a free victory point.
> > >
> > > Not necessarily.
> >
> > In this situation - combat with a stealth/bleed predator, it is. I was talking
> > about this situation exactly.
>
> It's not necessarily true that your grandpredator gets a VP. You make
> it sound like a foregone conclusion, which it certainly is not. If
> anything is "the problem" in this scenario, it's the weenie deck with no
> defenses, not the combat deck.

It's not necessarily true but it happens often enough that it's a major problem with
the combat deck archetype, IMHO.

> > The metagame is about guessing. You guess what you think will work based on your

> > experience with whatever group of people you're about to play with and your
> > opponents do likewise. The thinking is that this is a matrix game: guess right and
> > you're supposed to be rewarded.
>
> We have established that you don't think "not dying" is reward enough.

It can be if it's easy enough, I suppose. If I throw in a relatively small number of
cards and completely confound my predator's deck from doing anything to harm me or bleed
much from my pool, that's actually a pretty good advantage to have in a game. That
sounds like a reward to me. I just question whether you can do that do a good, dedicated
rush combat deck without using a huge amount of deckspace, which would greatly lessen
the reward.

> > Guess wrong and you get punished. The trouble I find with combat is
> > that its neighbors seldom get rewarded no matter what they guess. If they guess
> > right vs. the combat deck, much of the payoff still seems to go to the guys across
> > the table, who in fact tend to get paid off no matter whether the combat decks
> > neighbors guess right or wrong. Combat decks are just bad news to sit next to and
> > good news to set across from, no matter whether they themselves win or lose.
>
> You've said all this before, and I've argued against it. Your reward is
> that you don't die. You slow the combat deck down so that they can't
> oust you, and get ousted by their predator instead. The people across
> the table are irrelevant, much as they are between any other pair of
> decks.

I agree, that element exists. But the amount of deckspace needed to achieve it
mitigates the "reward". It's also hard to build the deck that does that and doesn't
die horribly to everything else in the metagame, which means it's really not the
answer.

The guys across the table get rewarded enough by various types of scenarios that
tend to come up at various times: the combat deck cripples its predator and then
suddenly gets handjammed trying to do the crosstable rush or doesn't draw any rush
cards for several turn is the usual one or runs into a grandpredator which is well
enough prepared or just plain lucky enough to withstand the crosstable rushes long
enough to get the oust. Things like that. They may not happen a lot with good
players. But even so they happen (in my perception) much more often than they do
with other types of decks.

> > Of course, if the combat deck does well, that's always somewhat bad for the guys
> > across the table in the same way that if anyone on a table really does well, it's
> > bad for everyone else. But relatively speaking, it's much worse for the combat
> > deck's neighbors because the guys across the table at least have some chance of
> > grabbing a VP before getting sucked under.
>
> Any deck which is slow to oust has this problem. It's not specific to
> combat.

If it were just being slow to oust (similar to a bloat deck, for instance), fine.
But here again, the dynamics are not the same. For instance, if the issue is destroying
the prey's minions and then having to send three vampires a turn to bleed at one each -
especially against a prey which refuses to spend more pool on more vampires and "help"
the combat deck - then the grandprey can run wild in a way that isn't possible when
its predator is still on the table with real minions. In fact, being slow to oust actually
has the opposite problem with most other decks: it's the prey who may gets more time to do
what he has to do. Though the random effects of that problem don't seem to be as bad or
happen as often as with combat decks.

> > But I hear others (e.g. Ian) don't really care for it either it. If it's a lot
> > of people, White Wolf would want to consider carefully to whether this is really
> > the type of game they want to design cards for and facilitate.
>
> It's been the same game for years and years. It would be highly
> daunting and/or highly unstabilizing to make the kind of fundamental
> change you seem to be advocating. Daunting to do it well, unstabilizing
> if it is not done well.

To restate what I say up at the top: I'm not demanding change to get rid of rush
combat. I'm just opposing change to support it. I'd also like to see new ways of
using combat cards to win games besides rushing and destroying minions.

> > > > People getting victory points based on the pure luck of
> > > > where they sit tends to make Jyhad suck when they happen. Pure play-balance
> > > > isn't the only thing to worry about.
> > >
> > > This happens _all_ the time. It has _nothing_ to do with combat decks
> > > specifically.
> >

> > What happens "all the time"? Luck? You're failing to make a distinction.

> > The luck of the metagame is a necessary element to CCGs. The luck of having

> > to sit next to someone who happens to be playing a specific type of deck that's
> > always bad news to its neighbors, on the other hand, is not necessary.
>
> Back to this. It is _not_ always bad news to sit next to a combat
> deck. I have explained this repeatedly. Back in Ithaca, when everyone
> had psychotic combat decks, Josh Duffin made a Ventrue deck with lots of
> combat defense and wrecked us all. He _wanted_ to sit next to combat
> deck; otherwise, all his combat defense cards went to waste. So, we
> started making non-combat decks and mixing things up. And the metagame
> evolved, as it's supposed to.

The problem with your response is that it doesn't solve the problem I'm pointing
at. A common mistake people make in understand the metagame of a CCG is that,
"If deck Y exists which will hose deck X, then deck X isn't all-powerful." The
trouble with that point of view is that if deck Y isn't good for much else besides
hosing deck X, then not that many people really want to play it and it doesn't do
that much for balancing deck X in reality. Deck X may not ALL-powerful, but it's
powerful enough that the metagame gets a lot less interesting.

In the case of combat, we're not struggling with combat decks being overly powerful
in terms of gaining victory points as much just finding a way to reward people who
guess right for sitting next to them. You can play dedicated fortitude decks and
win. But you usually won't because you can't do much else with such a deck. So
the *real life* thing that actually happens is combat decks vs. some degree level of
combat defense in the combat deck's neighbor which will delay it but never have a
chance of winning that game. Often that effectively rewards the people across the
table. Much more often than any other type of deck I see.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
>
> Fredrick wrote:
> >>Again (believe I made this point elsewhere multiple times),>>
>
> Of course you made it multiple times--I just chose to not accept it as a valid
> one :-)

Well, all right. But just understand that you're giving an answer I and other
people here automatically have a problem with. If you're trying to convince
yourself and those who already agree with you, you're probably doing a decent job.
I'm not sure why you'd see the need to do that, though.

> >>that's fine if the bleeds come early enough to make that decision. But once
> the 16 pool is already spent on vampires, you can't put them back in the
> uncontrolled area and retrieve your pool. That's what I meant by "mid or late
> game".>>
>
> That doesn't matter one way or the other. Bleed decks kill you by denyng you
> resources--your pool. If you lose it now or later, it is still less pool you
> have to spend on stuff you want. If you aren't ever bled for anything, you will
> have a lot more stuff/resources (vampires, master cards, whatever) than if you
> are bled for a lot. It doesn't matter when you lose the pool--if you lose it
> early, you lose the access to the resources early. If you lose the pool late,
> you lose access to the resources later. It doesn't matter. Each pool you lose
> is one less pool you have to spend on something useful.
>
> Rush decks kill you by denying you resources--your vampires. If you lose a
> vampire, you lose a vampire that cost you X pool, you have lost X pool in
> resources. The rush deck does it after the fact, while the bleed deck does it
> before the fact. The end result is the same--you are denied resources.

Please stop and think about this! Your prey spends 18 on vampires and 12 on
pool. It's done, the vampires are already out. So now you can attack him with
rush combat or stealth bleed him. If you rush him, you FIRST destroy his defense
THEN bleed him until he's dead. Between the time you've crippled him and when
you've ousted him by draining his pool, he's sitting there occupying a spot in
the chain without minions. This is completely different from trying to stealth
past him and get at his pool directly. Whether you succeed or fail, he still
has his minions to work with, defend himself, attack his prey and so forth.
Nothing happens to them until his last pool is gone - at which time he vanishes
from the chain. You can NOT tell me this "the same thing". It's not the same
thing, it doesn't play anything like bleed or vote, and the difference in how
it works seems damaging to the game and makes it less fun to play.
...

> Which is a reasonable belief--I never claimed that it was *fun* getting whacked
> by a Rush deck. In fact, it is not particularly fun at all.

This issue is not about it not being fun to lose the game. If my predator makes
a good deck and/or guesses right in the metagame and beats me, that's fine. For
one thing, I can learn from that. I can use his strategy and tactics in future
games and I can also learn that I need to defend myself from such things. That's
the cool thing about strategy games: when you don't win, you have the opportunity
to learn something.

The issue I'm raising is my perception that the combat decks neighbors will tend to
lose not so much because of bad choices (though that element is sometimes present),
but that they often lose simply because they were unfortunate enough to roll the
dice and wind up next door to combat deck. Even if they planned for it, they still
don't tend to do as well (unless, as I'm arguing with James, they planned a specific
anti-combat deck that doesn't do well against anything else). There's not much I
can learn from bad luck.

> >>Just pure play experience. You just often don't see the bleed or vote deck
> demolish its prey's resources so quickly that they don't even have a chance.>>
>
> I see that quite often, actually. If my predator is a well designed, quick
> Dom/Obf deck, I can easily lose upwards of 15 pool by turn 3.

All right. Absolutely different experiences, then. I don't see hardly see it
ever at all. We're in different worlds here. Not much else to say.

> >>And such decks do not usually attack their predator's resources at all (or at
> least not very much compared to rushing backwards), giving their predator a
> fighting chance to outrace them if nothing else.>>
>
> So? VTES is a mutli-player game, and by virtue of this, you deal with multiple
> players.

So it sucks to be combat deck's predator. You get attacked in ways you never
have to deal with vs. any other decks. Nothing to learn from this, nothing to
do about it. It's just bad luck. That's "so". It's a bad thing in a game to
have that kind of an element. That's "so". It makes the game suck.

> I see. You don't like Rush decks, and you don't like intercept decks. You
> basically don't seem to like any situation where a player can have any
> significant impact upon their predator at all, as you see this as "random".
> Check. You don't like situations where your grand predator gets an "undeserved
> advantage", because you did something bad to your predator. Check.

Yep. All this is true. Check.

As you like to say: so?

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Jeroen wrote:
>>with 10 cards you're defended against bleed AND vote, to protect yourself
from rush you'll need 14 cards. That would make a total of 24 purely
defensive cards (26.666666%) And because 8 of these cards only protect you
from 1 type of rush deck it's easy to see why they're the ones left out.>>

Yup. These are choices you have to make. If you are worried about bleed, you
include bleed defense. If you are worried about combat, you include combat
defense. Very simple.

If you are worried about combat decks, use combat defense, just like you use
bleed defense when you are worried about bleed decks. Do not, on the other
hand, choose to not use combat defense, get killed by combat, and then attempt
to justify how it was somehow not your fault that you got killed by a combat
deck (because you chose not to use combat defense) by attempting to brand Rush
decks as unfair, random, or chaos causing (and as such, unfit for play).

Messages.Body:
Derek wrote:
>>must... stay out of... other argument...

NAH, SCREW IT. WHEE!>>

Yaa! More folks are suckered in!

>>...whether or not you were ever intending to get the 6 point vampire
in the first place. Bleed decks can hamstring you somewhat by
bleeding for tons early on. After enough turns, though, you
potentially already have the vampires you've intended to get out, and
now that bleed for 6 is, while still aggravating, not quite as
limiting. And you ALWAYS get to have your first-choice vampire who
can at least make the deck hobble along, no matter how much you're
bled for in the first three turns.>>

And then you have one vampire to defend yourself with. And you'll probably die.
And then, again, you'll be in the same spot if all your vampires were blown up.
Dead.

>>If I have Dolphin Black, Boy Toy, and Yorik out, and someone
poofs Dolphin, I no longer have any intercept capability until I fetch
another vampire with Auspex.>>

If you were bled for 15 on the first three turns, you won't have Dolphin, Boy
Toy, and Yorik out at all. You might have one or two of them. If one of those
two isn't Dolphin black ('cause you couldn't justify the expenditure), it is
just like she was burned.

>>With one well-placed action, Rush can effectively remove a deck's
ability to function.>>

Or, it could burn a 6 point vampire, and then see that same 6 point vampire get
influenced out again the next turn. If I bleed you for 6, that is one less 6
point vampire you can bring out. If I burn a 6 point vampire, that is one less
6 point vampire you have out. If Dolphin is so durned important, A) Include
more of her in your crypt or B) keep her from getting killed.

>>If, in the situation above, I was the Rush deck's predator, then he is
probably almost REQUIRED to kill Dolphin before he gets repeatedly bled for 4
at stealth. But in killing Dolphin, he also removes my deck's ability to
defend against my
predator effectively.>>

Sad, that.

>>Against a fast predator, I'm probably on a death-spiral. So a 6-cap vampire
being burned is generally worth much more than 6 pool - situational costs
invariably come into play here.>>

Sometimes. Sometimes not. Sometimes the 6 point vampire is minion tapped for 5
before it gets killed. Either way, you are denied resources.

>>No. You are screwed much worse, since you've lost the 6 point vampire
that you wanted/needed and probably don't have another copy of in your
uncontrolled region.>>

Sad. Include more in your crypt. Or avoid getting burned. Combat defense isn't
that hard. People just don't *like* including it, because it is card intensive
and might not be important. This is a design decision that has to be made. If
you choose to not include combat defense then you are asking to get killed when
you sit next to a Rush deck.

>>If you had a bleed deck behind you, you simply wouldn't get 6 pool worth of
OTHER vampires. You would still get the vampire you wanted, however.>>

Not if you were bled to the point that you couldn't afford to bring it out.

>>Again, in the above case, if I were bled for 12 before I were able to get a
vampire, I would still have gotten Dolphin Black.>>

And then you'd still probably die.

>>Big difference.>>

Not seeing it.

>>Now, if we define 'blown up' as "sent to torpor", then we discover the
reason why Rush decks tend to not win.>>

I win all the time. I send all of my prey's vampires to torpor. They don't come
out unless they get more vampires. If they do, I send them to torpor too.

>>And if you kill ALL of someone's minions, then you definitely end
their game.>>

Just like if you bleed them to death.

>>This has an enormous destabilizing effect on the table;>>

How is it more destabilizing than bleeding someone to death?

>>if you kill all your prey's minions, your grandprey will have
completely free rein for the time it takes you to bleed out the
remaining 10+ pool.>>

Unless you beat them up too.

>>If you kill all your predator's minions, your grand-predator will likely use
the time to set up carefully so that he blows through your predator and then
you all in one turn.>>

So you need to make sure that doesn't happen either.

>>And if you start rushing your grand-predator's minions, then you are going
all
over the road and are starting to look like a "reckless" deck.>>

So? If I get the most VPs, I doesn't matter how reckless I look, or act for
that matter.

>>I bet I could turn a table against someone who was doing -that-, no matter
how necessary it was.>>

And I bet that I could convince whomever necessary that I was actually helping
them out, and that it was in their best interest to leave me alone, as I'll
leave them alone until they oust their prey, securing them at least 1 VP, which
is better than nothing.

>>It's easier to include bleed defense than it is combat defense.>>

Yup. Just like it is easier to bleed than it is to Rush.

>>To stop bleed decks cold, I simply include 6 Wakes and 8 Deflections.>>

14 cards. To stop a Rush deck enough you need, say, 4 Wakes and 10 Obediances.
Or 14 Superior Mettle. Or 7 Superior Mettle and 7 Skin of Steel. Or something
like that. No one questions the inclusion of 14 anti bleed cards in a deck.
Everyone questions 14 anti combat cards in a deck. That is why Rush decks work
in tournaments.

>>To stop a Rush deck cold, I need to have about 30% of my deck be
combat defense.>>

Incorrect. You don't need to stop a Rush deck cold. You need to slow the Rush
deck down enough so that it gets ousted before you get destroyed. This is what
kills me all the time. Someone has enough Obediance or Superior Mettle or Flesh
of Marble so about half of my Rush actions are foiled. I don't kill you, and
instead get ousted.

>>...This comes from the point of view of the combat deck, by the way.
=) I've found that if your deck has "light combat defense", it means
that I just have to use a little strategy and planning to thump your
guys, but I'll still get 'em... just a touch slower. You really need
about 30% of your deck being "go away" cards to seriously stop things,
and that's gonna be too much.>>

You don't need to seriously stop stuff. A deck with, say, 14 anti combat cards
(Flash? Superior Mettle? Obediance?) will slow my Rush deck down enough to get
me ousted. 14 cards. Just like the 14 cards you shut down a bleed predator
with.

Messages.Body:

>>Well, all right. But just understand that you're giving an answer I and
other
people here automatically have a problem with.>>

Which one is that?

>>Please stop and think about this! Your prey spends 18 on vampires and 12 on
pool. It's done, the vampires are already out.>>

And if I bleed him for 6 before he gets out that 18 on vampires, he will only
spend 12 on vampires (and it'll be just like I burned a 6 point vampire); or;

>>If you rush him, you FIRST destroy his defense THEN bleed him until he's

This is a much shorter time than one might think. Usually a turn or two at most

and then never spends any more after his vampires are burned, leaving a big
pool wall to get through, this is then the *prey* who is mucking up the table
and giving a free ride to his prey. I can't help people who refuse to bring out

>>This is completely different from trying to stealth
past him and get at his pool directly. Whether you succeed or fail, he still
has his minions to work with, defend himself, attack his prey and so forth.

Of course I can. I have, like, a billion times already. And I will continue to
do so, as you are yet to convince me that I am mistaken.

>>It's not the same thing, it doesn't play anything like bleed or vote, and the
difference in how it works seems damaging to the game and makes it less fun to
play.>>

To you. I disagree.

>>The issue I'm raising is my perception that the combat decks neighbors will
tend to lose not so much because of bad choices (though that element is
sometimes present), but that they often lose simply because they were
unfortunate enough to roll the dice and wind up next door to combat deck.>>

If they had enough combat defense (please see my reply to Derek), this would
not be the case. Again, people don't think twice about including bleed defense,
but don't think that it is fair to have to include combat defense as well. If I
am playing a deck that has no bleed defense, and I roll the dice and end up to
a S+B predator, I will be losing due under the exact same circumstances. You
may say "But *everyone* has bleed defense--if you don't that is a bad deck".
I'd say the same thing applies to combat defense.

>>Even if they planned for it, they still don't tend to do as well (unless, as
I'm arguing with James, they planned a specific anti-combat deck that doesn't
do well against anything else). There's not much I can learn from bad luck.>>

You can learn that you should have combat defense, or expect to die to a combat
deck. Just like if you have no bleed defense, you should expect to die to a
bleed deck.

>>All right. Absolutely different experiences, then. I don't see hardly see
it
ever at all. We're in different worlds here. Not much else to say.>>

Check. You never see anyone bleeding you for 15 on the first three turns.
Kooky.

>>So it sucks to be combat deck's predator.>>

It sucks to be an intercept deck's predator if you have no stealth. And it
sucks to be the predator of a deck with abundant bounce when all you can do is
bleed. And it sucks to be a Gangrel's predator when you have no damage
prevention. And it sucks to be a combat deck's predator if you have no combat
defense. Use combat defense, and this won't suck so much.

>>You get attacked in ways you never have to deal with vs. any other decks.>>

That is correct. That is why Rush decks can do well in tournaments, because
people don't expect to have to deal with them. This doesn't mean that people
shouldn't have to worry about them.

>>Nothing to learn from this, nothing to do about it.>>

Include combat defense. If you get bad luck and end up next to a S+B deck when
you have no bleed defense, the same stuff happens.

>>It's just bad luck. That's "so". It's a bad thing in a game to have that
kind of an element. That's "so". It makes the game suck.>>

There is no luck about it. Include combat defense. Would you say it is "just
bad luck" to end up next to a bleed deck when you don't have any bleed defense?
No, you'd say it was poor plannng. Same thing here. If you don't include combat
defense, you are asking to get killed by a combat deck. You just don't want to
have to worry about it. If you choose not to, you are making an informed
choice.

>>Yep. All this is true. Check.>>

Just making sure I understand.

Messages.Author: Pat Ricochet
Messages.Body:
Ok, one more into the mix, because there's finally a point that seems like
the actual meat of the argument to me. =)

>>> If you rush him, you FIRST destroy his defense THEN bleed him until he's
> dead. Between the time you've crippled him and when you've ousted him by
> draining his pool, he's sitting there occupying a spot in the chain without
> minions.>>
>
> This is a much shorter time than one might think. Usually a turn or two at
> most

I totally disagree with this number. A turn or two? One turn would
mean that all your minions bleed for one (no bleed cards, as this is a
Bajika Rush and only Rush deck, yes?), ousting your prey. How much pool
does your prey have, and how many minions do you have? I'll give the
benefit of the doubt that they're all small Potence-only weenies, but that's
4 or 5 guys, tops, since you haven't included any Effective Managements. So
you're assuming your prey spends himself down to 5 pool irregardless of you
obviously pounding them down into torpor (more on this later).
To borrow from another post, this:

>>if you kill all your prey's minions, your grandprey will have
>>completely free rein for the time it takes you to bleed out the
>>remaining 10+ pool.
>Unless you beat them up too.

and this:

>>If you kill all your predator's minions, your grand-predator will likely use
>>the time to set up carefully so that he blows through your predator and then
>>you all in one turn.
>So you need to make sure that doesn't happen either.

Which seems like either you ARE Rushing these people, keeping these
things from happening, OR you're bleeding for 4 and 5 a turn so you can oust
your prey in "a turn or two," assuming that they're down to 10 pool or less
after rushing all the minions. You're trying to have your cake and eat it,
too. The numbers don't add up, to me.
(if you want to say you can manage the table by threat alone, I would
say you play with weak-minded fools. But if you insist, go ahead, and the
argument is over, as we've nothing more to discuss.)

> (especially if Fame is factored in).

A trick you maligned as a waste of time for causing average 1.5 pool
loss for an average cost of one blood? Of a Unique Master? No, I won't
give you the benefit of the doubt of factoring that in. Unless you put 3
Fames in every deck, which, from what I hear, you don't.

> If my prey spends 10 points on minions,
> and then never spends any more after his vampires are burned, leaving a big
> pool wall to get through, this is then the *prey* who is mucking up the table
> and giving a free ride to his prey.

No, they ARE playing the game. This is her combat defense, just like
not blocking stealth bleed. If she thinks your predator can get you before
you can get her, or that you need to go whacking your grandpredator while
she "gets a free ride," she's best off not bringing out ANYONE.

> I can't help people who refuse to bring
> out
> vampires and try to play the game.

"It's not whether you win or lose, it's how you lay the blame."

If you kill every minion of your prey, consistently before they get to
do anything, and then she doesn't bring out more minions, and sits there
with 20 pool, waiting for you get get ousted, leaving a few pool on vamps so
she can bring one or two vamps out quickly and/or take the pool back, SHE
can blame YOU for the free ride his prey is getting, since she has no other
recourse. YOU can blame HER for not "trying to play the game," but I see it
as "playing into your hands."
You want to blame your prey for not playing by your rules, rules that
support your opinion that pool and resources are thoroughly interchangeable
quantities. But if they don't play by your rules, and don't allow
destruction of secondary resources to turn right back into destruction of
primary resources (by bringing out more vamps), your assumption fails. But
rather than seeing the difference, it seems you'd rather chalk it up to poor
playing on the part of the prey.

I can see you ousting your prey in "a turn or two" against a guy who
idiotically spends pool on guys as fast as he can, despite their imminent
death, until he can spend no more (smallest guy a 6 cap, and 4 pool left).
Other than that, it just takes longer, and your prey IS "sitting there

occupying a spot in the chain without minions."

--
Pat Ricochet
Soul Jar'rn Fool of Atlanta

Maybe. Maybe not. Maybe she is just giving her prey a free ride. I'm not saying
that this is necessarily bad, I was just using it as an example of someone
doing something that gives a free ride to their prey, which in the context of
the previous legs of this discussion, is, according to some involved, a Bad
Thing (keeping in mind that one of Fred's apparent biggest beefs with a Rush
deck is that it gives a free ride to it's grand prey).

>>If you kill every minion of your prey, consistently before they get to
do anything, and then she doesn't bring out more minions, and sits there
with 20 pool, waiting for you get get ousted, leaving a few pool on vamps so

recourse. YOU can blame HER for not "trying to play the game," but I see it

Yup, she could. I'm not the one caring about the free ride the grand prey is

>>You want to blame your prey for not playing by your rules, rules that
support your opinion that pool and resources are thoroughly interchangeable
quantities. But if they don't play by your rules, and don't allow
destruction of secondary resources to turn right back into destruction of
primary resources (by bringing out more vamps), your assumption fails. But

playing on the part of the prey.>>

No, I was just making an analogy. I'm not blaming anyone for anything. Fred

prey's vampires, his grand prey gets a free ride (or an "undeserved advantage",

>>I can see you ousting your prey in "a turn or two" against a guy who
idiotically spends pool on guys as fast as he can, despite their imminent
death, until he can spend no more (smallest guy a 6 cap, and 4 pool left).
Other than that, it just takes longer, and your prey IS "sitting there
occupying a spot in the chain without minions.">>

With a single Fame, my prey is ousted in 2 turns if he has 12 pool when his
last vampire is destroyed. This isn't at all unreasonable math. Without the
Fame, 8 pool is the number, again, not that unlikely.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <3ACCE37C...@math.wisc.edu>, James Hamblin
<ham...@math.wisc.edu> writes
>One problem I have is that it's hard to make an
>all-Gangrel combat deck, because Dog Pack is slow and expensive.
>Protean is a very combat-centric discipline, so maybe it should have a
>S:CE hoser. Then again, maybe not.

(Apologies for the delay. Much crashing and a brief weekend away.)

One of the great assets Jyhad has, partly by accident, partly by design,
it seems to me, is that none of the disciplines is *totally* good at one
thing. (Dominate is very good, however, probably the 'best'
discipline.)

Take Presence. It's good for bleeding, but can't get the stealth. It's
good for voting, but can't call the votes (stealth). It's good for
combat defence, but can't use that as a wall of blockers (lack of
intercept).

Similarly, Potence. It's excellent for hitting things. It can get lots
of damage. However, it can't maneuver, press, prevent or additional
strike with any efficiency at all.

Obfuscate - excellent for stealth, and a number of useful support combat
cards (Swallowed by the Night, Behind You! etc.), with minor bleed
(Spying Mission), but nothing for votes or offensive combat, really.

IMO, all disciplines should have holes. These holes should be, to some
extent, surmountable by discipline cross-over (efficient, useful cards)
or disciplineless cards (hampered by "Do Not Replace" etc.) Giving
Protean a "I beat you" card would give it maneuvers, aggravated damage,
stealth, presses, additional strikes, damage prevention and S:CE
prevention. A bad thing, IMO.

>Or, it could burn a 6 point vampire, and then see that same 6 point vampire get

You're TOTALLY missing the concept here, not to mention that I'm just
going to giggle at the idea of someone casually coughing up the same
6-point vampire in the face of a Rush deck. "Here, let me bleed

With zero vampires, it doesn't matter how much pool you have. The

>>>No. You are screwed much worse, since you've lost the 6 point vampire

>
>Sad. Include more in your crypt. Or avoid getting burned. Combat defense isn't

>you choose to not include combat defense then you are asking to get killed when

THIS is the key problem. Rush decks all too frequently grind to a
miserable halt, because they've slaughtered their predator, mugged
their prey, and then can't bleed out their prey before their
grandpredator blows through them all. Sure, it sounds like a neat
theory that you go forth and casually Rush people, but without some
very good table management skills and a little bit of luck, all you do
is tip things over to one end or the other, as you eventually hand-jam
or get bopped by the rest of the table to remove the reckless deck
from play.

Second... combat defense has become very hard as of Sabbat War. No
longer does "combat defense" mean figuring out something to deal with
the Gangrel and the Potence IG deck (maneuver or prevent). There are
all kinds of valid fight decks running about these days.

What do the Toreador include, for example? Majesty? No good against
Potence IG. Flash? Pesky Assamites and OBF/Gun decks. Sideslip?
Scorpion Sting for the Gangrel, not to mention IG again. Fight back?
Worthless against any deck with +1 intercept, since you can't get
something to use WITH that Celerity. Granted, combat is the
Toreador's weak point. But all the clans should be playable, not
forced to worry about if someone has trundled along the ever-failing
Rush deck.

If the problem were just "ok, i include prevent and no deflections,
and a bleed deck will win" or "i include deflections and no prevent,
and a Rush deck will win", then it'd be better. But the Rush deck
really does often just fizzle to a halt, hand jammed on no Rush and
forced to bleed for 1 lots, hoping, as its predator runs it over.

If this happens mid-game, then the table just collapses around you.
Bad.

>>>If you had a bleed deck behind you, you simply wouldn't get 6 pool worth of
>OTHER vampires. You would still get the vampire you wanted, however.>>
>
>Not if you were bled to the point that you couldn't afford to bring it out.

>>>Again, in the above case, if I were bled for 12 before I were able to get a

>
>And then you'd still probably die.

Nah. Wake/Tel. Misdirection, Wake/Block, and bleed backwards like a

>>>Big difference.>>
>
>Not seeing it.

Keep looking.

>>>Now, if we define 'blown up' as "sent to torpor", then we discover the
>reason why Rush decks tend to not win.>>
>
>I win all the time. I send all of my prey's vampires to torpor. They don't come

When was the last time Potence IG won a tournament? I notice in the
one all the Ithaca guys brought their combat decks to, that you were
the only one to make it to the finals... It's just not a winning
strategy anymore. People WILL cross-table you early on to remove the

People WILL wait and Dramatic Upheaval away your VP once you bleed
your prey down to 5. People have seen IG Rush. They know how to
handle it without just including piles of Fortitude and maneuvers and
letting the rest of the table go hang (which is exactly what the Rush
deck wants).

It served an excellent purpose when it was created; to move people off
the 15-Majesty decks. The metagame has since shifted, and it's just
too difficult to win with one anymore, frankly. We had a Rushy-grabby
deck at the Atlanta qualifier. It didn't win. I'm not even sure if
it qualified. (It ran into Flesh of Marble in one instance, and some
other problems in the others.) It sure hosed up some people's decks
though. Why encourage this too much? I'd much rather see cards that

(James argues that it's just as unfair to sit down next to a guy with deflections
as it is to sit down next to a combat deck. I reply that defending against deflected
bleeds is just like defending against bleeds that originated with one's prey.)

> > > > but if so, the stealth/bleeder's
> > > > grandprey is also guessing wrong in the metagame. At least he's involved in
> > > > his own fate.
> > >

> > involved in the metagame. You plan for your defense against stealth bleed.
>
