> always work.

Nothing always works. You're ignoring the point. Deflections per se are no more
different or "unfair" than dealing with bleeds your prey's bleeds. We've been
disputing whether there's a difference or not between bleed and combat in many
other places. Here, I was just replying that deflections as defense just sets
another guy's bleed offense on you. If you're involved in your defense against
bleeds, then you're involved in your defense against you're grandpredator's deflected
bleeds also.

> > > Well, they have to try. There are many ways to shut down a combat deck
> > > that don't require scores of cards in your deck. A non-additional
> > > strike Potence deck is shut down by a single Superior Mettle, for
> > > example.
> >
> > There's various fortitude cards that will shut down a combat deck for a
> > whole combat but none of them that you would sanely include in large numbers
> > just for one type of combat deck.
>
> Once again I'm repeating myself: you don't need scores of combat defense
> cards to screw a combat deck.

Once again I'm repeating myself: "screwing a combat deck" is not the issue.
Rewarding yourself against combat decks as neighbors are the issue. I wish
to God every time you feel the need to repeat that, you'd just mentally plug
in my automatic answer: it's one thing to screw a deck. It's another thing
to benefit from doing.

The thing I keep beating my head against the wall TIME AFTER TIME trying to
get through to you is that the Jyhad metagame is *NOT* a 2-dimensional zero-sum
game between any given set of predator and prey. The Magic metagame can be
describe that way because Magic is a 2-player game: what "screws" your opponent
ergo benefits you. No way 'round it. Not so Jyhad. In Jyhad, there are 4 or
5 players, hence the metagame payoff matrix is 4-dimensional or 5-dimensional.
It is eminently possible to "screw a combat deck" and by so doing, screw yourself
even worse. Or more often, to help yourself but not really help yourself all
that much. He's screwed in the payoff chart but you're not really rewarded.

I hate to go here because I'm positively frightened by the chance that you'll
misunderstand or go off on some tangent. But in order to try and clarify, I'll
use another type of deck. I'm going to possibly munge with how well the deck
works in practice so if you don't think it works this way in reality, please don't
correct my description of how the following deck works. I'm only trying to
create an example so you'll understand what bothers me about combat decks. Just
assume my comments about this deck are true for the sake of argument.

The deck I'm thinking about is the "Brainwash deck". Reputedly (I've never
actually tried it), you can usually slap enough Brainwashes out to be pretty
much assured of gaining a single victory point: your prey's. Maybe not but
usually. I suppose if your prey has all 1 or 2 cap vampires, he might survive
by getting 2 vampires out the first turn he has enough transfers to. But that's
a pretty unusual metagame choice. Outside of that, it doesn't matter _what_
type of deck your prey is running. His strategy and tactics are pretty much
irrelevant. He just loses because a guy behind wanted to play a Brainwash deck.

Brainwash is a card in the game and clearly not overpowered. It's just kind of
a fucked thing for someone to do. It's not a real problem in the game overall
so I wouldn't bother asking for Scott to ban it or anything. But if someone
started bitching and moaning that Brainwash decks don't work very well, I sure
wouldn't have much sympathy.

Combat is not as bad as Brainwash in that it has a realistic chance of sweeping
the table, not just producing a single victory point. Combat players are clearly
trying to win the game, unlike Brainwash deck players. So it's a lot more
respectable. Still, my perception is that combat decks are hard to play, so there's
some comparison with the Brainwash decks that are near impossible to ever get more
than one VP. And I also think that, like Brainwash decks, Combat decks are hard
to play counters to that get rewarded for sitting next to.

> I guess I finally understand, though it seems psychotic. You're saying
> you don't like rush decks, because there's no way to make a deck which
> makes you say "hurray!" every time a combat deck sits down next to you?
> That's insanity.

It's "insanity" not to like combat decks for that reason or it's "insanity"
because you believe that it's possible to make a counter deck that shows a
positive payoff? If the latter, I agree in some ways and disagree in others.
As you say, you can build a dedicated Fortitude deck that just neuters it
and chances are you can find a way to win - especially if both of your opponents
are combat decks. (If it's only one of the two, you may have problems.) But
is that deck a real player against anything else or just a one-trick pony?
If the latter, it's not much of answer to combat in the long run. If the
former, I'd like to see that sucker because I've never encountered one.

> > Mostly, in the metagame you just try to do things to _survive_ a combat
> > deck.
>
> Surviving is good enough. If you can survive a combat deck, you neuter
> it. If you can survive 1 out of every 2 or 3 combats, you stand a good
> chance of beating it.

How does surviving 1 out of ever 2 or 3 combat "beat" a combat deck? If
it's your prey, "beating it" happens when you oust it before getting ousted.
If it's your predator, "beating it" means having a good chance of ousting your
prey despite its efforts. Surviving 1 out of every 2 or 3 combats doesn't seem
to lead directly to either of these results. You have to bleed someone to
death on the side as well. This means you have to have enough deckspace to
have an offense of some sort, not just limp away from combats.

> > But I've never found a way to survive a dedicated rush combat deck
> > that works against anything else at all.
>
> Why should _combat_ defense cards work against anything but a _combat_
> deck? You seem to want Jyhad to be some kind of happy fairy land where
> you get to not think and never get screwed.

You seem to think shoving words in my mouth about what I want does anything
for your point.

Decks need to do more than survive combat because the decks that only solve
one archetype lose a hell of lot more games than they win. I'm not interested
in playing a deck just because it solves one possible opposing deck. It's
as if you think the fact some deck no one would usually want to play - unless
your whole metagame is positively overrun by combat decks - is worth considering
for its metagame value. It's not.

> > > Even if you put 15 Deflections in your deck, chances are you'll get
> > > caught with your pants down at some point. Even if your deck is 50%
> > > combat defense, the combat player will occasionally be able to make a
> > > kill. What's the difference?
> >
> > What do you need to know? The difference is that you usually *WON'T* get
> > caught with your pants down against bleed instead of being getting caught
> > with your pants down ALL THE TIME. The difference is the combat player
> > making an occasional kill rather than ripping you apart from the first
> > action. That's plenty of difference for me.
>
> Dude. You don't need to have gobs of combat cards to keep from getting
> ripped apart.

This is where you and I totally disagree. If it doesn't take "gobs of combat
cards to keep from getting ripped apart" then combat decks are easy to defend
against by all decks and they'd be mostly impossible to win with so no one would
ever play them so they'd never be a problem. The reason they're worth playing
is that the number of cards you have maintain in your deck to neuter them
severely cripples you from doing well against anything *else*.

> > That's not what I meant. You can also fit both bleed bounce and various
> > vote-only defenses (e.g. Delaying Tactics, your own voting vamps and vote-
> > producing cards, both masters and reaction cards and so forth) in the
> > same deck.
>
> Then you can fit combat defense cards into the same deck.

Nope. That's just not true. There isn't the single combat card (except for
S:CE) that just neutralizes an entire combat deck's whole action. Even Fortitude
cards usually have to played in multiples to neutralize the damage a good rush
deck does each and every combat.

> OK, I agree that combat defense cards don't do much unless there's a
> combat deck next to you. But that's part of the metagame. Your
> Delaying Tactics and Dread Gazes don't do shit unless there's a vote
> deck around, either.

Since there needs to be fewer of them, they can be discarded. The difference
is shear numbers.

> > > Dude. The example I gave was specific. There is a fast
> > > forward-pointing bleed deck in our group which can routinely oust my
> > > combat deck. So probably _not_ never, huh?
> >
> > It depends on your combat deck, I guess. Unless the combat deck is based on
> > larger vampires, I've never seen a weeny bleed deck that works well enough against
> > a combat deck. The combat deck just rushes and eats them too fast for them to
> > make much headway - even if you bring 4 out in the same turn.
>
> It's not going to win every time. But it has a very good chance.
> _Especially_ if the weenie player is smart and gets all their vampires
> out all on the same turn.

Sorry. That's not my experience. One rush, one dead weeny. They may get a few
bleeds off but it doesn't go very far.

> > I guess this an example of differing perceptions. This is completely outside
> > of my experience. Or maybe the problem is your combat deck, I don't know. It
> > doesn't seem like a reasonable claim to me.
>
> Yeah, that's right. I've only been playing rush combat decks since the
> game was first released. Yeah, my deck must just be for shit. <sigh>

I have no idea why you can't hunt down one mouse for pretty much every rush
you take. The combat deck I've seen Gomi play would eat a weeny bleed deck
for lunch.

> Well, I don't have a "chaosometer", so I can't use the magical chaos

> are released, the stupider this game will become. Archon Investigation
> is a trump card which was totally unnecessary. The way to fix AI is not
> to print an anti-AI card. There are many combat strategies, some of
> which are screwed by S:CE, some by Fortitude, some by maneuvers, etc. A
> better-than-S:CE trump card would be succeeded by a
> better-than-Immortal-Grapple anti-trump, and so on. Then we'd really be
> playing rock/paper/scissors.

I agree with that. I don't really want to print more anti-combat cards to
fix this problem. To me, it's an annoying problem with combat that makes me
opposed to doing anything to make rush combat easier. As I said, I just want
to find other productive ways to let players use combat cards to win games.

> > In terms of how to plan a deck that's a
> > reasonable metagame choice and wins *because* it's next to a combat deck, combat
> > decks do indeed need to be hosed more.
>
> Why does such a deck need to exist? I don't ever sit down and say
> "hurray! my predator is a malkavian stealth bleed deck!" Even if I have
> Deflections and/or other bleed defense, that defense doesn't _make_ me
> win.

Again, perceptions differ. Last week, one of the other players played a
weenie stealth presence bleed deck and I happened to be sitting in front
of it with a deck that a fair number of deflections. Hurray! My prey went
down to my predator's bleeds in no time flat, it was so easy it was like taking
candy from a baby. Trouble was, it was only a three-player game so I got wound
up losing anyway, but that's Deflection for you.

Yes, using Deflections will frequently win you the game if your predator is
stealth-bleed. Other bleed defenses? Right now, we think of combat which is
what this thread is about, and Archon Investigation which - weirdly enough -
has a "combat-like" effect of burning the minion, as the other bleed defenses.
What else am I missing?

> > I already conceded (in the middle of
> > all that text that you went off on) that it might not increase them, though
> > that strikes me as unlikely.
>
> Then there's nothing more to argue. The rest of your paragraph is you
> _still_ not understanding that 1+1=2.

No. That's just your warped interpretation of my paragraph. I'm not sure what
you think it buys you to interpret what someone says in a way would indicate
they don't understand basic mathematics. When I do that, I go back and try to
understand why I'm getting that impression and what they might have truly been
trying to say. If I can't resolve the difference, I ask them to please restate
the thing that seems to me like it obviously can't be true. I don't walk away
assuming the worst of them. Not much you learn that way.

Fred

So I'd like to know what about the above you "don't choose to accept as valid".
Once 16 pool is spent, it seems to me you're pretty much stuck taking your pool
losses out of the remaining pool. But if you get hit by a combat loss, you're
pretty much stuck taking your loss from your stock of minions.

> >>Please stop and think about this! Your prey spends 18 on vampires and 12 on
> pool. It's done, the vampires are already out.>>
>
> And if I bleed him for 6 before he gets out that 18 on vampires,

But you don't. The example given was bleeding him for 6 afterward.

In fact, even so Derek pointed out a difference with destroying a minion vs.
destroying pool at any time, so even the bleed beforehand example isn't
equivalent between bleeding and destroying a 6-cap.

> >>If you rush him, you FIRST destroy his defense THEN bleed him until he's
> dead. Between the time you've crippled him and when you've ousted him by
> draining his pool, he's sitting there occupying a spot in the chain without
> minions.>>
>
> This is a much shorter time than one might think. Usually a turn or two at most
> (especially if Fame is factored in). If my prey spends 10 points on minions,
> and then never spends any more after his vampires are burned, leaving a big
> pool wall to get through, this is then the *prey* who is mucking up the table
> and giving a free ride to his prey. I can't help people who refuse to bring out
> vampires and try to play the game.

Finally, a truly interesting answer to one of my points. I think even a turn
or two, plus the time he's maybe starting to get anemic but isn't yet quite
out of minions is plenty time to destabilize a game. If you can sweep a table
this way, I'd wouldn't be bitching about combat being too unfair to its neighbors.
Of course, I'd probably be bitching that combat decks are too powerful but that
would be another thread. But the truth is, combat, no matter who well played,
is seldom that clean. It's usually make a bloody mess of things, even when
it does well. It often runs out of gas mid-prey or mid-predator and stalls for
a turn or two or three and the half-killed thing winds up throwing the table
balance all out of whack in the meantime.

> >>This is completely different from trying to stealth
> past him and get at his pool directly. Whether you succeed or fail, he still
> has his minions to work with, defend himself, attack his prey and so forth.

>
> Of course I can. I have, like, a billion times already. And I will continue to
> do so, as you are yet to convince me that I am mistaken.

If you just want to claim truth by blatant assertion, we haven't much to talk
about. The two things appear different to me.

>
> >>It's not the same thing, it doesn't play anything like bleed or vote, and the
> difference in how it works seems damaging to the game and makes it less fun to
> play.>>
>
> To you. I disagree.
>
> >>The issue I'm raising is my perception that the combat decks neighbors will
> tend to lose not so much because of bad choices (though that element is
> sometimes present), but that they often lose simply because they were
> unfortunate enough to roll the dice and wind up next door to combat deck.>>
>
> If they had enough combat defense (please see my reply to Derek), this would
> not be the case. Again, people don't think twice about including bleed defense,
> but don't think that it is fair to have to include combat defense as well. If I
> am playing a deck that has no bleed defense, and I roll the dice and end up to
> a S+B predator, I will be losing due under the exact same circumstances. You
> may say "But *everyone* has bleed defense--if you don't that is a bad deck".
> I'd say the same thing applies to combat defense.

I guess I could say, please see my reply to James. People don't think twice
about including bleed defense because it's much easier to include and doesn't
leave your offense starving for deck space.

> >>Even if they planned for it, they still don't tend to do as well (unless, as
> I'm arguing with James, they planned a specific anti-combat deck that doesn't
> do well against anything else). There's not much I can learn from bad luck.>>
>
> You can learn that you should have combat defense, or expect to die to a combat
> deck. Just like if you have no bleed defense, you should expect to die to a
> bleed deck.

I can learn that a deck with combat defense - unlike a deck with bleed defense -
won't do much else and usually tends to do badly in any metagame that isn't
overrun by combat decks. But I already knew that.

>
> >>All right. Absolutely different experiences, then. I don't see hardly see
> it ever at all. We're in different worlds here. Not much else to say.>>
>
> Check. You never see anyone bleeding you for 15 on the first three turns.
> Kooky.

Check. You do. Kooky.

> >>You get attacked in ways you never have to deal with vs. any other decks.>>
>
> That is correct. That is why Rush decks can do well in tournaments, because
> people don't expect to have to deal with them.

I think that's your perception. The truth is that it's just harder to build
a deck that actually fully deals with them and wins against them. And when
you build such a deck, it does little else so it won't do well in the
tournament.

This is similar to the Magic "Black Summer" when Necropotence decks were all
the rage. There was Necropotence, anti-Necropotence, and a few other popular,
more balanced deck types. People would say, "Well, Necropotence isn't overpowered
because you can build decks to hose it." You could, but you'd never win the
tournament because they wouldn't win against anything else. People mostly just
decided they'd rather build another Necro deck and take there chances against
the other Necro decks. It was a decidedly unfun summer to bother with.

Combat decks are not overpowered. They mostly hose themselves from handjam
or something. Or get hosed by the occasional deck that can resist them long
enough to screw them but not win the game itself in turn. Or screw up the
table management that they constantly need to do to restore the balance they've
trampled all over. None of this helps its neighbors.

Fred

You could blame the man on the moon if you wanted to. But getting rid of him

Derek wrote:
>>A) is silly. B) is also a laugher, especially for the poor Malk Antis
who don't have much in the way of combat defense at all (even Voice of
Madness needs a younger vamp...)>>

A (being include more Dolphin in your crypt) is hardly silly--if a vampire is
so critical that your deck cannot function without one, you use multiples of
them. B is very difficult for the !Malks, yes. By playing them, you are in
effect, saying "I will be killed by a combat deck". You could be playing the
Gangrel or Ventrue instead.

Dunno. I hear Tom won recently in England.

>>I notice in the one all the Ithaca guys brought their combat decks to, that
you were the only one to make it to the finals... It's just not a winning
strategy anymore.>>

It's just as much a winning strategy as it ever has been. In the last big
tournament I went to, I got into the finals on 7 VPs (three games), and got the
only other VP out of the final (which went 4-1 to my predator of all people).
Not shabby, I'd say.

>>People WILL cross-table you early on to remove the threat instead of just
letting you smack minions down at will.>>

No they won't. This has never happened to me. Ever. The only time I can
remember getting specifically killed from across the table was after I messed
with them first. Which is rare.

>>People WILL refuse to influence minions out, forcing you to attempt to bleed
through 20 pool while your predator is nuking you repeatedly;>>

This is hardly a problem. It makes dealing with your predator much easier (only
having to fight on one front and all)--sure, maybe I'll only get 1 VP out of
it, but when my prey refuses to bring out minions, I am hardly foiled.

>>People WILL wait and Dramatic Upheaval away your VP once you bleed
your prey down to 5.>>

Maybe.

>>It served an excellent purpose when it was created; to move people off
the 15-Majesty decks. The metagame has since shifted, and it's just
too difficult to win with one anymore, frankly.>>

You'd be surprised.

>>We had a Rushy-grabby deck at the Atlanta qualifier. It didn't win. I'm not
even sure if it qualified. (It ran into Flesh of Marble in one instance, and
some
other problems in the others.) It sure hosed up some people's decks
though. Why encourage this too much?>>

I'm not asking anyone to encourage anything.

>>Right. How many Rush actions does your deck have again? Vamps have
gotten smaller and more durable. Decks hand jam, too. It's a given
that you can't beat down the entire table, but frankly, that's what
you're suggesting here.>>

Nah. You just need to manage the table well. Often managing the table means
making viable deals with other folks around the table--arranging to split the
table 2/3 for instance.

>>Unless you get dead because people didn't want to let the reckless
deck get started.>>

Yeah, that just isn't going to happen. Your grand predator has no incentive to
screw with you. Your grand prey has no incentive to screw with you. Sure,
everyone at the table can arbitrarily decide to kill you, but that can happen
to anyone at any time ("Hey! That guy won the last tournament! Let's destroy
him! Yaa!"). With a group of random tournament players, this just isn't going
to happen.

>>Anyone would also notice that if they remove the Rush deck, they have
a chance at a sweep, as opposed to a measly VP. =) Forcing the Rush
deck to begin capriciously killing cross-table, supporting my original
table-talk of the deck being reckless. :)>>

It just doesn't happen (the ganging up on). Perhaps you need to unionize?

>>Because 14 anti-combat cards just sit and jam your hand if nobody is
trying to kill you, while you can be almost 100% guaranteed that
someone will bleed you for at least 1?>>

Right. I'm not denying that combat defense is useless if you don't see a combat
deck. This is true. I'm also not denying that bleed defense is much more likely
to be useful. What I'm saying is that the option exists, take up less space
than most people attribute to it, and when you choose not to include it, you
are making an informed decision to get killed by the Rush deck you have a small
chance of sitting next to. This strikes me as a reasonable gamble to make ("I
probably won't have to deal with a combat deck, so I can improve my deck by not
mucking it upwith combat defense..."), but one you occasionally lose. All I'd
like to see happen is that when one loses this gamble, they say "Well, I
gambled and lost. Oh well." rather than "Combat is unfair! It destroys the
table! It kills you with luck! Yaa!" in some an attempt to justify a worldview
where combat defense is *always* unecessary.

>>I dunno. This really isn't my experience at all, although I do play a
lot of different combat, and not just plain old Potence IG. Someone
with a measly 14 cards' worth of combat defense is just plain going to
get whacked; except it's going to be a lot slower, giving him some
time to set up, influence more vamps, do some damage to his prey...
basically, to do a lot more of your work for you, and THEN you pounce
and toast some vamps all at once.>>

If I can get it to work out like that, all the better :-)

Usually, when I am foiled, it is by moderate combat defense--enough Obediances
to foil some necessary rushes, some Flesh of Marbles, enough manuvers,
whatever. If my momentum is toppled, I usually get ousted.

It *can*. But it won't, because that gets it killed very quickly.

(Patrick O'Shea has a slimmed-down version of it that he keeps built
to test decks around here; we consider that if your deck can't stand
up to sitting in front of the Crypt Machine, your deck needs to think
about whether or not it has enough bleed defense for a tournament.)

finishing 2nd there on a tiebreaker. The way you survive with a deck
like that (and the way he made it there) is to sit quietly at first,
gain some minions on the cheap, Deflect a bleed for 1 or 2
occasionally, hunt, and then bleed with 5 minions for 17 on about turn
6, with ridiculous amounts of Bonding, Sleeping Mind, and Seduction.

At that point, you're a target, but you already have your first VP and
are up and rolling. Bleeding for 12-18 on the first few turns just
makes you a target, leaves your prey with a couple vampires and 6
pool, and could get you made dead very quickly since everyone else
still has plenty of resources to point at you.

if you sit down as the original creator's predator in the first round,
who knows that the only thing you can do is kick the legs out from
under it before it even starts. =)

Norm and I had an interesting discussion about this at the qualifier.
We both agreed that the classic Malk stealth-bleed deck is simply too
reckless <-- there's that word again> anymore in the current
tournament environment. MANY people will be carrying Deflections, and
many people now know that the idea is to block, make them add stealth,
and THEN bounce the bleed.

I know that I personally am starting to think that initiating a bleed
for 6 at +2 stealth is like dropping a rock into the top of a large
drainpipe and listening to it rattle around for awhile; you never KNOW
where it's going to come out, and it certainly isn't going to keep
things very stable at all. I don't generally design decks anymore
that bleed for more than 3 in an action; this way I don't worry about
accidentally ousting someone if I get bounced all over the place, and
4 actions that bleed for 3 each are much harder to Deflect than 2
actions that bleed for 6 each. They might be easier to block since
smaller vampires can't get the superior disciplines as easily... but
getting one of your guys caught and dead is a better risk, IMO, than
handing the table to your prey.

>matter what.>>
>
>Yeah, see, this is where no one is going to be convinced one way or the other.
>I see the game differently.

I can't... I guess partly because I've seen the difference between one
vamp and no vamps too often. And also where I've completely shrugged
off anything my bleeding-voting-hideous-combat predator did, because I
had just enough vampires to make the oust next turn and refused to
risk losing one just to stop a bleed of 3.

Pool is important... but vampires to defend that pool and chew up
others' pool end up being more important. For the most part, if you
have tons of pool, you can always get more vampires. Not true sitting
next to a Rush deck, though.

>>>When was the last time Potence IG won a tournament?>>
>
>Dunno. I hear Tom won recently in England.

Yeah, he did mention that. I guess I missed the "win!" post, or no,
wait, I do remember that, it sparked off another Andrew Davidson
special about how Tom won by ousting his predator, etc. Which he
didn't. OK.

>>>I notice in the one all the Ithaca guys brought their combat decks to, that
>you were the only one to make it to the finals... It's just not a winning
>strategy anymore.>>
>
>It's just as much a winning strategy as it ever has been. In the last big
>tournament I went to, I got into the finals on 7 VPs (three games), and got the
>only other VP out of the final (which went 4-1 to my predator of all people).
>Not shabby, I'd say.

I'm of the opinion that it's possible to build decks that get to the
final consistently, but will lose in the final. And it's also
possible to build decks that can barely scrape into the final, but
have an excellent chance of winning once they're there.

I see finals played MUCH differently; everyone is conscious that the
whole table is a threat, and is ready to act accordingly.

>>>People WILL cross-table you early on to remove the threat instead of just
>letting you smack minions down at will.>>
>
>No they won't. This has never happened to me. Ever. The only time I can
>remember getting specifically killed from across the table was after I messed
>with them first. Which is rare.

Hmmmm. I dunno. As your grand-predator with a vote deck, I would
initially intend to do 3-1 to prey/you, since I'd want you as hurt as
possible when I finally ousted my own prey. Probably then, we get
into some table talk about who would get rushed if who got points of
damage, then I'd probably offer you the deal "I'll do the 1 to YOUR
prey if you kill some of my prey's minions (points at likely
interceptor, whether or not they have ever shown intercept). That'll
help keep you alive, and I'll help oust your prey for you." This is a
trap deal, but if you don't accept it, you WILL be getting the point,
since for you to rush me is WAY outside the lines of "useful strategy"
and I'm not especially afraid of it. Whether or not I have combat
defense in hand.

So my prey should be getting low quickly from our combined efforts,
and your prey will be getting low quickly as well. As soon as my prey
gets within oust reach, all my votes are going to start going 2-2 or
1-3: 1 to him, 3 to you, and if you live through the turn through
sheer amounts of pre-existing pool, I should still be able to retain
enough minions to zap you on my NEXT turn.

See, I play combat decks. I know better than to let them get into a
nice stable position with lots of minions and comfortable pool. =)
You have to kick the legs out from under them early on.

>>>People WILL refuse to influence minions out, forcing you to attempt to bleed
>through 20 pool while your predator is nuking you repeatedly;>>
>
>This is hardly a problem. It makes dealing with your predator much easier (only
>having to fight on one front and all)--sure, maybe I'll only get 1 VP out of
>it, but when my prey refuses to bring out minions, I am hardly foiled.

Getting 1 VP is not winning, though.

>>>People WILL wait and Dramatic Upheaval away your VP once you bleed
>your prey down to 5.>>
>
>Maybe.

A couple tournaments ago, I brought my flung-junk deck with bleed
enhancements. It pretty much terrorized everywhere it was near, but
only gained 1VP the entire day. Why? Two Dramatic Upheavals; one to
move me next to somewhere they thought I would be forced to do damage
to another deck (in front of the stealth bleed deck while I had only
two bleed cards in hand, giving the deck a free turn at me ANYWAY),
and one to swap with me when my vampire-less prey was at 3 pool, and I
had the Legal Manip in hand.

Tournaments see a lot of Dramatic Upheaval and the like, and a combat
deck generally doesn't have the vote power to stop it from happening -
and it's no good to Rush someone *after* they just stole your VP.

>>>It served an excellent purpose when it was created; to move people off
>the 15-Majesty decks. The metagame has since shifted, and it's just
>too difficult to win with one anymore, frankly.>>
>
>You'd be surprised.

I would indeed.

>>>We had a Rushy-grabby deck at the Atlanta qualifier. It didn't win. I'm not
>even sure if it qualified. (It ran into Flesh of Marble in one instance, and
>some
>other problems in the others.) It sure hosed up some people's decks
>though. Why encourage this too much?>>
>
>I'm not asking anyone to encourage anything.

Well, the original point of this argument was the whole S:CE-hoser
business. I don't want to see more S:CE *hosers*, because that makes
Rush decks -more- viable. Right now the truly "effective" Rush deck
is a Potence deck based around Immortal Grapple, one of the three true
S:CE hosers. I want to see more S:CE workarounds (TT, Psyche), which
would make bruise-and-X decks more effective and make combat more
popular, but NOT Rush decks (for the reasons all over this thread).
It's not that I don't think that Potence IG needs to exist, it's just
that encouraging Rush combat in varied forms as a strategy is likely
to lead to madness.

>>>Right. How many Rush actions does your deck have again? Vamps have
>gotten smaller and more durable. Decks hand jam, too. It's a given
>that you can't beat down the entire table, but frankly, that's what
>you're suggesting here.>>
>
>Nah. You just need to manage the table well. Often managing the table means
>making viable deals with other folks around the table--arranging to split the
>table 2/3 for instance.

2VP doesn't win the final, though...

>>>Unless you get dead because people didn't want to let the reckless
>deck get started.>>
>
>Yeah, that just isn't going to happen. Your grand predator has no incentive to
>screw with you. Your grand prey has no incentive to screw with you. Sure,

"Fear of having to sit next to you" isn't an incentive?

I went over the grandpredator bit above. A wise grandprey would begin
making sure his predator never quite entirely died, by whatever means
necessary (rescuing the Prince so he can 5th and possibly Minion Tap),
using the excuse "I don't want to have to sit next to it." If nothing
else, it slows you down and could put a real wrench in things.

>everyone at the table can arbitrarily decide to kill you, but that can happen
>to anyone at any time ("Hey! That guy won the last tournament! Let's destroy
>him! Yaa!"). With a group of random tournament players, this just isn't going
>to happen.

I talk FAST. =)

>>>Anyone would also notice that if they remove the Rush deck, they have
>a chance at a sweep, as opposed to a measly VP. =) Forcing the Rush
>deck to begin capriciously killing cross-table, supporting my original
>table-talk of the deck being reckless. :)>>
>
>It just doesn't happen (the ganging up on). Perhaps you need to unionize?

Heh. Oh, it DOES happen. =) Just not in the way you think. =)

>>>Because 14 anti-combat cards just sit and jam your hand if nobody is
>trying to kill you, while you can be almost 100% guaranteed that
>someone will bleed you for at least 1?>>
>
>Right. I'm not denying that combat defense is useless if you don't see a combat
>deck. This is true. I'm also not denying that bleed defense is much more likely
>to be useful. What I'm saying is that the option exists, take up less space
>than most people attribute to it, and when you choose not to include it, you
>are making an informed decision to get killed by the Rush deck you have a small
>chance of sitting next to. This strikes me as a reasonable gamble to make ("I
>probably won't have to deal with a combat deck, so I can improve my deck by not
>mucking it upwith combat defense..."), but one you occasionally lose. All I'd
>like to see happen is that when one loses this gamble, they say "Well, I
>gambled and lost. Oh well." rather than "Combat is unfair! It destroys the
>table! It kills you with luck! Yaa!" in some an attempt to justify a worldview
>where combat defense is *always* unecessary.

Right. I'm not attempting to justify THAT worldview. I just want to
see lots more new bruise-and-X options, as opposed to lots more Rush
options.

>>>I dunno. This really isn't my experience at all, although I do play a
>lot of different combat, and not just plain old Potence IG. Someone
>with a measly 14 cards' worth of combat defense is just plain going to
>get whacked; except it's going to be a lot slower, giving him some
>time to set up, influence more vamps, do some damage to his prey...
>basically, to do a lot more of your work for you, and THEN you pounce
>and toast some vamps all at once.>>
>
>If I can get it to work out like that, all the better :-)
>
>Usually, when I am foiled, it is by moderate combat defense--enough Obediances
>to foil some necessary rushes, some Flesh of Marbles, enough manuvers,
>whatever. If my momentum is toppled, I usually get ousted.

The Rush deck's true weakness - once it kicks one leg out from under
the table, it has to keep kicking or the table falls right on its
head. Again, the animation short "Balance" is an EXCELLENT visual...
and it even has five different bits! =)

Messages.Body:

aren't showing up. My apologies for these being in the wrong place...)

Fred wrote:
>>I guess I could say, please see my reply to James. People don't think twice
about including bleed defense because it's much easier to include and doesn't
leave your offense starving for deck space.>>

That, and you are much more likely to need bleed defense. Thus, bleed defense
is sort of a no brainer. Combat defense, on the other hand, is much less likely
to be needed. By choosing to not include it, you are making an informed
decision to leave a hole (albeit a small one) in your deck strategy. If your
combat defense is "hope they don't have blasters", then when you end up next to
a combat deck, you will die. You seem to want to attribute this to bad luck (of
being fated to sit next to a combat deck). I want to attribute this to making
an informed decision.

>>I can learn that a deck with combat defense - unlike a deck with bleed
defense -
won't do much else and usually tends to do badly in any metagame that isn't
overrun by combat decks. But I already knew that.>>

Again, this is a decision for you to make when building a deck. When you are
going to a tournament, you need to say "Hmm. Might I run into a combat deck?"
If you think the answer is yes, then you'd be a fool to not plan defenses. If
you think the answer is no, you'll be killed when you end up next to one, and
only have yourself to blame.

>>Check. You do. Kooky.>>

Hoo hoo. That's why I like you Fred. You're funny.

>>I think that's your perception. The truth is that it's just harder to build
a deck that actually fully deals with them and wins against them. And when
you build such a deck, it does little else so it won't do well in the
tournament.>>

Ok. Then build a deck that can't deal with combat, and get killed by some. I
fully understand that it is not easy to defend against combat (although 14
cards will slow it down quite nicely). But rather than accepting that by not
using combat defense you are simply playing the odds, you seem to want to not
have to worry about the whole thing by indicting combat is unfair and
destabilizing. When playing a Rush deck in a tournament, I am playing the
odds--in all likelyhood, the folks I sit next to A) won't be playing much
combat defense and B) won't be playing other combat decks. When I am correct, I
do very well. When I am wrong, I don't. Luckily, I am usually not wrong.

>>This is similar to the Magic "Black Summer" when Necropotence decks were all
the rage. There was Necropotence, anti-Necropotence, and a few other popular,
more balanced deck types. People would say, "Well, Necropotence isn't
overpowered
because you can build decks to hose it." You could, but you'd never win the
tournament because they wouldn't win against anything else. People mostly just
decided they'd rather build another Necro deck and take there chances against
the other Necro decks. It was a decidedly unfun summer to bother with.>>

But you don't need to build specific anti-combat decks to stop a combat deck.
You need to have enough combat defense to slow them down, throw off their
momentum, and get them killed. If you choose not to, that is fine, but in the
event that you end up next to a combat deck, you will die. This is not bad
luck. This is informed decision making.

Derek wrote:
>>B is definitely a problem for the Malks. But combat defense, well,
see below. I don't think 14 cards is -near- enough. =/>>

Really? I have found that very often, not that much combat defense is enough to
slow me down, or at least keep you alive. Generally, my prey needs more than my
predator to convince me that I am screwed--if my Predator has somewhat
significant combat defense (i.e. they sucessfully Obediance my first 2 rushes),
I'll let them be, unless they are in significant danger of ousting me. See, I
really like to oust my prey and only endeavor to get my predator ousted if
absolutely necessary. I'd still say that about 14 cards of combat defense is
enough to slow me down or get me killed. But, ya know, whatever.

>>Pool is important... but vampires to defend that pool and chew up
others' pool end up being more important. For the most part, if you
have tons of pool, you can always get more vampires. Not true sitting
next to a Rush deck, though.>>

True, true. I have actually lost complete track of what my point was originally
about that whole 6 pool=6 point minion thing. I'm easily confused :-)

>>Yeah, he did mention that. I guess I missed the "win!" post, or no,
wait, I do remember that, it sparked off another Andrew Davidson
special about how Tom won by ousting his predator, etc. Which he
didn't. OK.>>

Oh, yeah--that was a good one. Weren't you in that one?

>>I'm of the opinion that it's possible to build decks that get to the
final consistently, but will lose in the final. And it's also
possible to build decks that can barely scrape into the final, but
have an excellent chance of winning once they're there.>>

Absolutely--a standard intercept deck (ya know, the ones that get 2 VPs every
game) will pretty much always get into the finals, but never win. From my past
rush deck experience, however, it isn't that dire--you can regularly get 4 VPs
from a game (I do at least once every tournament), and can do so in the
finals--as always, it is a matter of the seating as much as anything else.

>>Hmmmm. I dunno. As your grand-predator with a vote deck, I would
initially intend to do 3-1 to prey/you, since I'd want you as hurt as
possible when I finally ousted my own prey.>>

Which is playing loose cannon, and asking to get killed. I am in no way above
throwing away my game to take someone else with me, if they decided to piss me
off first. If, in this situation, you, as my grand predator started hitting me
for 3/1, I'd make it very clear that I would remove you from the game, at the
expense of my own game. I'd much rather play nice, but if someone across the
table is going to screw me, I'm going to take them down with me.

Just 'cause I don't want to be reckless doesn't mean I won't be if necessary...

>>Probably then, we get into some table talk about who would get rushed if who
got points of damage, then I'd probably offer you the deal "I'll do the 1 to
YOUR
prey if you kill some of my prey's minions (points at likely interceptor,
whether or not they have ever shown intercept). That'll help keep you alive,
and I'll help oust your prey for you.">>

Yeah, I generally don't like making deals that start off with people screwing
me. The end result of this is us both losing, which I am comfortable with. On
the other hand, if you accept the position of my grand predator, and happily
accept the aid I am giving you (by messing up your prey) and leave me alone
until your prey is dead, then we are both in a happy place.

>>This is a trap deal, but if you don't accept it, you WILL be getting the
point,
since for you to rush me is WAY outside the lines of "useful strategy"
and I'm not especially afraid of it. Whether or not I have combat
defense in hand.>>

But you should be. If I can play the game to win, I do. If, on the other hand,
the table conspires against me to make me lose by circumventing the normal
predator/prey relationship, I *will* make you lose with me. I fail to see how
this is to your benefit.

See, I look at the table like this--My prey is just screwed. My grand prey is
in a very safe spot, in fact, the best, and it is in their best interest to not
anger me, as they can easily gat a VP by the time I get to them, and it is
perfectly likely that they will have enough momentum by then to keep going by
the time I get to them. My predator is mostly screwed, but I'm not above making
a "I'll split 3/2 with you, rather than get you ousted" deal with them, if I
think I can pull it off. My grand predator is going to have a lot of trouble
with their predator (as they are in the best spot at the table), and will be
benefitting from my abuse of my predator. If someone across the table decides
to bust up this wonderful environment, again, I am not above making them lose
with me. This is not something I want to do, but will if pushed into it.

>>So my prey should be getting low quickly from our combined efforts,
and your prey will be getting low quickly as well. As soon as my prey
gets within oust reach, all my votes are going to start going 2-2 or
1-3: 1 to him, 3 to you, and if you live through the turn through
sheer amounts of pre-existing pool, I should still be able to retain
enough minions to zap you on my NEXT turn.>>

And again, if this becomes the case, we both lose--you spend your effort
getting me ousted, and I spend my effort killing you. The table is completely
destabilized and someone else is going to win. I don't sign up for these
situations, but will play them out if someone else volunteers me.

>>See, I play combat decks. I know better than to let them get into a
nice stable position with lots of minions and comfortable pool. =)
You have to kick the legs out from under them early on.>>

But if you do this from across the table, you'll get killed--I expect this from
my predator or prey, but my grand predator has no buisiness doing this, and
I'll act accordingly. What is the point of playing a deck that has the
capability of going completely rogue if you aren't going to take advantage of
it if you need to?

:-)

>>Getting 1 VP is not winning, though.>>

No, it isn't, but it is better than 0 VPs. If my prey is going to do everything
in their power to deny me a VP (i.e. never getting out a single vampire the
whole game), I figure that getting 1 is a fine way to settle.

>>A couple tournaments ago, I brought my flung-junk deck with bleed
enhancements. It pretty much terrorized everywhere it was near, but
only gained 1VP the entire day. Why? Two Dramatic Upheavals; one to
move me next to somewhere they thought I would be forced to do damage
to another deck (in front of the stealth bleed deck while I had only
two bleed cards in hand, giving the deck a free turn at me ANYWAY),
and one to swap with me when my vampire-less prey was at 3 pool, and I
had the Legal Manip in hand.>>

Sometimes you get screwed.

>>Well, the original point of this argument was the whole S:CE-hoser
business. I don't want to see more S:CE *hosers*, because that makes
Rush decks -more- viable. Right now the truly "effective" Rush deck
is a Potence deck based around Immortal Grapple, one of the three true
S:CE hosers. I want to see more S:CE workarounds (TT, Psyche), which
would make bruise-and-X decks more effective and make combat more
popular, but NOT Rush decks (for the reasons all over this thread).
It's not that I don't think that Potence IG needs to exist, it's just
that encouraging Rush combat in varied forms as a strategy is likely
to lead to madness.>>

Nah. I don't think it would lead to madness. I think it would lead to a shift
in the environment. If, suddenly, the Assamites became viable somehow (which
would take quite a bit of work, mind you...), some of the folks who were
playing IG Rush might switch to Assamite Rush, which would make no difference
to the non combat decks (you get killed by combat or you don't), but would
trump the IG decks something fierce. Thus, the IG decks would probably fade out
of the circut.

>>2VP doesn't win the final, though...>>

No, no, that was pre-final. In the final, I either get 4 VPs, or I lose :-)

>>"Fear of having to sit next to you" isn't an incentive?>>

It is worth worrying about that later on, if you get a VP out of it.

>>I went over the grandpredator bit above. A wise grandprey would begin
making sure his predator never quite entirely died, by whatever means
necessary (rescuing the Prince so he can 5th and possibly Minion Tap),
using the excuse "I don't want to have to sit next to it." If nothing
else, it slows you down and could put a real wrench in things.>>

Could. Or, my grand prey could completely ignore me and attempt to get as many
VPs as possible before I got to him. Might even make a deal with me.

>>Right. I'm not attempting to justify THAT worldview. I just want to
see lots more new bruise-and-X options, as opposed to lots more Rush
options.>>

That'd be interesting, but I still don't think it would be any more effective.

and if I jump you with 3 guys in the same turn, you'll likely be out
after the first combat (i'm fond of Celerity; it lets me use things
like "press to continue" after that silly Skin of Steel, and it lets
me use things like "Blur" to avoid that pesky Superior Mettle, and
Dodge makes me laugh) and the next two people are going to be just so
many body parts.

And after that particular round of beatings has ended, I can get back
to the regularly scheduled business of ousting-my-prey.

how much it costs to bring them out. Once they're out, they become
worth more or less than 6 pool rapidly. (Minion Tap = this minion is
worth 1 pool. Owl Companion + 2 Raven Spies = this minion is worth
ALL of your pool. You get the idea.)

Yeah, I waded in for awhile. It was mostly Tom and a couple others

position to contribute his view.

But the decks with the most VP going into the finals have choice of
seating. Sometimes that's good; in the case of Rush and intercept
decks, though you might find that vulnerable people refuse to sit near
you. I got to the finals of one War Room tourney with Hideous
Tzimisce Intercept and had to sit 2nd; three other people deliberately
chose to sit as far away from me as possible. Oops.

>>>Hmmmm. I dunno. As your grand-predator with a vote deck, I would
>initially intend to do 3-1 to prey/you, since I'd want you as hurt as
>possible when I finally ousted my own prey.>>
>
>Which is playing loose cannon, and asking to get killed. I am in no way above
>throwing away my game to take someone else with me, if they decided to piss me
>off first. If, in this situation, you, as my grand predator started hitting me
>for 3/1, I'd make it very clear that I would remove you from the game, at the
>expense of my own game. I'd much rather play nice, but if someone across the
>table is going to screw me, I'm going to take them down with me.

Nah. That's not loose cannon. There's only two logical ways for 3/1
to go, you know: prey/grandprey, or prey/predator. The first is
aggressive, the second is solidifying. But neither is random.
Chucking it to your grandpredator, on the other hand, is pretty damn
random, or doing 1/3 to prey/grandprey, etc...

Although I have called multiple KRCs as 1/3 to prey/predator when I
was afraid I'd be ousted if I didn't kill him that turn. 3 points is
better than nothing. =)

>Just 'cause I don't want to be reckless doesn't mean I won't be if necessary...

Oh, I'm sure. But I also am NOT going to give you a free ride, since
from my point of view, your existence is making my predator really
climb down my back. So it is, after all, in my best interest to give
you a BIT of poking, and maybe get you to back off my grandpredator a
bit. =)

Table dynamics can be fun. ;) I find this is where the real game
comes into play... identifying who is ACTUALLY a threat to you. My
prey and grandpredator are totally non-threats, as my prey is
sammiched between me and Rush, and my grandpredator is probably toast.
This leaves my predator, an obvious threat, and YOU, a non-obvious
threat enabling my predator. =)

>>>Probably then, we get into some table talk about who would get rushed if who
>got points of damage, then I'd probably offer you the deal "I'll do the 1 to
>YOUR
>prey if you kill some of my prey's minions (points at likely interceptor,
>whether or not they have ever shown intercept). That'll help keep you alive,
>and I'll help oust your prey for you.">>
>
>Yeah, I generally don't like making deals that start off with people screwing
>me. The end result of this is us both losing, which I am comfortable with. On
>the other hand, if you accept the position of my grand predator, and happily
>accept the aid I am giving you (by messing up your prey) and leave me alone
>until your prey is dead, then we are both in a happy place.

Right. I'd probably stop before officially announcing the terms and
say "I *could* do this 3/1. What does everyone think about that?"

I am also comfortable with both of us losing, in that situation. If I
blithely oust my prey while not touching you, I am going to be in the
same position my prey was in at the start of the game; screwed, except
you'll have a lot more minions and a REAL incentive to nuke me. This
gets me dead. Since 1VP isn't sufficient to win, I'll go ahead and
sacrifice the sure 1VP to give myself a chance at 3. (if I get you, I
get your vampire-less prey as well.)

But then again, I also don't intimidate/threaten easily. =) And I
also don't make deals during the EARLY portions of the game to split
the table; I prefer to give myself a chance to get all 5. The time
for such a deal would be when I got down to almost ousting my prey,
and it became time either to begin hosing you as well, or to begin
carving up table pieces for us both.

>>>This is a trap deal, but if you don't accept it, you WILL be getting the
>point,
>since for you to rush me is WAY outside the lines of "useful strategy"
>and I'm not especially afraid of it. Whether or not I have combat
>defense in hand.>>
>
>But you should be. If I can play the game to win, I do. If, on the other hand,
>the table conspires against me to make me lose by circumventing the normal
>predator/prey relationship, I *will* make you lose with me. I fail to see how
>this is to your benefit.

It's not to your benefit either though. I assume that people are
going to make their best attempt to gain something for themselves;
odds are you end up accepting the 'trap deal', since it makes the most
sense for both of us as opposed to nuking each other and letting the
guy between us sweep. But it also gives me lots of time to set up for
the big kaboom at the end, where I either gain 3 all at once and
possibly sweep, or I fail to draw into cards and explode gloriously.

>See, I look at the table like this--My prey is just screwed. My grand prey is
>in a very safe spot, in fact, the best, and it is in their best interest to not
>anger me, as they can easily gat a VP by the time I get to them, and it is
>perfectly likely that they will have enough momentum by then to keep going by
>the time I get to them. My predator is mostly screwed, but I'm not above making
>a "I'll split 3/2 with you, rather than get you ousted" deal with them, if I
>think I can pull it off. My grand predator is going to have a lot of trouble
>with their predator (as they are in the best spot at the table), and will be
>benefitting from my abuse of my predator. If someone across the table decides
>to bust up this wonderful environment, again, I am not above making them lose
>with me. This is not something I want to do, but will if pushed into it.

Yep. But again, I rely on the fact that it's not something you WANT
to do. =) I won't chuck TOO many points of damage around early on...
but without any deal in place, I will make sure that a few land down
there. Can't have you getting 5 minions in a comfortable position and
be able to wipe out anything nearby as necessary.

>>>So my prey should be getting low quickly from our combined efforts,
>and your prey will be getting low quickly as well. As soon as my prey
>gets within oust reach, all my votes are going to start going 2-2 or
>1-3: 1 to him, 3 to you, and if you live through the turn through
>sheer amounts of pre-existing pool, I should still be able to retain
>enough minions to zap you on my NEXT turn.>>
>
>And again, if this becomes the case, we both lose--you spend your effort
>getting me ousted, and I spend my effort killing you. The table is completely
>destabilized and someone else is going to win. I don't sign up for these
>situations, but will play them out if someone else volunteers me.

Well, no play is COMPLETELY without risk. I'm betting that I can draw
the cards quickly enough, with enough actions, to get you BEFORE you
can even Rush me. If I fail, I'm also betting that you don't
completely kill all my vamps, which will hopefully leave me in
position to oust you NEXT turn... and will gain me 2 VPs as opposed to
the 1VP I am pretty much guaranteed if I just zotz my prey and ignore
you. =)

I might lose, and get us both ousted. But I might win, and get 3 or
more VP; definitely worth the risk.

>>>See, I play combat decks. I know better than to let them get into a
>nice stable position with lots of minions and comfortable pool. =)
>You have to kick the legs out from under them early on.>>
>
>But if you do this from across the table, you'll get killed--I expect this from
>my predator or prey, but my grand predator has no buisiness doing this, and
>I'll act accordingly. What is the point of playing a deck that has the
>capability of going completely rogue if you aren't going to take advantage of
>it if you need to?

...What's the point of going rogue if you know it won't actually stop
the person from taking those actions?? Nice little vicious circle,
no?

>:-)

O=)

>>>Getting 1 VP is not winning, though.>>
>
>No, it isn't, but it is better than 0 VPs. If my prey is going to do everything
>in their power to deny me a VP (i.e. never getting out a single vampire the
>whole game), I figure that getting 1 is a fine way to settle.

True, but it does begin to argue against the deck TYPE. Intercept
decks can get 2VPs consistently; this a flaw in their deck type, not
in the play of the people next to them. Rush decks can be best
defended against by not getting out more than 1/2 vampires and hoping
your grandpredator packed his Obediences that day, or that someone
else will kindly rescue your guys from torpor.

>>>A couple tournaments ago, I brought my flung-junk deck with bleed
>enhancements. It pretty much terrorized everywhere it was near, but
>only gained 1VP the entire day. Why? Two Dramatic Upheavals; one to
>move me next to somewhere they thought I would be forced to do damage
>to another deck (in front of the stealth bleed deck while I had only
>two bleed cards in hand, giving the deck a free turn at me ANYWAY),
>and one to swap with me when my vampire-less prey was at 3 pool, and I
>had the Legal Manip in hand.>>
>
>Sometimes you get screwed.

Yeah, but there are a LOT of Dramatic Upheavals in tournaments, was my
point. This isn't too uncommon to see.

>popular, but NOT Rush decks (for the reasons all over this thread).
>It's not that I don't think that Potence IG needs to exist, it's just
>that encouraging Rush combat in varied forms as a strategy is likely
>to lead to madness.>>
>
>Nah. I don't think it would lead to madness. I think it would lead to a shift
>in the environment. If, suddenly, the Assamites became viable somehow (which
>would take quite a bit of work, mind you...), some of the folks who were
>playing IG Rush might switch to Assamite Rush, which would make no difference
>to the non combat decks (you get killed by combat or you don't), but would
>trump the IG decks something fierce. Thus, the IG decks would probably fade out
>of the circut.

unless, of course, the IG decks shifted to the pot/CEL paradigm, which
could pack as many maneuvers as the Assamite Rush decks. And they
would slaughter each other and remain in the circuit.

I don't think Assamite Rush would necessarily trump IG Rush.

>>>"Fear of having to sit next to you" isn't an incentive?>>
>
>It is worth worrying about that later on, if you get a VP out of it.

Goodness, no. 3VP over 3 rounds won't make the final. =) At some
point you're going to have to thump an entire table. Some
opportunities are better than others. ;)

>>>I went over the grandpredator bit above. A wise grandprey would begin
>making sure his predator never quite entirely died, by whatever means
>necessary (rescuing the Prince so he can 5th and possibly Minion Tap),
>using the excuse "I don't want to have to sit next to it." If nothing
>else, it slows you down and could put a real wrench in things.>>
>
>Could. Or, my grand prey could completely ignore me and attempt to get as many
>VPs as possible before I got to him. Might even make a deal with me.

He could. I wouldn't; not right away, at least. I'd wait to see if
your deck rush-jammed, or whatevered, before being TOO nice about
anything. And in the meantime, I would set up into a good strong
position, possibly oust my prey if I get the option... maybe not.
This also depends on what OTHER decks are threats at the table, too,
since I'm in the best position.

>>>Right. I'm not attempting to justify THAT worldview. I just want to
>see lots more new bruise-and-X options, as opposed to lots more Rush
>options.>>
>
>That'd be interesting, but I still don't think it would be any more effective.

wow, I dunno about THAT. bruise-and-vote with the !Brujah is a
particularly vicious way to go (stealth = Torn Signpost), and a lot of
clans are better designed for bruise-and-X than they are for just
bruise. Toreador, Tremere, even the Brujah.



Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Derek wrote:
>>Hm. I always look at it a bit differently; 14 cards is ONLY 14 cards,
and if I jump you with 3 guys in the same turn, you'll likely be out
after the first combat (i'm fond of Celerity; it lets me use things
like "press to continue" after that silly Skin of Steel, and it lets
me use things like "Blur" to avoid that pesky Superior Mettle, and
Dodge makes me laugh) and the next two people are going to be just so
many body parts.>>

True, true, but more often than not, it is that one guy that survives that gets
me killed. Most people around here seem to have the attitude of "Well, unless I
can stop every single attack you make, I am removed from the game just 'cause I
sat next to you...", which simply isn't the case. It is that one guy my
predator has that I really need to kill, lest I get bled for 6 and ousted on
his next turn, who manages to survive due to a couple Flashes or something, and
leaves me with a rushless hand jam, and then kills me where this whole thing
falls apart. The Rush deck lives on a knife edge, as you well know...

>>I've never been sure what the point IS of it all, actually.>>

Well, as far as I can tell from my own scattered logic, here is how I see the
game: If I bleed you for 6, that is one less 6 point vampire you can bring out.
If this is early in the game (i.e. before you get out all the vampires you
planned on getting out in the first place), he result is identical to had I
burned a vampire--you are out 6 pool, and have no 6 point vampire. If this
happens later on (after all your vampires are out that you plan on getting
out), that is still one less 6 point vampire you have access to. If you had the
6 pool still, you could have made another vampire. 'Cause you don't have it any
more, you can't. The potential is gone. In many situations, burning a 6 point
vampire is far worse than just losing 6 pool (it has all sorts of
equipment/retainers; it is the most important vampire you have, and you don't
have another one in your crypt), and in many situations it isn't (you have
minion tapped it for all of its blood; you have another in your crypt just
waiting to get out), so the specifics of the situation is a wash. The effect on
my grand prey is similar--if I bleed them for 6, that is one less 6 point
vampire to affect them. If I burn a 6 point vampire, that is one less 6 point
vampire to affect them. Either way, it is a 6 point loss for my prey, and 6
points less of pressure on my grand prey.

>>I just don't think that a 6 point minion is worth 6 pool -except- as far as
how much it costs to bring them out. Once they're out, they become
worth more or less than 6 pool rapidly.>>

That is why you have to kill them before this amount changes :-)

In a recent tournament experience, my prey was playing some !Ven deck. He got
out his first 7 or 8 point vampire, not knowing what my deck did, and I
torporized him immediately. He then got out his next middle sized vampire (Why?
I dunno. He had some fortitude? Maybe he didn't think I could do it again?
Maybe he just wanted to try?),and I torporized it immediately again. He was now
out, like, 15 pool in vampires, and a couple points from me bleeding him,
leaving him at, like, 11-12 pool with no active minions. The result is very
similar to if I had just bled him for an awful lot really quickly--with little
pool and limited vampires. He then chose to get out another vampire (Again, I
don't know why. Maybe he didn't want to sit around at the table and do
nothing.), which I Famed, and killed. I ousted him very quickly after that. The
pointof this story? Sometimes killing vampires is more effective than just
bleeding. Sometimes not.

>>But the decks with the most VP going into the finals have choice of
seating. Sometimes that's good; in the case of Rush and intercept
decks, though you might find that vulnerable people refuse to sit near
you. I got to the finals of one War Room tourney with Hideous
Tzimisce Intercept and had to sit 2nd; three other people deliberately
chose to sit as far away from me as possible. Oops.>>

Seating is key in the finals. Far more important than what deck you happen to
have.

>>Nah. That's not loose cannon. There's only two logical ways for 3/1
to go, you know: prey/grandprey, or prey/predator. The first is
aggressive, the second is solidifying. But neither is random.
Chucking it to your grandpredator, on the other hand, is pretty damn
random, or doing 1/3 to prey/grandprey, etc...>>

Ohh. I misunderstood--I thought you were doing 1 to your prey and 3 to me. If
you were doing 3 to your prey and 1 to me, I wouldn't care at all. That
wouldn't cause any recklessness. I might make threats, but I wouldn't damage my
position over it.

>>I am also comfortable with both of us losing, in that situation. If I
blithely oust my prey while not touching you, I am going to be in the
same position my prey was in at the start of the game; screwed, except
you'll have a lot more minions and a REAL incentive to nuke me. This
gets me dead. Since 1VP isn't sufficient to win, I'll go ahead and
sacrifice the sure 1VP to give myself a chance at 3. (if I get you, I
get your vampire-less prey as well.)>>

But is it worth doing this at the risk of incurring the wrath of your grand
prey? You are already having to deal with two players--why make it three?

>>It's not to your benefit either though. I assume that people are
going to make their best attempt to gain something for themselves;
odds are you end up accepting the 'trap deal', since it makes the most
sense for both of us as opposed to nuking each other and letting the
guy between us sweep. But it also gives me lots of time to set up for
the big kaboom at the end, where I either gain 3 all at once and
possibly sweep, or I fail to draw into cards and explode gloriously.>>

Ahh, I am always a big fan of the glorious explosion...

>>Yeah, but there are a LOT of Dramatic Upheavals in tournaments, was my
point. This isn't too uncommon to see.>>

I don't see them that often, and wonder why...

>>unless, of course, the IG decks shifted to the pot/CEL paradigm, which
could pack as many maneuvers as the Assamite Rush decks. And they
would slaughter each other and remain in the circuit.

I don't think Assamite Rush would necessarily trump IG Rush.>>

Well, the long range Assamite CEL/qui deck would kill the IG close range deck
quite nicely--the IG deck just can't have that many manuvers, where the CEL
deck can.

>>Goodness, no. 3VP over 3 rounds won't make the final. =) At some
point you're going to have to thump an entire table. Some
opportunities are better than others. ;)>>

In all likelyhood, you aren't going to see a Rush deck in more than one game.
If you sweep 2 tables, and happily take the 1 VP in the game with the Rush
deck, you are set.

>>wow, I dunno about THAT. bruise-and-vote with the !Brujah is a
particularly vicious way to go (stealth = Torn Signpost), and a lot of
clans are better designed for bruise-and-X than they are for just
bruise. Toreador, Tremere, even the Brujah.>>

I have never found Bruise/Anything to work so well for the obvious reasons--you
need to mix up card types, so you never have the right ones when you need them;
your combat cards don't do you any good when no one blocks you, and they just
jam up your hand; you have limited ways to defend yourself against your
predator. More cards that make Bruise/X work just, well, aren't going to work.



Messages.Author: Pat Ricochet
Messages.Body:
> On Wed, 11 Apr 2001, Derek Ray wrote:
>
>> He played it in the Atlanta qualifier and made it to the finals,
>> finishing 2nd there on a tiebreaker. The way you survive with a deck
>> like that (and the way he made it there) is to sit quietly at first,
>> gain some minions on the cheap, Deflect a bleed for 1 or 2
>> occasionally, hunt, and then bleed with 5 minions for 17 on about turn
>> 6, with ridiculous amounts of Bonding, Sleeping Mind, and Seduction.
>
>> -- Derek
>
> As the player of the Rush deck at the Atlanta qualifiers,
> I'll just hop in here and note bemusedly that the only round in which *I*
> had much luck with the deck was the third, in which Pat was my prey,
> the woman from LA with the weeny OBF bleed was grand-prey, and Ass-mites
> as predator.

Robin's Nossie bloat was your predator, actually. Getting hammered hard
by weenie bleed, so it wasn't doing much.

> It was an interesting example of the table-control that a
> good rush deck must establish, as I needed to leave Pat with enough
> minions to keep his prey down, who was Tributing like mad, but still keep
> in the kill zone (note.... the deck was smattered with Presence bleed and
> so not technically a completely focussed rush-deck, but the emphasis by
> far was on rush).

Which helped you in this game, by my look at it. You always had a rush
when you needed it, but got me ousted by the last bleed of one. If you had
had no Legals, that would have been an entire turn more, and that turn would
have been enough for me to dump my hand out bleeding Niki, possibly getting
her. (damn you! =)

> In this case, the crypt machine was good, since it gave
> me plenty of targets to keep cycling while still focusing almost
> exclusively on my prey, so I don't think it was too "destablizing" in the
> way you guys are discussing.

And yet, as you said, it subverted the rush deck paradigm. Unless you
killed all my guys dead, I could Govern out more guys, which brings out
minions without spending their full pool cost. I was bringing out more
guys, but killing a 4-cap after 5-cap after 4-cap wasn't costing me 4 and 5
pool to replace each time. It was costing me 1 pool. =)
Now, the "solution" to this, by the Bajika school of Rush, is to kill
ALL my guys, period. Niki *definitely* would have blown through Robin
earlier, not needing to leave anyone untapped, ever. And then have too many
minions for you to rush all of.
Also, that was a 4 player game, which is much easier for the Rush deck
to fight with everyone, which you did, some, than in a 5 player game.
Beating up on me gives your grandprey who IS your grandpredator free reign,
who beats up on your predator. Rob Treasure detailed this dynamic for 4 and
5 player games in a recent newsletter. He pretty much stuffed it in one
sentence, like "A kills B, C kills D, and A and C play the 2 player game."
Which, despite the *very* good game of complete table management it was,
for all 4 players, (all players agreed, one of the best games we've played
in a tournament) is what it came down to. You killed me, Niki killed
Robin, and then Niki got you. Despite your best efforts, you had to keep me
down enough to keep me from ousting, allowing Niki to blow through even
Robin's bloat.

I think you got the 1 VP that you could get guaranteed, since the Crypt
Machine has *0* combat defense (other than the Coven =). You could have
gotten that VP earlier, even, but would have thrown away any shot at 3 VP.

--
Pat Ricochet
Soul Jar'rn Fool of Atlanta

> I've never been sure what the point IS of it all, actually. I just
> don't think that a 6 point minion is worth 6 pool -except- as far as

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
>
> (my newsreader is pissing me off and the messages I am trying to respond to
> aren't showing up. My apologies for these being in the wrong place...)
>
> Fred wrote:
> >>I guess I could say, please see my reply to James. People don't think twice
> about including bleed defense because it's much easier to include and doesn't
> leave your offense starving for deck space.>>
>
> That, and you are much more likely to need bleed defense. Thus, bleed defense
> is sort of a no brainer. Combat defense, on the other hand, is much less likely
> to be needed. By choosing to not include it, you are making an informed
> decision to leave a hole (albeit a small one) in your deck strategy.

You act as if you're making this decision in a complete vacuum. Like having a
bleed defense is a matter of pushing a button and an automated arm comes out and
drops combat cards in your deck and it's done. But the question of the which decks
you're going to encounter is not the only one which matters. There's also the
question of what it does to your deck to try to defend against them and of what
use are the cards you use to defend against them in doing anything else.

This is the Necropotence deck experience all over again. There's a deck out there
that can hose Necropotence (in Magic during the "Black Summer") but it's useless
against anything else. So it's not really an effective answer in the metagame.

> >>This is similar to the Magic "Black Summer" when Necropotence decks were all
> the rage. There was Necropotence, anti-Necropotence, and a few other popular,
> more balanced deck types. People would say, "Well, Necropotence isn't overpowered
> because you can build decks to hose it." You could, but you'd never win the
> tournament because they wouldn't win against anything else. People mostly just
> decided they'd rather build another Necro deck and take there chances against
> the other Necro decks. It was a decidedly unfun summer to bother with.>>
>
> But you don't need to build specific anti-combat decks to stop a combat deck.
> You need to have enough combat defense to slow them down, throw off their
> momentum, and get them killed.

(Sigh.) For the umpteenth time, if all you're trying to do is, "get them killed"
this isn't an answer. This just means you're surviving, limping away with your
ass. I can build defenses against bleed and vote that allow me an offense as well.
Which just reinforces my original point: Combat decks just fuck the guys they sit
down next to. Woopee, I can throw a bunch of combat cards into my deck and slow
down how quickly that thug next door waxes my minions. Wake me when it's over so
I can count the number of ousts my prey has achieved in the meantime...

Fred

Well, assuming the attempts to oust it the first turn are successful. It

and/or the rusher may find himself compelled to rush the minions of other

Yea, you're right as far as that goes but reality is often more complicated

(and its predator identifies it as being out of Rush actions, an
important concept; outright lying has saved MY butt numerous times)
it's dead in the water. A deckful of combat cards is worthless
without a way to get into combat, and so i've grown skittish of
putting -that- many combat cards in unless I can back them up with
permanent Rush or something. (Templar = rewly)

>>>I've never been sure what the point IS of it all, actually.>>
>

>game: If I bleed you for 6, that is one less 6 point vampire you can bring out.

If it's early in the game. If it's later in the game, I'm 6 pool
closer to being ousted that I wasn't going to use on vampires at ALL.

>If this is early in the game (i.e. before you get out all the vampires you
>planned on getting out in the first place), he result is identical to had I
>burned a vampire--you are out 6 pool, and have no 6 point vampire. If this

Right. Early in the game, the 6 pool = 6 point vampire is a valid
comparison; either you need to GET a 6 point vampire, or you just GOT
a 6 point vampire.

>happens later on (after all your vampires are out that you plan on getting
>out), that is still one less 6 point vampire you have access to. If you had the
>6 pool still, you could have made another vampire. 'Cause you don't have it any
>more, you can't. The potential is gone. In many situations, burning a 6 point

But in most cases, the potential remains unused. It's just 6 pool,
and it's there merely to serve as an "oust timer". So a bleed for 6
EARLY denies resources, but a bleed for 6 late is just closer to the
actual oust.

>vampire is far worse than just losing 6 pool (it has all sorts of
>equipment/retainers; it is the most important vampire you have, and you don't

This is where I don't agree. I don't consider it a wash at all; I
consider it to be far too situational to be pigeonholed in this
manner. It's GOING to be worth more or less than 6 pool at that point
in the game; either you totally need that vampire, or you're just
lobbing someone out there with full blood to take rescue actions and
be a target/disposable blocker.
