extra Master Phases playing vastly more useful cards.

> So what your analysis fails to show above is that to get that same 2
> pool, there has to be another ascendance choking up your hand....

Unless you play with poor players, small card limits, and/or libraries
larger than 90 cards (all of which means your person experience can't be
compared to ANY useful discussion here), games just DON'T last that long. A
"quick" game is about 8 turns, a normal game 11 or 12, a "long" game
somewhat more than that.
With only 12 Master Phases, on average, for ALL game, you want to spend
4 of them, a third of your Master resources, on gaining 2 pool?! I can play
one Blood Doll, and easily gain 2 pool from that without affecting the
usefulness of the vampire I took the 2 blood from.

If you think Ascendance sucks, keep in mind that it's one card. If you
put in all of 2 Ascendances, you gain 2 pool in half the time, and half the
MPA's of the STI. STI might as well read: "Gain 2 pool; lose 4 Master Phase
actions."

Consider this: You might argue "what are you crazy what about the
Parthenon? i have it in every deck and take 2 pool off my STIs every turn"
Okay. Parthenon: Pay 2 pool to gain X master phase actions, where X is
the number of turns left in the game. Play one STI immediately, and take 2
off next turn. And 1 the turn after that. Card slots in your deck: 2.
MPA's used: 2. Net gain: 0.
Put in 2 Ascendances, instead. Card slots: 2. MPA's used: 2. Net gain:
2.
Okay, put in another STI:
Turn 1: Parthenon, STI. -3 pool
Turn 2: Get 2 pool back. -1 pool.
Turn 3: Get 1 pool back (burn STI), play STI. -1 pool.
Turn 4: Get 2 pool back. +1 pool.
Turn 5: Get 1 pool back (burn STI), and play your favorite Master. +2 pool.

Let's put in 3 Ascendance instead:
Turn 1: Ascendance: +1 pool.
Turn 1: Ascendance: +2 pool.
Turn 1: Ascendance: +3 pool.
Turn 4: Play your favorite Master.
Turn 5: Play your next favorite Master (say, a Storage Annex, to keep away
from Master hand jam)

BOTH take up 3 Master slots. Ascendance isn't jamming your hand any
more than the Parthenon/STI combo at even 2 STI's, and you're still an MPA
ahead WITHOUT the Parthenon. If you think Ascendance sucks, STI sucks MORE,
even WITH the Parthenon.
Not to mention that trick requires the Parthenon to show up *first* in
that combo. If you put in one copy, it'll show up, on average, halfway down
your deck (I'll give you the benefit of the doubt that you design and play
your decks not to have cards left over at the end of the game) meaning, on
turn 6. If the STI's show up after that, you've gained 3 pool, and the game
is almost over. If they show up before that, you'll be on turn 8 before
you've gained the 4 pool the STI's and the 8 MPA's get you. If you put in
*more* copies of the Parthenon, *they* can jam your hand as bad or worse as
any Ascendance.

Now, don't get me wrong: I think Ascendance is a waste of deck space.
it sucks.
But, Ascendance sucks and "STI rocks?" I hope you meant to say "STI
sucks rocks."

Let's talk "same card slot" math for a second: If I put 1 Ascendance
in my deck, I gain 1 pool when I play it. Yay! I gained a pool.
This could save my ass from being ousted by an Anarch Revolt for one
extra turn.

If I put 1 STI in my deck, I have to survive an extra two turns after
I play it to gain 1 pool, AND I have to waste my next two Master
actions as well.

I could only see using STI's in a deck that chucked around Rumors of
Gehenna and Parthenon liberally; when you have 36 Master phases per
game, it makes a lot more sense to use 12 of them on something like 3
STI's. Although the net gain is STILL only 6 pool, you can at least
pull from your Investments as MPA filler when you don't have a Master
card in hand.

There's an interesting experiment - check your decks and see how much
pool you REALLY gain at any given point in time. Use 30 counters of
the same color to start with, and 15 of a separate color. Vampire
blood is always from the original 30. Anything that goes into your
pool somehow comes from the 15, and anything that comes out of -that-
pool goes into a separate container and isn't reused, so you can tell
how much you've actually gained at the end of the night. Should be
interesting to see if 6 is "lots", or 6 is "puny". I'm going to bet
on "puny" since things like a Consanguineous Boon will usually give
you a free 3-4, +1 for Bribes, +2 for Voter Cap... Tribute is at least
4, a Blood Doll will usually give about 3-4 all on its own, while a
Minion Tap is normally for at -least- 6. But I wonder if some decks
don't survive remarkably well with almost nothing like that.

Aw, cmon. It's USENET tradition to not back up what you say with
facts. Besides, how else would people get good, honest flamewars
started?

Although I think you had it here simplest, and Talonz should look at
it like this (restated in painfully-obvious mode):

You have approximately 12 turns in a game. Yes, we DID test this by
keeping track over about 3 months, and at several different
tournaments. Games rarely if EVER last longer than 15 turns, and
12-13 is easily the average.

By extension, you have approximately 12 Master Phase Actions in any
game. Parthenon and Rumors will double or triple this, of course, but
for now we'll leave those out to make things simple.

A Short Term Investment costs 1 pool, and requires 1 MPA to play.

To make playing an STI a non-losing proposition (wasted MPA, and
negative pool), you MUST use an additional MPA at some point to take 1
pool back off the STI. So for the cost of 1 card slot in your deck
and 2 MPAs, you have successfully reached ground zero.

Twice in the future, you can then spend one MPA to gain a pool. This
totals out to 4 MPAs and a gain of 2 pool - a full THIRD of your total
MPAs for a game. You will only be playing 8 other Master cards this
game. Select carefully. You can conceivably be playing 10 other
Master cards this game, but in that case the STI is a wash, and why
did you bother to put it in your deck?

A much better option is to use the same MPA slot for a Blood Doll,
which can convert 2 vampire blood into the same 2 pool at the cost of
only 1 MPA - leaving you 3 free MPAs.

If you add things like the Parthenon and Rumors of Gehenna into your
deck, cards like STI become much more effective, as you suddenly have
the potential of 24 or 36 Master Phase Actions to play with. Since
you probably still haven't included much more than 18-20 Master cards
in your deck, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to determine that you
are likely to have spare MPAs lying around that a STI would fill
nicely.

However, two last thoughts: first, a Parthenon isn't guaranteed to
get out on turn 1, so you can't assume that the Parthenon
automatically doubles ALL your MPAs. It only doubles the ones after
it shows up.

And second, a Parthenon costs 2 pool, which is identical to the gain
from an STI. If you intend to use STI to gain pool in this fashion,
you may wish to include several.

>"You can't make a fact out of an opinion by raising your voice."

Spurious logic. First show how "used in winning decks" necessarily implies

The reason not to neuter the most-used card for merely being most-used is
trivially shown by applying the method (neuter the most-used cards)
iteratively.

> [...]

> If the cards were given MRP of this form in Final Nights then, using
> LSJ's sophistry, this wouldn't be errata.

It's not sophistry, it's just definitions. And it's not just "my" defintions,
it's standard usage. Errata is the term used for a list of corrigenda, or
for the corrigenda themselves. A corrigendum is a change made that doesn't
get made in the actual printed material but rather gets made too late to
be included in the printed work and is shown on another medium. Changes from
1st edition to 2nd edition of a printed work (that appear in the 2nd printing
of the work) are not errata after the 2nd printing is made. See Webster.

Conversely, attempting to call printed card text "errata" would be sophistry
if it were clever.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson

On Tue, 24 Apr 2001 08:55:36 -0400, LSJ wrote:

>Right. So we agree that your previously-stated (although somehow snipped from
>above) conditions are not sufficient to show that a card is broken.

What they demonstrate is that the game is broken. You can express the
problem in two ways - that the overused cards are too good or that the
underused cards are not good enough. How do you choose between these
two positions? What determines the correct balance point or norm?

In the case of the pool gain cards, we have two cards that are used
almost exclusively and ten or more cards that are little used
(Ascendance, Powerbases, Investments, etc). It's natural to focus
first on the exceptional cases - are these the source of the trouble?

It could be that if these two cards were amended to make them weaker
then they would just join the other cards in oblivion. If levelling
down is likely to produce this result then one should consider
levelling up. This is more of a challenge. I could suggest sensible
improvements to each and every weak card but is such a program of
upgrades feasible? I did something of the sort in Shadowfist (the
RetroFist variant) and this was well received. Levelling down causes
trouble because unwary players are told that their cards no longer
perform as well as expected and this can hose their decks. Levelling
up is more acceptable, because, if there's a surprise, it tends to be
a pleasant one.

But which alternative would produce the best effect upon the metagame?
If pool gain were harder then then the game might be faster and that's
probably desirable. If pool gain were easier, then more strategic
options would be possible - players could have more minions and/or
better ones. That's good too.

Doing nothing is not an option if you are continuing to print new
cards. You could print new pool gain cards to replace the existing
coasters. You could print helper cards which magnify the poor cards
or hosers which hurt the good ones. But reprinting the existing cards
in amended form is the most efficient course because you have the art
and layout all ready to use.

If you'd rather level up than level down in this case, here's a
fitting upgrade for Ascendance:

Master. Gain 1 pool for each Ascendance in your ash pile.

I'm not quite sure what should be done about the Powerbases though. I
thought they were some good already but winning players think
otherwise and you can't argue with success.

Andrew

>see some better Necromancy cards in Final Nights. But will they help
>the existing ones?

In some ways, the very presence of other cards which encourage people to
make decks round them will help existing ones.

If we pass through Necromancy as a discipline, there are lots of really
quite usable cards in it. Spectral Divination is a nice utility card,
providing minor stealth and intercept, both of which are valuable to a
discipline. Whispers from the Dead is a good utility cards, allowing a
deck to adapt to the game (if you find your vote defence is useful, you
can recycle it, ditto bleed etc.) Soul Stealing is certainly very good,
hampered slightly by the current vampire selection (POT/NEC is
difficult, only two vampires) and also by the lack of a solid maneuver
in Necromancy, Dominate or Potence.[0] Jar the Soul has utility for tap
and bleed, though many people choose stealth and bleed in preference.
Possession has some good potential defensively, and also for interesting
Might of the Camarilla, Goodnight and Sabbat Inquisitor (or similar)
tricks. Spectral Intervention is a solid defensive combat card. Compel
the Spirit is good defensively, and has a gorgeous piece of artwork on
it, one of the best in the game. (Matt Green currently owns it, IIRC,
and I would sell body parts to steal it from him.)

Eyes of the Dead, Torment the Soul, Release of the Shackled Soul (due to
the rareness of allies, due to their power problem) and Death Pact are
all a bit sucky.

However, with the exception of Possession, none of the cards are
essential game-winners. None of them leap out and say "Build round me".
And with the problems that the Giovanni crypt selection gives us, we
have even more problems. And Possession requires weird crypt
one-trick-pony decks really.

More cards can give us exciting strategies. That, in itself, gives the
other cards more use. We have more vampires with sensible discipline
selections, and more necromancy cards. Building a solid Necromancy
based deck is no longer a chore, requiring intense effort and selection.
Spectral Divination becomes much more useful because we have more cards,
more vampires, more solid Necromancy decks, all[1] of which could quite
happily do with a little stealth, a little intercept, that dodge or
Combat Ends from Intervention, the burning blood from Soul Stealing and
so on.

That's Necromancy's bane at the moment. Quite a few really nice solid
support cards which are scuppered by vampire selection and nothing to
really go *well* with them.

[0] As a result, one card I'd like to see is a maneuver for Necromancy.
Maybe a maneuver at basic and some necromantic weirdness at superior, or
somesuch, making it doubly useful.

[1] Of course, not *all*. You know what I mean.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <3ae8d0aa.73613223@news>, Talo...@hotmail.com writes

>Not exactly the best example there. Dominate is widely regarded as
>the best disc out there, and necromancy, welll.......

Dominate is an excellent discipline. However, much of its power comes
through its diversity. It's an excellent solo discipline, along with
Fortitude.

Very few of the cards have ever been, intrinsically, broken. Thoughts
Betrayed and Mind Rape were two. However, in the current card set,
Dominate is not "broken". However, Necromancy is, currently,
under-powered. Not that its cards are intrinsically bad (some are), but
that it is hampered for a number of other reasons too.

That's the point that Andrew missed (intentionally, I feel).

That one card is less powerful than another doesn't make the better card
"broken". It *might* be, and cases can be made for such. However, it's
not a case-closed scenario. The difference may be slight. One card may
have a far greater utility value, the other being more corner case, but
equally excellent *in that corner case*. One might be slightly
under-average, the other slightly above average. The distance between
the two may be quite large, but their individual variance from the mean
is much smaller.

Moving from "Blood Doll is more powerful than STI" to "Blood Doll is
broken" is a potential argument to have. It needs, however, careful
statistical analysis, thoughtful examination, thorough discussion and
plenty of experience. Andrew provides none of that.

weenie bleed already hampers a number of strategies, including
(interestingly) those built around the Powerbases.

- if someone goes to steal from your Powerbase, they aren't bleeding

- it doesn't cost you anything to take counters OFF

effects automatically happen during your untap. You don't sacrifice
Master phases for it, meaning you can conceivably play:

on your first four turns, and just sit on your butt and defend those,
while gaining something around 3 pool per turn. (the Omaya deck does
just that.) Again, if people steal from your Powerbases... they
aren't bleeding you for 6. In any deck that can reliably stop casual
0- or 1-stealth "i grab the powerbase" actions, they're definitely
worth it.

Ok let's go back to the original point then and start at the top.
Minion Tap is broken - there is no question in my mind about this.
Why?

1. With a single master phase action you can score yourself up to 11
pool - a huge amount compared to other cards.

2. Return to Innocence was banned because it could generate pool
swings of this size. A precedent.

3. It can be readily combined with minion stealing cards like ToGP
and Hostile Takeover to loot and pillage other players' minions rather
than your own.

and refill the same minion.

>1. With a single master phase action you can score yourself up to 11

"Because". Justify that. You state it like fact, which it isn't.
There are *many* reasons why RtoI was banned. Pool swing was among
them, but wasn't the only one.

>3. It can be readily combined with minion stealing cards like ToGP
>and Hostile Takeover to loot and pillage other players' minions rather

Certainly. Which could already have been emptied, and which you've
quite possibly had to pay a great deal of pool for.

>4. It can be readily combined with 5th Tradition to repeatedly drain
>and refill the same minion.

True. That combos exist doesn't make one card broken. It might mean
there are several *good* cards which combo well together. Identifying
which one is the problem card takes time and effort.

The finger, there, could equally be levelled at 5th.

>5. With NCL there is no limit to the number that you may include in a
>deck.

Indeed not. But with NCL, you can be hoisted by your own petard, by
including too many. And it is very possible to include too many.

>6. It doesn't do what it says. You can Minion Tap a minion until it
>has no blood at all but it still isn't tapped.

Since when has a card's title counted for anything in mechanics?
Temptation of Greater Power doesn't mean you have greater power. Blood
Doll doesn't create a small plastic Barbie. Drain Essence drains some
blood, not some of a creature's essence. Short Term Investment can be
left for as long as you want, and a Protracted Investment can be emptied
first.

(By the way, Andrew, if you're going to troll intentionally, and want to
do it effectively, including pointless pieces of wank like this one give
them game away.)

>7. The empirical evidence from the analysis of winning decks

You have thrown together a few numbers.

Presenting numbers does not constitute "analysis". I sincerely hope any
person who's been involved in teaching you any mathematical or
scientific discipline wondered why you were so stupid.

>shows
>that this card is so effective at winning tournaments that it makes a
>wide swathe of lesser cards worthless.

Not true. Many other cars have places regarding blood and pool
management. However, their places are not necessarily the same place as
Minion Tap.

For instance, what *can't* Minion Tap do? It can't *lower* your pool
size, for a start. Nor can it add blood to a minion - one of Blood
Doll's great advantages. Blood Doll, once in play, can slowly lower
your pool if you want it, or it can slowly increase a vampire's blood,
and so on. Different functions.

The Investment style cards give you very different functions. They
don't allow blood management, only pool management. This, in and of
itself, means that they are extremely different cards. One powerful
function a card can have, regardless of what form it takes, is
flexibility. Blood Doll can help you defend your pool, deplete your
pool, defend a vampire or deplete a vampire depending on your needs.
Short Term, once in play, can only help you generate pool. That's all
it can do. Adding restrictions to Minion Tap/Blood Doll can't really
seriously affect that dual-edged flexibility.

Consider a hypothetical idea:

Parity Shift, in terms of pool swing, is the most powerful 'damage' vote
in the game. (Compare KRC and ConAg.) Yet its inherent restriction
comes from the fact that it can't be pulled off easily multiple times -
you end up with lots of pool - especially against a single target - they
end up with very little pool indeed.

Can Blood Doll help? Not easily. It's slow to pull off. Can Minion
Tap? Not at all. It can't deplete your pool rapidly at all.

Try an interesting idea for a vote deck, then.

Toreador vote, maybe a few Grand Balls to stop blocks (Toreador have
problems with stealth, of course). Presence helps the vote pass. Anson
would make a good 'key' vampire. Two votes and his extra master
special. Generate pool via Parity Shift. Deplete pool, as necessary,
via Secret Horde. Gather Secret Horde back via Anson and the Parthenon
as necessary. Pass Rumors, if necessary.

A game-winner? Potentially. It's not going to run riot round the
tournament scene, but it could do a lot towards shaking up a play-group.

That cards have limited applications (thus, their utility function is
much lower than a common or garden card) doesn't make them unplayable.
Creative thinking helps makes them playable. Intelligent playing and
deck construction - realising that two cards do *not* have the same
function and shouldn't be treated as carbon-copies except for one being
weaker than the other - contributes greatly.

Yes, a card can be difficult to use. It can be 'weak' even when it
works. However,

>If you have a better way of
>proving that a card is broken, then let's hear it.

Were any of your statements:

- true
- backed up with actual evidence, not proof through assertion
- weighty
- represented a view of things as a whole, not one small section

you might have a case to make. Thus far, you haven't done anything
beyond say "This is broken, hear me roar."

>A straw man. Cards don't have to be identical to be balanced

Balanced, no. But to have an identical power/utility function - what
you seem to want - they would.

Some cards being "below" the average and some being "above" will happen
in any situation where there is a differential. "Balanced" isn't a
single point, it's a grey area. Some cards are more 'powerful' than
others, some are less.

We all accept that there are some differences. Moving from "There are
differences" to "This card is broken" isn't a supportable proposition
without a *lot* (one helluva lot) more work on your part.

It surprised me too at first. The Parthenon would seem to be an
excellent card, allowing you two Master phases per turn... thus
letting you put many more Masters in your deck... and so on.

But what happens if you don't draw the Parthenon up early, and you've
included, say, 20 Masters? Well... you probably explode gloriously
with a handful of grey cards that you can't get rid of and can't play
quickly enough. Bad.

The immediate solution is to include more Parthenons. But then you
GUARANTEE that you'll be discarding the others later; and you've upped
it to say, 24 Masters now counting the extra copies. Is it REALLY
worth it to have 24/90 Masters in a deck? Perhaps if they're good
enough, and you can always play them... a few extra Golcondas, Hostile
Takeovers, and the like are never bad, and chucking two Hostile
Takeovers in a turn is usually enough to trash someone's game,
especially if you trick them into paying a large amount to keep their
vampire on the first one.

What it comes down to is that the Parthenon requires a lot more
support to use effectively than would be indicated at first glance -
simply chucking a bunch more Masters in your deck won't cut it.
Hence, the number of tournament winning decks who simply passed up the
Parthenon and put fewer Masters in to simplify the issue.

----
[The following numbers of Andrew's were taken out of only 87 decks,
indicating that multiple cards have been counted/used in some cases.
Right next to these numbers should be one reading how many of those
DECKS out of 87 actually used the card... unless that's what your
previous numbers were. Upon examination, they couldn't possibly have
been, as you have Minion Tap listed at '96', which is more than 87.
THOSE numbers would be lovely to have.]

>164 Minion Tap
>153 Blood Doll
> 90 Sudden Reversal

This is important, and while Direct Intervention is a fairly new card
(Sabbat), I would be curious to see how many winning decks were
carrying at least a copy of DI -- that number would surely reveal
something.

What it indicates is that the effects of Master cards are becoming so
widely varied, that it's almost NECESSARY to carry Sudden Reversals to
prevent them ruining your day. Especially with things like Temptation
of Greater Power, Hostile Takeover, etc. running around.

> 31 Tribute to the Master
> 27 The Parthenon
> 5 Ascendance
> 4 Short Term Investment
> 4 Powerbase
> 3 Blood Puppy
> 0 Protected Investment/Secret Horde

Not surprising: STI is better on the cost-to-MPA-to-pool ratio than
both. Protracted is pay 3, use 7, gain 3. STI is pay 1, use 4, gain
2. If you pay 3, Secret is just another Protracted. But if you pay
1, it's only a gain-1.

>So the fans of Ascendance can now claim a small victory over the
>supporters of STI. And the gulf between Minion Tap, Blood Doll and
>the rest is even greater than it first appeared.

Again, the numbers are somewhat misleading; multiple copies of a card
in a deck do not indicate as much as the card's very presence in a
deck would. Both numbers taken together side-by-side would provide a
very accurate picture, as it would show how many of any given card
tend to be put in a deck. I'd expect Sudden to show 1 or 2 per, and
be in almost EVERY deck, and MT/BD to show multiple per but not
necessarily be in every deck.

IF the numbers matched that, it would seem to indicate that Sudden is
a far more critical card to winning than Minion Tap or Blood Doll...
even though there's only 1 or 2 in a deck. You can poolgain in many
ways, but you HAVE to stop the crucial Hostile.

may change in the future with ridiculous pool-gain/Parthenon/Rumors of

master. However, this definitely indicates that at least one DI can
certainly save your ass if used at the right time - and it'd be good
to include one in each deck.

>>in a deck do not indicate as much as the card's very presence in a

>
>55 Blood Doll

and your numbers were:

164 Minion Tap
153 Blood Doll
90 Sudden Reversal

So that leaves us with:

a little less than a 4:1 ratio for Minion Taps/deck,
almost exactly a 3:1 ratio for Blood Dolls,
a bit less than a 2:1 ratio for Sudden Reversals,
and about a 1.5:1 ratio for Direct Interventions.

this seems fitting, and I'd say it adds Sudden Reversal and DI to the
list of "cards that should go in every tourney deck". Minion Tap
being a transient and Blood Doll being a permanent reasonably account
for the ratio point difference, and the Sudden/DI numbers also seem
logical.

>Note that this is more than half of the decks in every case. I'm not
>sure if this can be extrapolated to the field in general but it seems
>worse than the infamous Necro Summer of Magic during which 50% of the
>decks would typically be packing Necroptence.

However, this is the difference: as I understand the Necro Summer,
you either had Necropotence, or anti-Necropotence, or you died
miserably. The antis to MT/BD/SR/DI are not quite so 'direct'...
indeed, they're quite varied.

Minion Tap leaves you with a near-empty vampire. The problem doesn't
come in when Minion Tap gains you the pool - it comes when you find a
way to reload the vampire, meaning you have a resource for almost
free. There are numerous ways to reload the vamp - there are also
numerous ways to stop the reload (intercept is a biggie, but there's
always the old "beat their ass while they're empty" idea too). If you
didn't reload the vampire, he wouldn't have any blood to play all your
cool cards. =) And if you Minion Tap for 6 in the face of a Malk S&B
deck, you can rest assured that you've probably simply put a
'band-aid' onto a large, gaping wound.

Blood Doll is significantly stronger, permitting you to either drain
or assist the vampire as need be - and it's a permanent that can't be
removed. However, the fact that it can be a DRAIN on your pool (have
you never seen someone pushing 3-4 pool through multiple Blood Dolls
in order to arrange rescues from torpor, etc?) means it's definitely
not broken; it's simply an excellent resource management tool. The
Powerbases fall short not because of the blood gain - they fall short
because they do nothing BUT gain pool, and can't even put it onto your
vampires. With no blood on vampires, Blood Doll doesn't make pool
gain; and VERY frequently in the endgame, there's just no blood on
ANYONE's vamps.

Sudden Reversal and DI speak for themselves. But they cost your next
Master phase action, and if you don't have them in hand, you can't use
htem. If you put enough in the deck to have them in hand always, you
run out of room for the beneficial Masters, and you end up losing, as
you can't Sudden all your prey's AND predator's Masters.

What we have here is just simply a case of some cards being inferior
to the norm. If anything is to happen, it should be to improve the
Powerbases in some fashion... perhaps that Chicago automatically
gained a counter every untap, and you could burn a Master Phase to get
ALL the counters yourself, or anyone else could take a 0-stealth
action? Wild speculation, here, since wallpaper doesn't get upgraded
that much. :)

On Sun, 6 May 2001 18:50:09 +0200, "Roger Carhult"
<rogc...@student.luth.se> wrote:

>I can't think of any non-discipline (although I came to think of a few
>discipline ones now like Black Metamorphosis) non-directed actioncard at the
>momment that isn't at +1 stealth, and most disciplinecards are as well. Also

Classifying 5th as "non-discipline" is technically accurate, but not
necessarily a good measure: it requires a Prince or Justicar, which
is its own restriction. Same with Blood Hunt and the Traditions -
sure, they're disciplineless, but they need a Prince/Justicar.

Of the totally restrictionless actions, there are several exceptions:
Cull the Herd and Blood Bond have +1 stealth despite being (D), while
Revelation of the Sire has NO stealth itself.

>most directed ones aren't at stealth either unless they're disciplinecards
>where the superior version adds a stealth (e.g. Mind Nimb). Maybe it's just
>an impression I've got that nobody else have, but when you look at the game
>overall it's pretty much like this.

"pretty much" isn't a basis for a good assessment, though, what with
all the exceptions floating around.

A better one would be that the cards which produce powerful effects
tend to either have high blood cost (Blood Bond's 2 blood) or zero
stealth (Arson, Black Metamorphosis, Shadow of the Beast) or require
superior in a discipline (Mind Numb, the Haunting). The weaker effects
(Rave, the Embrace, Army of Rats) come with a built-in stealth to make
them even worth doing in the first place; if you notice, very few of
the no-restriction, low-cost cards do very much at all.

Messages.Body:
On Sun, 6 May 2001 22:53:46 +0000 (UTC), go...@best.com (Gomi no
Sensei) wrote:

>In article <tf4bft8fjcvbpn6h7...@4ax.com>,
>Derek Ray <lor...@yahoo.com> wrote:
>
>[minion tap v. 5th]

Warning. Long post. Mash "N" now if you don't want to see an
in-depth analysis. =/

>note that the Sabbat have a perfectly useful equivalent to
>Minion Tap/Fifth: Tribute/Blood Feast. It's slightly more
>limited in its realistically attainable maximum pool gain
>per cycle (MT/5th: 6-9 pool, TttM/BF: 3-6 pool), but works
>in quite an analogous fashion. Both can increase to theoretical
>infinity (with capacity-increasing cards for MT/5th and Embraces
>for Tribute/Feast).

Blood Feast is a great card, and TM/BF is certainly a nice combo. But
the comparison tends to fall short when put into practice. =/ (see
below)

>But both involve a master card that moves vampire blood to
>Methuselah pool, followed by an +1 stealth action requiring
>a title that replaces the vampire blood just lost.

Correct - and again, there are a couple of gotchas involved.

>Kendrick and Korah are the cheapest vampires able to play Blood
>Feast, at 7 capacity. While, with Tap/Fifth, lower capacity makes
>the combo less effective, Tribute/Feast works better with a lower
>cap titled guy since you can afford more guys to Tribute.

Here's the problem. Let's compare the two deck styles. Minion
Tap/5th requires large titled vampires - lending itself well to a vote
deck. TM/BF requires a large number of vampires - lending itself well
to a weenie lemming horde bleed-deck. So trying to build each of
these...

Kendrick/Korah are 7-caps with Obfuscate; this permits you to use
Forgotten Labyrinth on your Blood Feast and pretty much guarantee it
actually happening. The rest of your crypt can be a bunch of 2-caps
(if you Tribute away from a 1-cap, he has to hunt, rendering Blood
Feast worthless) - which gives you a risk of crypt-screw right away if
you don't get Kendrick or Korah early on. Safest bet is 2 Kendrick
and 2 Korah - with 4 out of 12, you should almost always have 1 in
your opening crypt.

To even the playing field, let's use Murat, Nikolaus, Greger, and
Gilbert - who are also 7-caps with Obfuscate, letting you drop
Forgotten Labyrinth on your 5th Tradition. The rest of your crypt can
be any Prince or Justicar of any capacity; restricting ourselves to
big ones with some form of OBF, we find Lucian, Sheldon, Selma, Klaus,
Francois, Suhailah, and Queen Anne. That gives us 11 vamps; and I'd
probably choose to add Lucretia in here as the 12th. She can't use
the Traditions, but as a 10-cap she makes an excellent Minion Tap
target, and her +1 stealth on all actions can't help but be good.
Here also, with 4 out of 12, you should almost always have a 7-cap in
your opening crypt; but you have no duplicates, and even if you get a
poor draw, your larger vamps can still 5th with OBF. Also, with 5
Nossies, you can include some of the Nosferatu clan toys - and if
you're brave, you can use the 3 Malkavians in the same way.

The crypt selection is definitely in favor of MT/5th.

Let's assume that you get good seating position (3rd) and an excellent
crypt draw; Kendrick and three 2-caps for the Sabbat, and Nikolaus,
Selma, Sheldon, and Lucian for the Camarilla. On turn three, both
decks are ready for their first action. Let's also assume that
libraries flow perfectly, just to simplify things - and nobody
voluntarily lowers themselves to a level where they can't play
Forgotten Labyrinth. Total pool amounts assume no predator, again to
simplify things.

Turn 3:

Camarilla: Nikolaus uses his special to move 1 blood to Sheldon.
Minion Tap for 4, then Nikolaus plays 5th Tradition on himself to
refill completely. 4 transfers to Sheldon, and done. Total pool:
23.

Sabbat: Tribute from Kendrick for 1, and whether he plays Blood Feast
or not, his blood level remains at 6. 4 transfers, bringing out two
2-caps, and done. Total pool: 20.

Turn 4:

Camarilla: Nikolaus doesn't use his special (pointless), Minion Tap
for 5, and he plays 5th tradition to refill. 4 more transfers,
Sheldon comes out, and done. Total pool: 24.

Sabbat: Tribute for 3, then Kendrick plays Blood Feast. The two
2-caps can take an action if they choose, and Kendrick's blood level
is currently at 5. Transfer 2, bring out the next 2-cap, and done.
Total pool: 21.

Turn 5:

Camarilla: Minion Tap Sheldon for 7. Sheldon plays 5th Tradition on
himself, refilling. Nikolaus may take an action - with 5 votes on the
table already, he has a good chance of passing his vote. 4 transfers
to Selma, and done. Total pool: 27.

Sabbat: Tribute for 4, and Kendrick plays Blood Feast (4 blood left
afterwards). The three two-caps may take actions. Spend 1 and 4
transfers, see the next vampire (a 2-cap), and done. Total pool: 24.

Turn 6:

Camarilla: Minion Tap Sheldon for 8. Nikolaus plays 5th on Sheldon.
Sheldon may call a vote, again with the 5 table votes. 4 transfers to
Selma, who comes out, and done. Total pool: 31.

Sabbat: Tribute for 4, Kendrick plays Blood Feast (3 blood left
afterwards). Three 2-caps may take actions, transfer 2 to the next
vampire who comes out. Total pool: 26.

So we're more or less one-third to halfway through the game. The
Camarilla bloat deck is 5 pool ahead; not an incredible amount, but
let's look at the inherent advantages.

The Camarilla deck has 3 minions and 7 table votes - its primary
offense. All its votes can be called with Forgotten Labyrinth if
necessary, which you are also using for your 5th Traditions and
therefore probably have in hand at any given time. We assumed that it
had no predator, but if necessary it can use 2nd Traditions to stop
actions that simply don't need to happen, with a good probability of
success. More likely, though, it has simply been ignoring its
predator, since it's gaining pool like mad. It can continue to do
this at the rate of 8 per turn, since now Nikolaus and Selma can each
spend a bit of their blood to take the "refill Sheldon" action -- and
with 7 votes, it may not be necessary to attempt to bring out Lucian
yet, although I'd probably put 6 blood on him and let it sit for
awhile.

The Sabbat deck has 5 minions and 3 table votes, but this isn't its
primary offense. Or should it be? It has 4 weenies available for its
use, but they have almost no disciplines in common - so are they
simply playing Computer Hacks each turn, and using disciplineless
Dodge and Fake Out cards to save themselves? Possibly, and this could
conceivably overwhelm a prey. Trying to have them call votes isn't
necessarily the best idea, with only 3 votes available; Bribes is not
a bad option, but it only goes so far. Early Crusades might help get
a voter deck up and running, but the weenies' votes will only be at +1
stealth due to a lack of OBF. And there is no equivalent for 2nd
Tradition in the Sabbat, so this deck relies a LOT more on its pool
gain working properly. Worst of all, Kendrick can only go one more
turn before the Tribute reduces him to 1 blood - and he no longer has
the protection of Forgotten Labyrinth on the Blood Feast.

So how to put a wedge in the pool gain? Obviously, kill the early
vampire with a Rush deck. (Any deck capable of consistently
generating +3 intercept will do, also; such decks are extremely rare,
however.)

If you kill Nikolaus after his first MT/5th, Sheldon still comes out
next turn. It's a swing of 5 pool and 2 votes, but Sheldon can
immediately 5th Nikolaus, who can then rescue himself with Forgotten
Labyrinth; the machine is back, merely slowed down. The ability to
play 5th Tradition on a vampire in torpor is huge. (The observant
reader will note that 6 of the above-listed vampires have Fortitude,
potentially making it quite difficult to even kill them.)

If you EVER kill Kendrick, the deck is in bad shape. The weenies must
immediately all take +1 stealth actions to rescue Kendrick, who will
have to hunt at +1 stealth - a prime intercept target. The weenies
themselves can still be Tributed from, so your pool gain is not in
quite as bad shape; but every so often they're going to have to be
taking hunt actions until they successfully get Kendrick back and keep
him - and then the problem comes of how to refill Kendrick enough so
that he can keep taking Blood Feast actions? The TM/BF combo removes
one from him every turn, necessitating that at some point he get a
Palatial Estate, Rack, or Hunting Ground - slowing down your pool
gain.

How about Sudden the pool grab? Well, Sudden Reversal hurts both
decks about equally, really; the Camarilla deck can still get Sheldon
and have 5 votes and 2 vamps for only 15 pool, while the Sabbat deck
can still quickly get the three weenies and at least have numerical
actions on its side for 13 pool.

How to improve the Sabbat deck, which is falling way behind here?
Well... the 2-caps can all go make Embraces as their actions, and
eventually it can be a deck that simply bleeds for 1 each with 30
minions. eyeballing the numbers quickly, we get:

Turn 4, starting with 20 pool. No Tribute, the 2-caps need their
blood. They and Kendrick Embrace, and the Embraces get skill cards
and hunt. A 2-cap is transferred out; total pool 18 and Kendrick on 4
blood.

Turn 5, Tribute for 5 (three Embraces, Kendrick, and the fresh 2-cap).
The 2-caps all hunt, as do the Embraces. Kendrick calls a Blood Feast
afterwards, filling everyone up. Spend 1 and 4 to see one; total pool
22, Kendrick on 3 blood, and three 2-caps and three Embraces all on 2
blood.

Turn 6, Tribute for 7. Kendrick calls the Blood Feast, and six
minions can take any actions they like with 2 blood each. If you
bring out the next 2-cap, your total pool sits at 27; one better than
the previous example, and you have three extra minions from the
Embraces. If you Tribute for 8 next turn, Kendrick will lose the
protection of Forgotten Labyrinth for his Blood Feast action; however,
it's sort of nice to have 8 minions in comparison to the Camarilla
deck's 3.

This looks much better, except for the problem of all the +1 stealth
Embrace actions, and all the +1 stealth hunt actions. People blocking
the Embraces' hunts is bad, because they can be easily punched into
torpor and then the creating minion will have to hunt. People
blocking the Embrace action is almost as bad, because it doesn't take
much effort to do 3 damage. And while you've got 8 minions, sure,
it's still not going to be easy to oust anyone, since your offense is
at 0 stealth. Putting some Psychic Veils in the deck and using
Obfuscate skill cards for the Embraces would be almost necessary.

The obvious conclusion: Minion Tap/5th Tradition gets started faster,
gains more pool overall, is more versatile/robust, and its pool gain
serves as a direct complement to a vote-deck offense, which is
inherently highly effective. Its natural stealth on the pool gain
also assists in the offense; it will be able to oust people rapidly
without needing to slow down its pool gain. It even has the option
for strong defense as necessary.

Tribute/Blood Feast, while gaining nearly as much pool and being a
good complement to an equally effective weenie-bleed-horde offense,
has an awful lot of moving parts, is slow-starting, and can be very
fragile once begun -- any defense it can muster simply can't match up
to the power of 2nd Tradition backed with Fortitude.

The even more obvious conclusion is that if there is a problem with
bloat decks being too powerful, it lies squarely with 5th Tradition;
one of the Tribute/Blood Feast deck's weakest legs is that Kendrick
will eventually run out of blood, and there is no easy way to get it
back on him.

Not necessarily.

It's the old ASD argument of "We see this is better, so therefore it is
the problem." (I know you're saying "if", but we still have to be
careful.)

Take away the context of Blood Feast. Is 5th, in and of itself, a
balanced card? Is the cost proper to its effect? Are the requirements
sufficient? If it is more powerful than the mean average, how much more
powerful is it?

Is part of the problem that of exponential utility, rather than
additive? Let me explain.

Let's assume we're creating a game where we decide that the ability to
invisible is worth 3 points <arbitrary numbers here, folks>, and the
ability to hit someone with a stunning punch is worth 3 points. Would
we then say the combined ability was only worth 4? Being able to go
invisible *and* hit someone hard - well, that makes the hit almost
guaranteed, and it makes your defence perfect, whereas on their own,
they're sensible - defence and offence. Could we say that the cost
might be closer to 3 *times* 3?

5th Tradition *and* Minion Tap are kind of part of the whole same thing.
Together, they allow offence *and defence, in large quantities. Getting
nine pool back from Queen Anne, and then allowing her to have full blood
again - it splits the usual "push"-"pull" of the pool/blood dynamic.

Under "normal" circumstances, you spend 5 pool to put 5 blood on a
vampire and make them ready. 5 on that vampire, plus 25 in your pool, =
30.

Hunting fundamentally allows that "rule" to be circumvented - fairly
sensibly, too. And it's hard to abuse hunting, since you can't get
blood back from the vampire. Giant's Blood is similarly hard to abuse -
only usable once a game.

And then you find cards like Restoration and Regeneration. Lots more
blood, but stiffer requirements. Again, balanced.

On the other side, we have Blood Doll. 1 blood off a vampire, 1 blood
into your pool. Equilibrium. Minion Tap similar. X blood off, X pool
in.

The interesting part is where these two interact, allowing the same
"rules bend" of one (in the sense of a card doing something not allowed
by the basic, inherent rules of V:TES) to impact on the same "rules
bend" of another.

Kinda interesting thing to ponder, and I'm glad we're having this debate
regarding Minion Tap and Fifth. It's one that's not been dug out for a
while, and "now" we have interesting cards like Blood Feast and Media
Influence to consider in line with it, it's useful to have it.

Interesting side note: the Priscus "block" doesn't change voting as
much as it seems. more casual crud:

You control the lone Priscus, so you effectively have 3 votes.

Someone hostile brings out a Cardinal. Votes tie 3 to 3.
Someone hostile brings out a Priscus. Votes tie 0 to 0.

A THIRD person brings out a Priscus. Votes pass or fail 3 to 0,
depending on how the subvote goes and if anyone abstains from it.

If you control a Cardinal, and two other people bring out Cardinals,
votes will pass or fail 9-0 or 6-3... depending on how people vote and
if anyone abstains. Same thing, but the numbers are x3.

About the only thing you really can't do with a Priscus is stack
multiples of them in a deck and provide quick vote lock for YOURSELF -
you will only ever control 3 votes.

The Camarilla's strength is its organization - the Traditions
represent that organization. The Sabbat's strength is its raw
brutality - the extra-nasty combat available to the Sabbat clans
represents that brutality.

2nd Tradition ends up being somewhat less than impressive against a
Tzimisce combat deck, for example - who -really- wants to untap and
block Meshenka from getting a Revenant, possibly losing their vampire?

>never played with.
>

>First tradition: VERY powerful card, but can turn the whole table against

No need for it to be, either. Since it's a vote, not an action, it
falls in the same category as Parity Shift. Strong card, yes, but so
is Cardinal Benediction, which is something the Camarilla can't even
remotely match.

>Second Tradition: untap + 2 intercept, without Aus or ani.

Matched up (somewhat) by Eternal Vigilance, which provides a permanent
untap opportunity, but no intercept. EV is significantly weaker, yes,
but the Sabbat -does- have an option if you choose to go that route.

>Fourth: Can be copied by a vamp with DOM or PRES
>Fifth: Most powerful of 'em all.
>
>Anybody still wondering why Cammie decks are still the big majority?

Are they? The Camarilla is presently a hair more powerful than teh
Sabbat, but in my eyes it's mainly because of 5th Tradition. 2nd is
very strong, but again, it's becoming more and more hazardous to
casually block actions these days without using Obedience - and the
Sabbat don't have a WHOLE lot of Dominate floating around at high
levels, unlike the Camarilla. The classic Ventrue "I block everything
with 2nd, pool gain with 5th, and vote you to oblivion" deck tends to
get its vampires beat up these days - so they start excluding the 2nd
except for emergency situations.

Of course, the Sabbat would rather block and thump you, so they don't
need the Dominate. =)

Messages.Author: Flux
Messages.Body:
"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message
news:0xntBeZK...@obeah.demon.co.uk...

> Take away the context of Blood Feast. Is 5th, in and of itself, a
> balanced card? Is the cost proper to its effect? Are the requirements
> sufficient? If it is more powerful than the mean average, how much more
> powerful is it?

I'd say yes. On average, it will usually provide some 5+ blood to a vampire,
as a +1 stealth action that requires a title. A prince title, for example,
costs as much as an inferior discipline (in the point system for vamps),
though all titled vampires are of large capacity, so we might compare it to
a superior discipline. Still, compare to a few other cards with similar
effects by themselves:
Restoration: only 3 blood max, and only for the acting vampire. No blood
cost though, but that's only 1 blood anyway.
Govern the Unaligned: 3 blood and 3 transfers, but only on a younger
vampire. It does have the added bonus of flexibility though.
Blood Feast: on average, 3-4 blood. The acting vampire himself never gets
anything from it.
Media Influence: similar to Blood Feast.

5th Tradition seems to have been designed around the assumption that it'd be
used on half-full vampires. Then the Minion Tap/5th Tradition combo would be
fairly balanced with these other cards. This points the 'blame' to 5th
Tradition, since Minion Tap can be equally combo'd with any of these other
cards, yet it's effect won't be considered abusive.

<snip>

You make some interesting points, but I feel they are of no relevance here.
Combo's are the heart of VTES (and most other CCGs), and they have to be
considered when judging a card's balance (like RTI+DtD+Soul Gem, or the old
Fame 'I-shoot-myself-in-the-foot' decks), but in this case we can compare
5th Tradition's effects directly with other existing cards, and I'm afraid
the conclusion can only be that 5th Tradition is not balanced by itself.

Flux
